en/16-20-body-f6081ba7.mp3.text: Those deluded beings, born again and again into shadowed births, never reach me and sink into a lower state. Notice how the verse pairs two ideas. The deluded enter shadowed births birth after birth, and they do so because they never reach me. The shadowed birth is not a random fate; it is the direct result of never turning toward the divine. Krishna then names the three gates of ruin that keep people locked in this cycle.

en/16-20-intro-958e4f90.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the dark nature of destructive people. Now he shows the end of that path, where the deluded are trapped in shadowed births.

en/16-21-body-27a8b38c.mp3.text: Desire, anger, and greed are the three gates of ruin. Abandon these three. Krishna does not list these as separate sins. He calls them a threefold gate, a single entrance that leads the self into ruin. Freed from these three gates, a person acts for their own good and reaches the highest state.

en/16-21-intro-c2cf7361.mp3.text: Krishna names the three inner enemies that block the path of right action. Listen to how he groups them.

en/16-22-body-bd63cc21.mp3.text: Freed from these three gates of darkness, a person acts for their own good and reaches the highest state. Krishna says that once a person is freed from those three gates of darkness, they act for their own highest good, and from that action they reach the highest state. But Krishna warns that a person who ignores this path and follows only their own desire will not find happiness or the highest state.

en/16-22-intro-e5985e07.mp3.text: After naming the three gates of ruin, Krishna now asks what happens to the person who walks through them. Listen for the path that opens up.

en/16-23-body-5af0ee77.mp3.text: Whoever sets aside scripture and acts on desire alone does not attain perfection, happiness, or the highest state. The verse names three losses, one after the other, showing that a life driven only by desire misses the highest aim. Krishna then tells Arjuna to treat scripture as his only authority for deciding how to act in the world.

en/16-23-intro-05d5903a.mp3.text: Krishna has just listed three inner gates of ruin. He now warns what happens when a person ignores right guidance and acts only on impulse.

en/16-24-body-5250fab5.mp3.text: Therefore, scripture is your authority for deciding what should be done and what should not be done. Knowing the duties laid out in scripture, you should act here in the world. The word is shastram, scripture, and it is called pramanam, authority, for deciding what should be done and what should not be done. Arjuna then asks about those who worship with faith but set aside scriptural rules.

en/16-24-intro-cdb26e5e.mp3.text: Krishna concludes his teaching by offering a single standard for deciding right and wrong action. Listen for the word that names that standard.

en/16-3-body-ccb5f9d3.mp3.text: Splendor, forgiveness, steadiness, purity, absence of hostility, and lack of pride belong to the one born with divine qualities, O Bharata. Listen to naatimanita, lack of pride. In a list of virtues, this is the quality that stops a person from looking down on anyone else. Next, Krishna names the demonic traits, beginning with hypocrisy and arrogance.

en/16-3-intro-13a2359d.mp3.text: Krishna finishes his list of noble traits. Listen for the quality that keeps a person humble.

en/16-4-body-aefc0a73.mp3.text: O son of Pritha, hypocrisy, arrogance, self-importance, anger, harshness, and ignorance are the marks of one born with demonic qualities. Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance mark the demonic nature, Krishna tells Arjuna. Krishna now explains that the divine nature leads to liberation while the demonic leads to bondage.

en/16-4-intro-68f6e655.mp3.text: Krishna lists six qualities that signal a demonic nature. Keep your ears on the very last word of the list.

en/16-5-body-19f73003.mp3.text: The divine nature leads to freedom; the demonic nature leads to bondage. Do not grieve, Pandava. You are born with the divine nature. Krishna directly addresses Arjuna as Pandava at the end. The word means born of Pandu, and by using it he reminds Arjuna of his lineage and the divine nature he already carries. Krishna then turns to describe the shadowy qualities that bind a person to the world.

en/16-5-intro-cd381f49.mp3.text: Krishna has just finished describing the demonic traits. Now he turns to Arjuna directly and gives him a single command.

en/16-6-body-98926733.mp3.text: In this world there are two kinds of beings: the divine and the shadowed. I have already described the divine in detail; now listen to the shadowed, Arjuna. Krishna says there are two broad kinds of human nature. He has already spoken in detail about the divine, and now he tells Arjuna to listen to the shadowed, asuric nature. Next, Krishna describes the shadowed nature as lacking purity, truth, and self-control.

en/16-6-intro-0d0ecbd4.mp3.text: Krishna has just finished describing the divine qualities. Listen for the second category he now turns to.

en/16-7-body-cf714107.mp3.text: People of a shadowed nature do not know what should be pursued and what should be withdrawn from. In them, there is no purity, no noble conduct, and no truthfulness. The asuras do not know what to pursue and what to withdraw from, and because they cannot make this basic choice, they end up without purity, conduct, or truth. They say the world is unreal and born only of lust, and they deny any moral order.

en/16-7-intro-2324a408.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the divine nature. Now he asks what happens when a person cannot tell right action from wrong withdrawal.

en/16-8-body-dd760902.mp3.text: They say the world is unreal, without foundation, and without a ruling order, born only from the union of male and female. They say desire alone is its cause, and nothing else. Listen to the word asatyam, untrue. They call the world untrue and without a ruling lord, denying any higher order. Holding this view, deluded people with ruined discernment and fierce actions arise only to destroy the world.

en/16-8-intro-80924afc.mp3.text: Krishna now names the worldview of those with a shadowed nature. Listen to how they explain the world.

en/16-9-body-9a866a23.mp3.text: Holding this view, deluded people with ruined discernment and fierce actions arise only to destroy the world. Listen for the word nastaatmanah, those whose inner being is lost. The verse says these people arise for the destruction of the world, and the reason is that they have already lost their true inner self. Next, Krishna describes those who take refuge in desires that can never be filled.

en/16-9-intro-7c1c0424.mp3.text: Krishna has just described a mindset that denies all order and truth. Now watch for one word that names the inner state of the people who hold it.

en/17-1-body-e4a212fe.mp3.text: Arjuna says: O Krishna, what is the standing of those who worship with faith while setting aside the rules of scripture? Is it sattvic, rajasic, or tamasic? Arjuna asks what quality rules people who worship with faith while setting aside scriptural rules. Krishna answers that this faith is born of a person's own nature and then describes the three kinds.

en/17-1-intro-5f32cc08.mp3.text: Arjuna asks Krishna what kind of faith rules those who worship with devotion while setting aside the rules of scripture.

en/17-10-body-27460b94.mp3.text: Food that is half-cooked, tasteless, foul-smelling, stale, leftover, and impure is dear to people ruled by tamas. The word gatarasam means devoid of taste. It shows that tamas is a lifeless state, where even flavor has faded from the food and the mind. Next, Krishna describes the sacrifice of those who act without desire for reward. They offer it simply because it must be done.

en/17-10-intro-56fdf666.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the restless food of passion, and now he names the diet of tamas: stale, lifeless, and foul. Listen for what this reveals about the mind.

en/17-11-body-76ca6486.mp3.text: A sacrifice performed according to scriptural rule by people without desire for reward, with the mind settled on “it must be done,” is sattvic. Sattvic sacrifice follows the rule, wants no reward, and rests on one thought: this ought to be done. Krishna then turns to the next kind of sacrifice, one performed for reward or show.

en/17-11-intro-bf7cdfce.mp3.text: Krishna turns from the food people eat to the action they perform. Listen to how he defines the purest kind of offering.

en/17-12-body-f7c9c6a0.mp3.text: But, best of the Bharatas, know that sacrifice to be rajasic when it is performed for reward or for show. The word dambhartha, for display, is what exposes the ego. A sacrifice done to be seen is classified as rajasic, driven by restlessness and a desire for reward. Krishna then names the third kind of sacrifice, one that is performed without faith, rule, or care.

en/17-12-intro-02ad84f9.mp3.text: How do you know if a good deed is really good? Krishna gives one test. Listen for the motive behind the action.

en/17-13-body-95d8bbb9.mp3.text: They call a sacrifice dark when it lacks scriptural rule, food offering, mantra, fee, and trust. Listen to the word tamasam, dark. A sacrifice without rule, food, mantra, fee, or trust is a dark, lifeless act that leaves the worshipper unchanged. Next, Krishna moves from sacrifice to a different kind of discipline, the austerity of the body.

en/17-13-intro-8e147b89.mp3.text: Krishna is describing the lowest kind of sacrifice, one that misses every essential element. Listen to what a ritual without trust actually looks like.

en/17-14-body-728b9dc5.mp3.text: Worship of the radiant beings, the wise, the teacher, and the enlightened; purity, simplicity, celibacy, and non-violence, these are called bodily austerity. The word shaucham, purity, is named here as bodily tapas. It shows that physical discipline is keeping the body clean and simple. Krishna now turns from the body to the tongue, defining austerity of speech.

en/17-14-intro-44d11bb8.mp3.text: Listen closely for the word shaucham, purity, as Krishna lists what counts as bodily tapas.

en/17-15-body-5bd31a44.mp3.text: Speech that does not agitate, is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, together with study and practice, is called austerity of speech. Krishna names the austerity of speech. It is about words that do not agitate the listener, that are true, pleasant, and beneficial. After speech, Krishna turns to the austerity of the mind, where silence and self-control take over.

en/17-15-intro-7e131415.mp3.text: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how inner discipline takes shape in daily life. He has just finished bodily austerity and now moves to how we use our voice.

en/17-16-body-194550e3.mp3.text: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-control, and purity of feeling are called mental austerity. The first quality is manahprasadah, cheerfulness of mind. It means the mind is not agitated or fearful, but settled and clear even in hardship. Krishna now brings these three disciplines together into a single sattvic way of life.

en/17-16-intro-37fce372.mp3.text: Last time Krishna defined austerity of speech. Now he turns to the mind. Listen to the five qualities that make up mental austerity.

en/17-17-body-a827ecdb.mp3.text: That threefold discipline of body, speech, and mind, performed with supreme trust and without craving results, is called sattvic. The verse names one quality, paraya, supreme trust. It is supreme trust placed in the practice itself, and that alone makes the threefold discipline sattvic. Krishna now turns to the next kind of austerity, the one done for praise and honor.

en/17-17-intro-a0559415.mp3.text: Why is some tapas pure and some not? Listen to the two conditions that turn discipline into sattva.

en/17-18-body-a84a3a90.mp3.text: Austerity done for honor, praise, and worship, or with a show of display, is said to be rajasic here. It gives unstable, temporary results. The Sanskrit word dambhena means with pretence or show. When austerity is done for this reason, it is called rajasic, and its results are unstable and impermanent. Krishna then moves on to the tamasic kind of austerity, one that is done with foolish stubbornness.

en/17-18-intro-b8795a0b.mp3.text: Krishna now turns to the third kind of discipline, the kind done to impress others. Listen for the motive behind the practice.

en/17-19-body-0ecf933b.mp3.text: Austerity done with foolish stubbornness, by torturing oneself or harming others, is called tamasic. The word pida, meaning pain, appears in the phrase of torturing oneself, showing that this austerity harms the one performing it. Krishna then describes the third kind of austerity, which is done to harm others.

en/17-19-intro-69803d86.mp3.text: Listen for the word pida, pain. How does the way pain is used here reveal the nature of this austerity?

en/17-2-body-e5a64019.mp3.text: The faith of embodied beings is born of their nature. It is of three kinds: sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. Listen to this. Krishna does not call faith a choice. He says it is born of nature, shradha, and that it is threefold, sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic. Krishna tells Arjuna that a person is made of faith, and whatever a person trusts, that is what they become.

en/17-2-intro-71814363.mp3.text: In Chapter 17, Arjuna asks why people worship in such different ways. Krishna begins his answer with a single idea.

en/17-20-body-de2354db.mp3.text: A gift given with the feeling that giving is a duty, offered to a worthy person at the right place and time, is called sattvic. The word daatavyam, to be given, shows that the giver acts from duty. They give because giving is the right thing to do. They do not give because they expect thanks or a return. Krishna then turns to the opposite kind of giving, which is done for a return or a desired result.

en/17-20-intro-119c2621.mp3.text: After Krishna dismisses giving that harms others or seeks reward, he points to the purest kind of charity, one given only because it is right.

en/17-21-body-f248abb2.mp3.text: But charity given in return, or for a desired result, and given grudgingly, is said to be rajasic. Charity given for a return, for a hoped-for result, or grudgingly, is what Krishna calls rajasic. Krishna now moves to the lowest kind of giving, the tamasic gift given with contempt and without respect.

en/17-21-intro-8fd7c8dc.mp3.text: Krishna continues his teaching on the nature of giving. Listen for the exact moment a gift becomes impure.

en/17-22-body-755ba1db.mp3.text: Charity given at the wrong place and time, to an unworthy recipient, without respect and with contempt, is called tamasic. The word tamasam, tamasic, appears at the end, and it is attached to four conditions: the wrong place, the wrong time, the wrong person, and contempt. The next verse moves from the act of giving to the three syllables that name the supreme reality.

en/17-22-intro-b667de16.mp3.text: Krishna has just described a giving that is mixed with self-interest, and now he names the lowest form. Listen to the four ways a gift can fail.

en/17-23-body-345b105e.mp3.text: Om, Tat, and Sat are the three names by which the supreme reality is known. By that, the Vedas, the priests, and the sacrifices were established in the beginning. The verse pairs Om, Tat, and Sat as the three names of Brahman, and then links them directly to the origin of the Vedas, the priests, and the sacrifices. Krishna now says that all sacred acts begin with the utterance of Om, for those who speak of Brahman.

en/17-23-intro-a8ae5d88.mp3.text: Krishna shifts the teaching from charity to the source behind all sacred action. Listen for the ancient names he names.

en/17-24-body-2e6787d3.mp3.text: Therefore, the ritual acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity prescribed by scripture are always begun by uttering Om, for those who speak of Brahman. Listen for the word udahritya, having uttered. It shows that the sacred sound comes first, before any physical act of giving or sacrifice begins. He then states that seekers of freedom perform these acts thinking they are for the Supreme Reality, without desire for a result.

en/17-24-intro-622fecc0.mp3.text: Krishna has just named Om, Tat, and Sat. Now he tells you that those who speak of Brahman always begin their prescribed acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity by uttering Om.

en/17-25-body-5c4874fb.mp3.text: Thinking “all this is for the supreme reality,” seekers of freedom perform many kinds of sacrifice, austerity, and giving without wanting the result. Notice the word Tat, meaning that supreme reality. The seeker of freedom performs sacrifice, austerity, and giving without aiming at any result, because the act itself is the offering. Krishna now moves from the inner state to the outer word, sat, which names existence and noble action.

en/17-25-intro-0e876363.mp3.text: Krishna speaks to Arjuna about the inner state behind every act. Listen for the word that keeps a seeker from looking back for a reward.

en/17-26-body-3e98f01f.mp3.text: O Partha, the word sat is used for existence itself, for noble being, and for praiseworthy action. Krishna explains sat: the word covers what exists, what is good, and any action worth praise. Krishna now moves from the word to the quality itself, calling steadfastness sat as well.

en/17-26-intro-2c1ca34f.mp3.text: Krishna now names the word that covers all three, and he says it in one breath.

en/17-27-body-859be09f.mp3.text: Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and giving is called sat. Action done for that purpose is also called sat. The word sat here is not just the fruit of a ritual or a donation. It is the steadfastness, the inner state of being in sacrifice, austerity, and giving. Krishna now turns to the opposite, calling action without faith unreal.

en/17-27-intro-d9539bf0.mp3.text: How can a single word, sat, cover both a state of being and a physical action? Listen for the link.

en/17-28-body-377bb66f.mp3.text: O Partha, sacrifice, charity, austerity, and any deed done without trust are called unreal. Its fruit exists neither here nor after death. Krishna calls all of it asat, unreal. A sacrifice, a gift, or a penance done without faith is not just empty; it is called unreal, with no fruit here or after death. Arjuna then asks about the exact truth of renunciation and relinquishment.

en/17-28-intro-f73e9263.mp3.text: Krishna has just defined true action, and now he warns what happens when trust is missing. Listen for the word he uses for empty rituals.

en/17-3-body-c9cf3f9b.mp3.text: O Bharata, each person's trust matches their inner nature. A person is made of trust; whatever trust he holds, that is what he becomes. Listen to one word, shraddhamayah, made of trust. The verse says a person is made of trust, and whatever a person trusts in, that is what they become. Krishna now names the three kinds of people and what they worship.

en/17-3-intro-428a020b.mp3.text: Krishna sets aside the battlefield and speaks directly to the nature of the listener.

en/17-4-body-cf81d273.mp3.text: The sattvic worship radiant beings; the rajasic worship yakshas and rakshasas; the tamasic worship spirits and hosts of the dead. The word yajanate, worship, binds all three types together. Yet the objects of their worship split them into three: the clear worship radiant beings, the restless seek intermediaries, and the confused turn to spirits and ghosts. Krishna then turns from worship to the harsh austerities people perform without wisdom.

en/17-4-intro-0c61b36c.mp3.text: Krishna is sorting human nature into three types. Listen for the single word that names the act they all share, and how the objects of their worship divide them.

en/17-5-body-e5cdf8d8.mp3.text: People who perform harsh austerities without scriptural guidance, driven by vanity, ego, desire, attachment, and stubbornness, are not purified by them. The word anvitah means endowed with or joined to. These people are joined to desire, attachment, and stubborn force, which is why their severe austerities do not purify them. Krishna then names the ultimate consequence of such misguided self-punishment.

en/17-5-intro-3d37c11a.mp3.text: The Gita looks at the inner state behind outward practices. Listen to the hidden motives Krishna names.

en/17-6-body-9d16076e.mp3.text: Those who are ignorant and perform terrible austerities without scriptural guidance, wasting away the body’s elements and Me dwelling within the body, should be known as having demonic resolve. Notice the word antahsharirastham, the one dwelling within the body. The text says these people waste away the very elements of the body, and they also harm Me, the one dwelling within it. Krishna now turns to the food a person eats, and how that too is divided into three kinds.

en/17-6-intro-50e84c98.mp3.text: Carry on from the last verse, where Krishna called out false worship; now he turns to false fasting. Listen for who suffers.

en/17-7-body-fe9d0e4d.mp3.text: Food, sacrifice, charity, and austerity are each of three kinds. Listen to these distinctions. The word trividhah, threefold, appears in this verse. It tells us that even food and sacrifice are not single things but come in three varieties, and we are about to hear what they are. Krishna now begins to describe the threefold nature of food, starting with what the sattvic person finds dear.

en/17-7-intro-bc728cb7.mp3.text: Krishna has just condemned lawless austerity. Now he asks Arjuna to listen to something that sounds simple but is not.

en/17-8-body-38db1c84.mp3.text: Foods that increase life, purity, strength, health, happiness, and cheerfulness, and are tasty, smooth, firm, and pleasing, are dear to the sattvic person. The word rasya means tasty, pointing to food that is rich and nourishing. The word snigdha, smooth, points to food that is unctuous and easy on the body. Krishna now turns to the food that feeds a passionate nature, which is bitter, sour, and painful. Listen to how he names its effects.

en/17-8-intro-3938ed15.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from the battlefield to the kitchen, explaining the food that steadies a clear mind. Listen for the qualities that define this sattvic diet.

en/17-9-body-acac1090.mp3.text: Bitter, sour, salty, overly hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are dear to the passionate person. They bring pain, grief, and illness. Bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent and dry foods please the rajasic, and bring pain and illness. Krishna now turns to the tamasic pattern, describing the foods that dull the senses and cloud the mind.

en/17-9-intro-1e3d3384.mp3.text: Krishna contrasts the foods that build health with the foods that destroy it. Listen for the specific quality that makes the rajasic person choose these foods.

en/18-1-body-d50d20c7.mp3.text: Arjuna says: O mighty-armed one, O master of the senses, O slayer of Kesi, I wish to know the distinct truth of renunciation and relinquishment. Arjuna asks to know the distinct truth of sannyasa and tyaga separately. He does not ask for new rules, but for the exact border between two ways of giving up. Krishna answers by defining sannyasa as giving up desire-born actions, and tyaga as giving up the results of all actions.

en/18-1-intro-320ee882.mp3.text: The war has paused, and Arjuna stops Krishna to ask for the final distinction: what exactly is renunciation, and what is relinquishment? Listen for the difference he wants.

en/18-10-body-e2b98751.mp3.text: One who neither rejects unwholesome action nor clings to wholesome action is a wise renunciate, free of doubt and established in clear seeing. Listen for one verb, anushajjate, clings to. The wise one does not cling to wholesome action, the very thing most people chase. This is how a renunciate acts. Krishna now explains why total renunciation is impossible for any embodied being.

en/18-10-intro-0ad23e15.mp3.text: Listen for one verb. It shows how a wise person acts without attachment to results.

en/18-11-body-fd8696b2.mp3.text: For embodied beings, total renunciation of action is impossible. Therefore, one who renounces the fruits of action is called a renunciant. The verse turns on one word, karmaphalatyagi, the renouncer of the fruit. Krishna says the one who drops the reward while the action stays on is the true renunciant. The next verse explains the three results for those who cling to the fruit, and the freedom of those who do not.

en/18-11-intro-f5678a0a.mp3.text: Krishna answers the question of how to truly give up. He points to the one who bears a body and the one who gives up the fruit.

en/18-12-body-1337db15.mp3.text: For those who do not renounce the fruits of action, action produces three kinds of results, pleasant, unpleasant, and mixed, even after death; but for those who renounce the fruits, there is no such result anywhere. Krishna names the three kinds of fruit: pleasant, unpleasant, and mixed. These three results continue for those who cling to outcomes even after death. Krishna then tells Arjuna to learn the five causes behind all actions.

en/18-12-intro-7fc00767.mp3.text: Krishna now answers the question of what happens to those who still expect results. Listen for the threefold fruit of action.

en/18-13-body-b5d617fc.mp3.text: O mighty-armed one, learn from Me these five causes, taught in the Sankhya system, for the accomplishment of all actions. The text says these five causes are taught in Sankhya, a philosophy of knowledge. Krishna cites it to show that human action is not as simple as one person deciding and doing everything alone. Krishna names the five factors, starting with the field, the doer, and the instruments.

en/18-13-intro-82830475.mp3.text: Krishna asks Arjuna to understand that every action depends on five causes, and not on one person deciding to do it alone. Listen for the five causes.

en/18-14-body-882d9f22.mp3.text: The field, the doer, the instruments, the many efforts, and the fifth factor, the unseen force, all shape every action. The verse names five factors, and the fifth is daivam, the unseen force. This shows that behind every deed stands a power beyond the doer. Krishna then says that whatever a person does, right or wrong, carries these same five causes.

en/18-14-intro-b2ae8282.mp3.text: Krishna now breaks every action into its hidden parts, showing that no one acts alone. Listen for the five causes he lists.

en/18-15-body-7d0918e6.mp3.text: Whatever action a person begins through body, speech, and mind, right or wrong, has these five causes. The word to hear is sariravangmanobhih, through body, speech, and mind. It shows that a person acts with all three at once, and that every action, whether right or wrong, is driven by the same five causes. Krishna then says that anyone who thinks the pure self alone is the doer has not seen rightly, because the five causes are always present.

en/18-15-intro-15aab17f.mp3.text: Krishna is about to name the five forces behind every action. Listen for the one word that tells you what a person actually uses to act.

en/18-16-body-20777e91.mp3.text: But one who sees only the pure self as the doer, even though these five causes are present, has not seen rightly; such a confused mind does not understand. Krishna calls the person who sees the pure self as the sole doer confused, blind to the five causes. Next, Krishna continues.

en/18-17-body-4959e26c.mp3.text: One who has no sense of separate self and whose understanding remains unstained does not kill, even by killing all these beings, and is not bound. Listen to the word lipyate, which means to stick or cling. A mind that does not cling to the act is a mind that is not bound. The next verse names the three things that drive every action and the three parts that make it up.

en/18-17-intro-ee5f448f.mp3.text: Krishna now turns to the person who acts without that false sense of doership, and names the two qualities that keep the mind pure.

en/18-18-body-89953110.mp3.text: Knowledge, the object known, and the knower, these three drive action. Instrument, act, and actor, these three make up the whole of action. Krishna lists the knower, the known, and the knowing as the impulse to act, and the instrument, the act, and the actor as the whole of action. Krishna now shows how each of these three parts is itself threefold, linking them to the three qualities. Listen to that next.

en/18-18-intro-500d85e6.mp3.text: How does action actually work? Listen to how Krishna breaks it down into its simplest parts before Arjuna can let go of the idea of being the doer.

en/18-19-body-faf977e9.mp3.text: In the analysis of the three qualities, knowledge, action, and the doer are each said to be threefold. Listen now to these distinctions as they truly are. Using the three gunas, Krishna announces that knowledge, action and the doer each come in three kinds. Krishna then defines sattvic knowledge as seeing the one undivided reality in all divided beings.

en/18-19-intro-dd179609.mp3.text: Krishna explains how the three qualities shape the world. Listen for how they divide knowledge, action, and the doer into three kinds each.

en/18-2-body-d51eefaa.mp3.text: The wise call renunciation the giving up of desire-born actions. The discerning call renunciation the giving up of all results of action. Krishna gives two definitions in this verse. The wise call renunciation the giving up of desire-born actions, while the discerning call it the giving up of all results of action. Krishna now warns against the extreme view that all action should be abandoned as flawed.

en/18-2-intro-83201b3e.mp3.text: Krishna answers Arjuna’s question by naming two kinds of renunciation, then defines each one.

en/18-20-body-4c61a9c5.mp3.text: Know that knowledge to be sattvic by which one sees the one imperishable reality in all beings, undivided among the divided. The pivot is the word avibhakta, undivided, placed right beside vibhakta, divided. The knowledge is sattvic because it sees the one unbroken reality inside every single being. Krishna then turns to the opposite vision, the one that sees many separate beings. Listen to how he names that knowledge.

en/18-20-intro-bd60175f.mp3.text: Listen for the single word that tells you whether a person sees reality as one or many. Krishna points to the quality of the vision itself.

en/18-21-body-a2aa590f.mp3.text: But know that knowledge as rajasic by which one sees many different beings as separate and distinct in all beings. Notice the word 'tu', but. Krishna places this divided seeing against the unity he described in the previous verse, marking it as a lower state of understanding. Krishna then describes the lowest kind of understanding, the dark, that clings to a single body as the whole truth.

en/18-21-intro-417e296b.mp3.text: Krishna has just described clear vision that sees unity. Now he turns to the restless mind. Listen for how he names the divided view.

en/18-22-body-2ddfebf1.mp3.text: But knowledge that clings to one body as if it were the whole, without reason, without truth, and petty, is called dark. Krishna calls this tamasic knowledge because it clings to one limited thing, a single body or action, and mistakes it for the whole. It lacks clear reason and misses the truth. Krishna then turns to action, describing the sattvic kind that is done without craving or attachment.

en/18-22-intro-cb5e0959.mp3.text: Krishna has just named rajasic knowledge, which sees many separate beings. Now he names the lowest kind, tamasic knowledge.

en/18-23-body-226922dd.mp3.text: Action that is guided by duty, free from attachment, and done without craving results is called sattvic. The verse says sattvic action is prescribed, free from attachment, and done without craving fruit. It is action performed as duty, stripped of the pull of likes and dislikes. Krishna next describes rajasic action as that driven by desire for pleasure, ego, or great strain.

en/18-23-intro-18016d21.mp3.text: Krishna now asks what makes an action truly sattvic, guiding us to the quality of selfless duty.

en/18-24-body-2513ec2c.mp3.text: But action done with desire for pleasure, or with ego, or with great strain, is said to be rajasic. The verse says that action done with ego, or with great strain, is called rajasic. The word sahankarena is the key, because it means with ego, and that ego is what makes an otherwise busy action restless. Next, Krishna names the third kind of action, one done in delusion without regard for the consequences.

en/18-24-intro-a0724f84.mp3.text: Krishna is sorting action into three qualities. This time, he names the restless kind, driven by desire, ego, and strain.

en/18-25-body-f2916c2e.mp3.text: Action begun in delusion, ignoring its consequences, harm, and one’s own capacity, is called tamasic. Listen for the word anupreksham, without considering. A tamasic actor looks at the world and simply refuses to weigh the consequence, the loss, the harm, or their own capacity to finish it. Krishna then describes the opposite kind of actor, one who is steady and unchanged by success or failure.

en/18-25-intro-759646f3.mp3.text: Krishna has just described passionate action. Now he tells us about the worst kind. Listen for the four things a dark actor refuses to consider.

en/18-26-body-a6a36d6d.mp3.text: The doer who is free from attachment, free from ego, endowed with steadiness and enthusiasm, and unchanged by success or failure is called sattvic. The sattvic doer works free of attachment and boasting, with resolve and zeal, unmoved by success or failure. The next verse describes the passionate doer, ruled by craving and chasing results.

en/18-26-intro-5e1d81c6.mp3.text: Krishna is now judging the person behind the action, showing Arjuna the ideal doer who works without attachment or ego.

en/18-27-body-7fd01273.mp3.text: The doer ruled by craving, chasing results, greedy, violent in nature, impure, and tossed by joy and sorrow is called passionate. Krishna calls the rajasic doer impure, and that word reveals a restless mind that wants the reward, resents the loss, and cannot rest. Next, Krishna names the doer who is careless, crude, and lazy, the tamasic doer.

en/18-27-intro-009129ff.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the steady doer; now he names the restless middle path.

en/18-28-body-6a0546f6.mp3.text: A careless, crude, stubborn, deceitful, lazy, gloomy, and procrastinating doer is called tamasic. This verse lists seven marks, but one stands out: procrastination. The doer is not merely lazy, he is delaying, which traps him in a cycle of gloom and inaction. Krishna now turns to the three qualities that shape how a person understands and acts.

en/18-28-intro-3e722cbb.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the passionate doer. Now he names the third and lowest type. Listen for the seven marks that define it.

en/18-29-body-3e83f105.mp3.text: O Dhananjaya, now hear the threefold distinctions of understanding and steadfastness according to the three qualities, fully and separately explained. Krishna turns to buddhi and dhriti, the mind and resolve, and promises to separate each into its three qualities. Sattvic buddhi is the clarity that knows what binds and what frees.

en/18-29-intro-a5ff8979.mp3.text: Krishna now turns to the inner equipment of the mind, the tools of understanding and steadfastness.

en/18-3-body-763c7be6.mp3.text: Some wise people say all action should be abandoned as flawed. Others say sacrifice, giving, and disciplined effort should not be abandoned. Here are two camps of the wise, and Krishna does not yet take a side. One camp says action itself is flawed and must be abandoned. The other camp says sacrifice, giving, and austerity must never be abandoned. Krishna now steps in to give his own settled view on what true renunciation actually is.

en/18-3-intro-a15bdf7d.mp3.text: Krishna answers Arjuna's final question about letting go by showing that even the wise cannot agree. Listen for the two camps.

en/18-30-body-dea5a7c2.mp3.text: O Partha, the intellect that knows what leads forward and what withdraws, what should be done and not done, what is fear and fearlessness, what binds and what frees, is sattvic. The word buddhi, intellect, appears in the verse, and the verse says it knows. It is a knowing that separates action from withdrawal, duty from non-duty, fear from fearlessness, and bondage from freedom. Krishna now turns to the mind that mistakes action for right action and non-action for wrong action, calling it rajasic.

en/18-30-intro-36547e02.mp3.text: Krishna is sorting the mind into types. Listen for the one word that names the tool of knowing.

en/18-31-body-e9decea1.mp3.text: Arjuna, the intellect that does not truly know right action and wrong action, duty and what should not be done, is rajasic. Krishna warns that a rajasic intellect gets dharma and adharma wrong. It cannot tell the difference between duty and what to avoid, and so it misreads the right action. Krishna next describes the intellect that is completely covered by darkness and calls wrong action right.

en/18-31-intro-b43479cb.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the sattvic intellect that sees clearly what frees and what binds. Now he turns to the mind that lacks that clarity.

en/18-32-body-f951cf17.mp3.text: The mind covered by darkness calls wrongdoing right and reverses everything. The word tamasi, covered by darkness, is the engine of this verse. It is the darkness itself that makes the buddhi call adharma righteous and reverse every aim. Krishna now turns to the steadiness that holds the mind, senses, and life-force in place through yoga.

en/18-32-intro-fd66b4cc.mp3.text: Krishna moves from the confused to the darkest understanding. Listen to how a mind completely covered by darkness names evil as good.

en/18-33-body-af14505f.mp3.text: O Partha, that steadfastness by which one holds steady the functions of mind, life-force, and senses through unwavering yoga is sattvic steadfastness. Sattvic dhriti holds mind, breath and senses steady through unwavering yoga, Krishna tells Arjuna. Krishna now turns to the steadiness that clings to pleasure and wealth while craving results, which he calls passionate.

en/18-33-intro-9db43e7a.mp3.text: Krishna is now answering the question, what is true inner strength? Listen to how he names the one strength that keeps the mind, breath, and senses steady.

en/18-34-body-a6eb487c.mp3.text: Arjuna, the steadiness that clings intensely to duty, pleasure, and wealth, while craving results, is passionate steadiness. Krishna names a lower steadiness that still holds dharma but for reward. It is still discipline, but mixed with craving. Krishna then turns to the lowest kind of steadiness, where a dull mind clings to sleep, fear, and pride.

en/18-34-intro-1de5c701.mp3.text: Krishna is sorting out the different kinds of inner steadiness a person can have. Listen to how he describes the passionate kind.

en/18-35-body-eaff4422.mp3.text: The dull-minded one does not let go of sleep, fear, grief, sorrow, and pride. That steadfastness is tamasic, Arjuna. The word to hear is dhriti, steadfastness. Here it is tamasic, a dull resolve that will not let go of sleep, fear, grief, and pride. Krishna now turns to the three kinds of happiness, starting with the one that first feels like poison.

en/18-35-intro-174bbadf.mp3.text: Krishna is listing the qualities of resolve, and he names the lowest kind. Listen for the word that means the stubborn grip of a dull mind.

en/18-36-body-8419efd8.mp3.text: O best of the Bharatas, hear from me now about three kinds of happiness. The happiness that comes from practice, ends sorrow, and first feels like poison but later like nectar is called sattvic. Krishna begins on the three kinds of happiness: sattvic joy grows with practice and brings an end to sorrow. Krishna then turns to the happiness that seems like poison at first and like nectar in the end.

en/18-36-intro-a44eaef0.mp3.text: Krishna finishes his teaching by pointing to a happiness that grows through practice. Listen to how he describes its end.

en/18-37-body-cb1beff2.mp3.text: That happiness is called sattvic, which seems like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from clarity of the discerning mind and the peace of inner understanding. Krishna pairs two words, visha, poison, and amrita, nectar. The highest happiness begins as poison and ends as nectar, showing that true joy can feel bitter at first. Krishna now turns to the second kind of pleasure, the one that begins like nectar but ends like poison.

en/18-37-intro-5163f8ee.mp3.text: Krishna continues by describing the first of the three kinds of happiness, using a single striking image.

en/18-38-body-43907285.mp3.text: The pleasure that begins like nectar from contact between the senses and their objects, but ends like poison, is called rajasic pleasure. Krishna gives two exact words, agraha, at first, and pariname, in the end. The pleasure starts like nectar, but it ends like poison, and that is why it is called rajasic. Krishna now turns to the third kind of pleasure, one born of sleep, laziness, and negligence.

en/18-38-intro-01eb2f7c.mp3.text: Krishna has just described a steady, lasting joy. Now he names the pleasure that tempts us, born from our senses touching the world. Listen for its two stages.

en/18-39-body-e16d89aa.mp3.text: That pleasure, born of sleep, laziness, and negligence, deludes the self at the beginning and at the end; it is called tamasic. Krishna points to a pleasure born of sleep, laziness, and negligence, and says it deludes the self from the very beginning to the very end. Krishna then reminds us that no being on earth is free from these three qualities.

en/18-39-intro-99f155fa.mp3.text: Krishna finishes sorting the three kinds of pleasure. Listen to how he describes the lowest one.

en/18-4-body-2f31425c.mp3.text: Arjuna, first hear my settled view on renunciation. Renunciation is said to be threefold. Krishna calls Arjuna bharatasattama, best of the Bharatas, to honor him before giving this final teaching, and immediately adds that tyaga, renunciation, is threefold, so the path forward must be understood with precision. Sanjaya will soon describe how the armies stand arrayed, ready for the war to begin. Listen for the first sounds of the battle.

en/18-4-intro-c735914e.mp3.text: Krishna pauses to settle the debate between action and withdrawal. He tells Arjuna to listen to his settled view on renunciation.

en/18-40-body-686018c0.mp3.text: There is nothing on earth, in heaven, or among the radiant beings that is free from the three qualities born of nature. Notice the word gunaih, three qualities. Krishna lists earth, heaven, and the gods to show the scope is total; no being in the material order is exempt. Krishna then explains how the four social duties are divided according to these same three qualities.

en/18-40-intro-a780aea2.mp3.text: Listen for one word that covers every realm of existence. Krishna is about to explain that no being is exempt from the three gunas.

en/18-41-body-f5a55515.mp3.text: O scorcher of foes, the duties of priests, warriors, merchants, and workers are divided according to the qualities born of their nature. Krishna speaks to Arjuna, the warrior, and calls him parantapa, scorcher of foes. In this same breath, he lists the four classes of people, showing that the structure of society is as natural as the qualities that drive it. Krishna continues by showing that the natural duty of a brahmin is self-control and knowledge.

en/18-41-intro-4909df58.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna that every being is woven from three qualities. Now he names the four kinds of people who act from those qualities. Listen to how he calls them.

en/18-42-body-96f2567b.mp3.text: Self-restraint, control of the senses, austerity, purity, forgiveness, honesty, knowledge, realization, and faith in the supreme reality are the natural duties of a brahmin. The words shama, control of the mind, and dama, control of the senses, appear together here, and they reveal that a Brahmin's work is rooted in mastering the inner self. Krishna now turns from the qualities of a brahmin to the outer life of a warrior, listing the qualities that define a kshatriya.

en/18-42-intro-32e15e4b.mp3.text: Krishna has just shown how every human nature carries its own work. Now he turns to the inner qualities that define a Brahmin's path.

en/18-43-body-41fbc54b.mp3.text: Valor, radiance, firmness, quick skill, never fleeing in battle, generosity, and leadership are the natural duties of a warrior. Valour, vigour, firmness, skill, not fleeing battle, generosity and leadership make up the kshatriya's natural duty. Krishna then lists the natural work of farmers, cattle-herders, and merchants.

en/18-43-intro-d1b80fed.mp3.text: If a thinker's work is self-control and knowledge, what is a warrior's work? Listen to the list of qualities that belong to a kshatriya.

en/18-44-body-d8db4aa2.mp3.text: Farming, cattle-keeping, and trade are the natural work of the merchant class. Service to others is the natural work of the worker class. The word swabhavajam means born of nature. It tells us that farming, cattle-keeping, trade, and service are not random jobs, but duties that belong to particular people by their very nature. A person devoted to their own work attains perfection. Krishna now explains how that devotion leads to perfection.

en/18-44-intro-5bcb65a2.mp3.text: The Gita has described the duties of warriors, teachers, and rulers. Now it names the work of merchants and service workers, showing how society holds together.

en/18-45-body-525d8986.mp3.text: A person devoted to their own work attains perfection. Listen as I explain how a person devoted to their own work reaches that perfection. Listen to the phrase sve sve, in each one's own. It appears twice to insist that a person finds fulfillment only by staying devoted to their own work. Krishna promises to explain how a person reaches that perfection through their own work.

en/18-45-intro-b6a858b4.mp3.text: Listen for a phrase that tells a person to stay in their own lane. Krishna is about to explain exactly how that works.

en/18-46-body-eb274848.mp3.text: By worshipping the one from whom all beings arise and by whom this whole world is pervaded, a person attains perfection through their own work. Krishna names the same source twice: from whom all beings arise, and by whom all this is pervaded. That one being is the origin of life and the ground of all action, so any work done for that being becomes a path to perfection. Krishna then moves from the source of all life to the choice of your own work.

en/18-46-intro-a2cc1171.mp3.text: Krishna has just answered why work is necessary, and now he answers how it becomes sacred. Listen for the single source that connects every action to the divine.

en/18-47-body-fb5669ee.mp3.text: One's own duty, though imperfect, is better than another's duty well performed. Doing the work set by one's nature, a person does not incur wrongdoing. A single word, svadharmah, one's own duty, does the heaviest lifting here. It beats paradharmah, another's duty, even when that other path is flawless, and it frees you from kilbisam, wrongdoing. Next, Krishna continues.

en/18-47-intro-d04888b6.mp3.text: Krishna sharpens his point: the duty born of your own nature is safer than copying someone else's path.

en/18-48-body-aea1915a.mp3.text: O son of Kunti, one should not abandon one's natural duty, even if it has flaws. All undertakings are clouded by some defect, just as fire is veiled by smoke. Krishna says all undertakings are clouded by some defect, just as fire is veiled by smoke. The smoke does not mean the fire is gone; it means the fire is hidden, and you must still do your natural duty. Next, Krishna continues.

en/18-48-intro-a0c24ff6.mp3.text: Before you leave a task because it feels imperfect, listen to how Krishna explains why no action is ever perfect.

en/18-49-body-0605436d.mp3.text: One whose mind is detached everywhere, who has mastered the self, and who is free from craving attains the highest perfection of non-action through renunciation. The verse places three qualities side by side, a mind without attachment, a self that has been conquered, and a heart free from craving. Together they make up the path to the highest perfection of non-action. Krishna now turns to the supreme reality that is reached when this state is fully attained.

en/18-49-intro-2866b326.mp3.text: Krishna describes the inner condition that makes duty possible. Listen for the state of a mind that no longer reaches outward.

en/18-5-body-1d1d9f71.mp3.text: Sacrifice, giving, and disciplined effort should not be abandoned; they must be done. These three actions purify thoughtful people. Krishna names three actions, yajna, dana, and tapas, and says they purify thoughtful people. He does not drop them from duty, but places them at the heart of it. Krishna then says these same actions must be done without attachment, without wanting their results.

en/18-5-intro-046c0535.mp3.text: Listen for three actions that Krishna says are purifying, and that even the wise should never abandon.

en/18-50-body-99515633.mp3.text: Listen to me briefly, O Arjuna, as I explain how one who has reached perfection attains the supreme reality, the highest culmination of knowledge. Listen for Para, supreme. It marks the highest point of knowledge, describing the ultimate reality that a perfected seeker attains. Sanjaya then describes the purified understanding and steady self that lead a seeker to this supreme culmination.

en/18-50-intro-2bc6ce6b.mp3.text: Krishna asks Arjuna to listen to a brief summary of how a perfected seeker attains Brahman. Listen for the word that marks the highest point of this knowledge.

en/18-51-body-766f729f.mp3.text: Endowed with purified understanding, holding the self steady with firm resolve, giving up sense-objects, and casting away attraction and aversion... Krishna speaks to Arjuna, guiding him back to inner steadiness. He describes one who seeks Brahman: a person with clear understanding steadies the mind, restrains the senses, gives up sense pleasures, and drops attraction and aversion. Krishna continues with the result: dwelling in solitude, eating lightly, and controlling speech, body, and mind, one stays absorbed in meditation, grounded in non-attachment.

en/18-51-intro-a642a8cf.mp3.text: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna, guiding him back to inner steadiness after the long discourse. Listen to how he describes the discipline of one who seeks the highest reality.

en/18-52-body-82a8489b.mp3.text: Dwelling in solitude, eating lightly, and controlling speech, body, and mind, one stays absorbed in meditation, grounded in non-attachment. The verse gives a single compound for three restraints, yatah vak kaya manah, meaning one whose speech, body, and mind are restrained. It shows the inner work is an active mastery of every outward and inward movement. Krishna then lists the final qualities, free from ego and anger, that make a person fit for the supreme reality.

en/18-52-intro-0188eed9.mp3.text: Krishna continues his description of the purified mind, now naming the daily disciplines that keep it steady. Listen for the three things he controls.

en/18-53-body-199c476b.mp3.text: Free from ego, force, pride, desire, anger, and possession, one becomes peaceful, without “mine,” and fit for union with the supreme reality. Notice the list of six poisons that must be dropped before the mind can become peaceful and fit for the supreme reality. When all six are dropped, the person no longer grieves or desires, and becomes equal toward all beings.

en/18-53-intro-8045c757.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the outer discipline of solitude and controlled eating. Now he asks: what must drop from inside to finish the job?

en/18-54-body-cbd36d89.mp3.text: One who has become Brahman, serene in mind, grieves not and desires not. Equal toward all beings, that person attains supreme devotion to Me. Notice the word prasannatma, serene-minded. It is the mind that has stopped grieving and stopped craving, and that is the very state that allows supreme devotion to grow. Krishna then tells the way to reach that state through loving knowledge.

en/18-54-intro-d9a4fe2a.mp3.text: Krishna now shows the fruit of letting go. Listen to the two things a free mind no longer does.

en/18-55-body-093218e5.mp3.text: Through devoted love, one truly knows Me as I am. Knowing Me in truth, one enters into Me at once. Listen for the word abhijanati, knows truly. It is not ordinary knowledge, but a deep recognition that reveals exactly how much Krishna is and what he is. Krishna now speaks of the devotee who takes refuge in him, acting in the world yet entering the eternal state.

en/18-55-intro-fc9b7e41.mp3.text: Krishna has finished describing the calm devotee, and now he points to the heart of bhakti. Listen for the word that names this direct knowing.

en/18-56-body-930872f8.mp3.text: A devotee who takes refuge in me, while always doing all actions, attains the eternal, imperishable state through my grace. Listen to two words, madvyapashrayah and matprasadat. The first means one who takes refuge in me, and the second means by my grace. The verse says the devotee does all actions, yet attains the eternal state only through my grace. Krishna then tells Arjuna to surrender all actions to him and remain constantly focused on him.

en/18-56-intro-638bcfd7.mp3.text: Krishna shows Arjuna the final shape of devotion, where acting in the world and surrendering to him become one.

en/18-57-body-7c8ed739.mp3.text: With your mind, surrender all actions to Me. Take refuge in the discipline of clear understanding and remain constantly focused on Me. The verse asks Arjuna to use his mind to place every action into Me, then to take refuge in the discipline of clear understanding, and to keep the mind fixed on Me. Centered in me, you will cross all obstacles through my grace. But if you do not listen because of ego, you will fall.

en/18-57-intro-d382fd1a.mp3.text: Krishna now gives the inner method for that surrender, and you will hear the mind itself made into the offering.

en/18-58-body-c3912c96.mp3.text: Centered in me, you will cross all obstacles through my grace. But if you do not listen because of ego, you will fall. The word ahankarat, from ego, names the inner force that makes Arjuna turn away from listening and brings ruin. Next, Krishna continues.

en/18-58-intro-c1500992.mp3.text: Krishna sums up his teaching with a promise and a warning. Listen to the single word that names the real danger to Arjuna's peace.

en/18-59-body-c20e6e9b.mp3.text: Relying on ego, you think, 'I will not fight.' That resolve is false; your nature will drive you into battle. Arjuna's vow 'I will not fight' rests on ego, Krishna says, and his own nature will overrule it. Krishna then says that Arjuna is bound by his own nature-born duty, and will act even against his own will.

en/18-59-intro-5dc7813e.mp3.text: Krishna strips away Arjuna’s final excuse to stay still. Listen for the word that names the pride behind this refusal.

en/18-6-body-443cad21.mp3.text: Even these actions, and all other actions, should be done without attachment and without wanting their results. This is my settled and best teaching, O Arjuna. Krishna calls this his settled, best opinion. He tells Partha that even these actions, meaning all duties including sacrifice and discipline, must be done without attachment and without wanting the results. Krishna warns that giving up prescribed action in confusion is a tamasic way to live. Listen to why he says that.

en/18-6-intro-6d5f542c.mp3.text: Krishna now gives Arjuna the final word on how to act, making his teaching on sacred duty absolutely clear.

en/18-60-body-3308354a.mp3.text: Bound by your own nature-born duty, you will do what you do not want to do in confusion. Even against your will, you will act. The word svabhava, your own nature, is the engine here. It tells Arjuna that his own blood and upbringing are already pushing him toward action, so his current refusal is only a surface hesitation. Krishna now says the Lord sits in every heart and uses maya to make beings spin according to their nature.

en/18-60-intro-2de89dc8.mp3.text: Krishna points to one word that will shape the rest of this chapter. Listen for what your own nature demands of you.

en/18-61-body-f2c9294d.mp3.text: O Arjuna, the Lord abides in the heart of all beings and, by His maya, causes all beings mounted on a body-machine to revolve according to their nature. The Lord sits in every being's heart, Krishna says, turning them by maya as if mounted on a machine. Krishna then tells Arjuna to surrender his whole being to this divine, so he can reach supreme peace and the eternal abode.

en/18-61-intro-905a72aa.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna that his own nature will force him to fight. Now Krishna reveals the deeper force behind all action: the Lord inside every heart, turning the body-machine by maya.

en/18-62-body-1f5333a1.mp3.text: Surrender to the divine with your whole being, Arjuna. By that grace, you will reach supreme peace and the eternal abode. The word refuge, sharanam, marks the final shift. It tells Arjuna to stop carrying the weight of the world and to place the burden entirely on the divine. Krishna steps back, telling Arjuna to reflect on this secret wisdom and then choose his own path.

en/18-62-intro-9a675ca7.mp3.text: Krishna has just shown him the hidden order behind all action and thought. Now he offers a final turn, a way to end the struggle.

en/18-63-body-c9661357.mp3.text: Thus I have explained to you the most secret wisdom. Reflect on it fully, and then do as you wish. Krishna tells Arjuna to think this over completely, then act as he wishes. He gives Arjuna the freedom to choose and act for himself. Krishna now calls Arjuna dear to him, and says he will speak one last secret word for his good.

en/18-63-intro-ad465913.mp3.text: After revealing the deepest secret, Krishna steps back and asks Arjuna to decide for himself. Listen for the moment he hands the choice back.

en/18-64-body-c9f7b645.mp3.text: Listen again to My most secret word. You are dear to Me, so I will speak for your good. Krishna names the reason for his final command: Arjuna is dear to him, and therefore he will speak only what is truly good for him. Because Arjuna is dear to him, Krishna now gives the final command to fix his mind on him.

en/18-64-intro-1e03d50e.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna to reflect on the secret wisdom and then choose his own path. Now he asks him to listen once more.

en/18-65-body-df59af54.mp3.text: Fix your mind on me, become my devotee, worship me, and bow to me. You will come to me; I promise you this truly, because you are dear to me. The key phrase is manmana bhava, with mind on me. Krishna asks for nothing but a focused mind, and in return promises that you will come to me alone. He seals this with his reason: you are dear to me.

en/18-65-intro-701c5845.mp3.text: Krishna now offers the simplest path. Listen for the instruction to fix the mind on Him.

en/18-66-body-edf9dba8.mp3.text: Abandon all duties and take refuge in Me alone. I will free you from all wrongdoing; do not grieve. Listen for sarva-dharman parityajya, having abandoned all duties. Krishna asks Arjuna to drop every other support, every other path, and take refuge in Me alone. Krishna then warns Arjuna never to speak this teaching to the faithless or the fault-finding.

en/18-66-intro-9458856c.mp3.text: Krishna has just promised his love. Now he gives the final command that closes the entire dialogue. Listen for the one instruction that asks for everything.

en/18-67-body-00339844.mp3.text: Never speak this to one without discipline, one without devotion, one unwilling to listen, or one who finds fault with me. The word anashushrushave, to one unwilling to listen, is the sharpest warning. After revealing the deepest secret, Krishna refuses to let it reach a closed mind. He then turns to the one who does share it, promising that they will come to Him without doubt.

en/18-67-intro-fa5631ea.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna to abandon all duties and take refuge in Him, and now He places a condition on the teaching itself.

en/18-68-body-f3b26f21.mp3.text: Whoever shares this supreme secret among my devotees, with devoted love for me, will surely come to me without doubt. The secret is not for everyone, but for those who already love Krishna. The word asamsayah, without doubt, seals the promise: anyone who teaches it with supreme devotion will come to me. Krishna then promises that no one on earth is more dear to him than the one who shares this secret.

en/18-68-intro-3f5ab64e.mp3.text: Krishna has just finished his final instruction, but he adds one more condition about who may hear it. Listen to that boundary.

en/18-69-body-79ebdf84.mp3.text: Among all human beings, no one does what is more dear to me than he does. On this earth, no one will ever be dearer than he is. Listen to priyakarittamah. It means the one who does the most dear service. This is the person who teaches the teaching, and Krishna places him above all others on earth. Krishna now says that the one who studies this dialogue will also worship him through the sacrifice of knowledge.

en/18-69-intro-68ea39d0.mp3.text: Krishna closes the dialogue with a final promise. Listen to how he names the person who will be dearest to him.

en/18-7-body-bf70031b.mp3.text: Abandoning prescribed action is not right. Giving it up in confusion is called tamasic. Krishna names the exact kind of renunciation he rejects: tamasah, the dark or dull kind. It is not the action itself that is wrong, but the confusion, moha, that makes a man drop his duty. Krishna now says that renouncing action out of fear of pain is a passionate failure that yields no fruit.

en/18-7-intro-5153eb93.mp3.text: Krishna has just told you to keep acting without attachment. Now he warns against a specific trap.

en/18-70-body-cac77187.mp3.text: Whoever studies this sacred dialogue of ours will also worship me through the sacrifice of knowledge; that is my view. Yajna is a sacrifice, and Krishna calls the study of this dialogue a jnana yajna, a sacrifice of knowledge. He says that anyone who reads these words is worshipping him directly. Krishna then says that even listening to this dialogue with trust frees a person from evil and leads to heaven.

en/18-70-intro-b1d76504.mp3.text: Listen for the word yajna. You might expect a blood sacrifice or a fire offering, but Krishna names a very different kind of offering.

en/18-71-body-9cf4fcdc.mp3.text: Even a person who listens to this with trust and without fault-finding becomes free and reaches the auspicious realms earned by noble action. Listen to the word anasyuh, without fault-finding. The teaching does not demand a scholar, only a listener who comes without mockery to hear what is said. Krishna asks Arjuna directly if his confusion is gone, closing the conversation he began.

en/18-71-intro-280ae0ce.mp3.text: Krishna finishes his teaching and opens the door to liberation beyond Arjuna. Listen to who else can enter.

en/18-72-body-8abfb54d.mp3.text: O Partha, have you heard this with one-pointed mind? O Dhananjaya, has the delusion born of ignorance been destroyed in you? Krishna asks two questions, one about listening and one about being free. The word krsna uses for listening, srutam, is just the past tense of hearing, and he asks if Arjuna heard this with ekagrena cetasa, a mind gathered into a single point. Arjuna answers that his delusion is gone and he will do as Krsna says.

en/18-72-intro-bf8475f2.mp3.text: Krishna has finished his long teaching and turns to Arjuna, checking whether the words have landed. The war still waits, but the real test is whether Arjuna's ignorance and confusion have been broken.

en/18-73-body-a92f8670.mp3.text: Arjuna says: By your grace, O Achyuta, my delusion is destroyed and memory restored. I stand free of doubt and will do what you say. Arjuna names one thing he has received, smriti, memory. Krishna's teaching has brought it back, and with it the confusion that clouded his sight. Sanjaya closes the Gita by calling this dialogue wondrous and hair-raising.

en/18-73-intro-d5caec96.mp3.text: In the final verse of the Gita, Arjuna answers Krishna. What has changed inside him? Listen for the word that tells you.

en/18-74-body-7ffa2887.mp3.text: Sanjaya says: Thus I heard this wondrous, hair-raising dialogue between Vasudeva and the great-souled Partha. Sanjaya names the two speakers as Vasudeva and the great-souled Partha. The word mahatmanah, great-souled, sits right beside Partha, marking that Arjuna has come out of his grief and into his true self. He closes by saying this same conversation was a supreme secret that he heard directly from the Lord of yoga himself.

en/18-74-intro-3ac6adfd.mp3.text: Sanjaya has watched the whole war. Now he tells Dhritarashtra what he heard. Listen to how he describes the talk between Krishna and Arjuna.

en/18-75-body-e0d59d52.mp3.text: By Vyasa's grace, I heard this supreme secret yoga directly from Krishna, the Lord of yoga, as he spoke it himself. The word is saakshat, directly. Sanjaya did not read a text; he heard this supreme secret spoken live by Krishna himself, a direct transmission from the Lord of yoga. Remembering this direct teaching, Sanjaya rejoices again and again, carrying the dialogue forward.

en/18-75-intro-2ea7e87a.mp3.text: Sanjaya now names the exact source of the teaching, and points to one word that seals its origin. Listen for it.

en/18-76-body-387c4501.mp3.text: O King, remembering again and again this wondrous, holy dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna, I rejoice again and again. Sanjaya calls the conversation between Krishna and Arjuna wonderful and holy, and he says he rejoices again and again every time he remembers it. He remembers the form of Krishna and feels wonder and joy again and again.

en/18-76-intro-91338dd5.mp3.text: Sanjaya finishes by telling the king that he does not merely report the Gita, but lives inside it. Listen to how he describes his own response.

en/18-77-body-6ba1cfbc.mp3.text: Remembering that astonishing form of Krishna again and again, I feel great wonder, O King, and I rejoice again and again. Recalling Krishna's cosmic form again and again, Sanjaya feels great wonder and keeps rejoicing. The vision of Krishna and Arjuna together is the source of all prosperity and victory, says Sanjaya.

en/18-77-intro-24f8cc8d.mp3.text: In the last verse, Sanjaya said he rejoiced at the holy dialogue. Now he returns to the vision that started it all.

en/18-78-body-54339bd7.mp3.text: Where Krishna, the master of yoga, is present, and where Arjuna, the bow-bearer, is present, there are prosperity, victory, glory, and firm justice. This is my conviction. Sanjaya's closing verdict: where Krishna and Arjuna stand together, prosperity, victory, glory and justice follow. Here the Gita comes to rest.

en/18-8-body-22b40872.mp3.text: If someone gives up action thinking it is only suffering and fearing bodily strain, that renunciation is passionate, and it brings no fruit of renunciation. Krishna calls this kind of giving up rajasa, passionate. It is not the calm of true release, but the restless recoil of someone who steps back from their duty simply because it hurts. Krishna now turns to the giving up that is done without clinging to results, the true sattvic path.

en/18-8-intro-7849e7c9.mp3.text: Krishna has been sorting the different kinds of giving up. Listen to the one that looks like peace but is actually fear.

en/18-9-body-784d9229.mp3.text: Arjuna, when fixed duty is done as only duty, without clinging to results, that renunciation is called sattvic. Krishna calls it sattvic tyaga, giving up both attachment and fruit at once, so the action is done purely because it is required. Krishna then speaks of the wise renunciate who neither rejects unwholesome action nor clings to wholesome action.

en/18-9-intro-0e7efdb2.mp3.text: Krishna now teaches the cleanest form of letting go. Listen to how he defines the highest sacrifice.

en/2-1-body-636acf8d.mp3.text: Sanjaya says: To Arjuna, overcome by pity, his eyes full of tears and clouded with grief, Madhusudana spoke these words. Madhusudana, the slayer of the demon Madhu, is the name Krishna takes as he begins this teaching to a weeping Arjuna. Krishna asks Arjuna where this delusion has come from in this moment of crisis.

en/2-1-intro-0e7eb08e.mp3.text: Sanjaya paints a picture of Arjuna sitting broken on his chariot, and then Krishna begins to speak to him.

en/2-10-body-d0c36c3b.mp3.text: Hrsikesa spoke to the grieving Arjuna, smiling slightly, in the midst of the two armies. Krishna speaks as if smiling at Arjuna's grief. The name Hrishikesha means lord of the senses, and here he stands between two armies to teach the master of the senses how to act. Krishna gently points out that Arjuna is grieving for the wrong reasons while speaking like a wise man.

en/2-10-intro-f2a1fbdc.mp3.text: Arjuna has just dropped his bow, saying he will not fight. What does Krishna say to him, standing right there between the two armies?

en/2-11-body-0fd2727e.mp3.text: The Blessed Lord says: You grieve for what should not be grieved for, yet speak words of wisdom. The wise do not grieve for the dead or the living. Krishna points to the contradiction between what Arjuna says and how he feels. Arjuna speaks प्रज्ञावादान्, words of wisdom, yet he grieves for the अशोच्यान्, the ungrievable. Krishna now tells Arjuna that he, Krishna, and the kings have always existed, and will always exist.

en/2-11-body-8a75f350.mp3.text: The Blessed Lord says: You grieve for what should not be grieved for, yet speak words of wisdom. The wise do not grieve for the dead or the living. Krishna points out the mismatch: Arjuna speaks like a wise man while grieving for those who need no grief. Krishna then reminds Arjuna that neither he nor the kings will ever cease to exist.

en/2-11-intro-58fd0886.mp3.text: The armies face each other. Arjuna has dropped his bow. Krishna begins his teaching by pointing out the gap between Arjuna's words and his feelings.

en/2-11-intro-822141ed.mp3.text: Krishna looks at Arjuna's words and actions, finding a mismatch. Listen for the gap between what Arjuna says and what he does.

en/2-12-body-c67ead2d.mp3.text: I was never absent, nor were you, nor these kings. Nor will any of us cease to be in the future. The word jaatu, meaning at any time, appears in the verse. By saying there was never a time when any of us were not, Krishna shows that existence has no beginning and no end. Krishna then explains how the embodied soul simply moves from one body to another like changing clothes.

en/2-12-intro-9324ebc3.mp3.text: Krishna is correcting Arjuna's grief by pointing to a word that keeps coming back. Listen for it.

en/2-13-body-50d50d47.mp3.text: Just as the embodied one passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too it passes into another body. The wise are not deluded by this. The word dehinah, the embodied one, is the subject here. It is the one who moves from childhood to old age and then into another body, and the steady one is not deluded by this. Krishna now brings in the senses and the heat and cold that come with them.

en/2-13-body-ccc14b0c.mp3.text: Just as the embodied one passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too it passes into another body. The wise are not deluded by this. Krishna compares childhood, youth, and old age to passing into another body, showing that the one who lives in it moves on. He now turns from the soul to the senses, O son of Kunti. They bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and they come and go. Endure them.

en/2-13-intro-6822f979.mp3.text: Krishna draws a simple picture from daily life. Listen to how he links the body to the one who lives in it.

en/2-13-intro-ab9b74c5.mp3.text: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna, who is terrified at the thought of killing his own kin. Listen to how Krishna uses a simple human experience to steady him.

en/2-14-body-240d28af.mp3.text: Contacts with the senses, O son of Kunti, bring heat and cold, pleasure and pain. They come and go; they are impermanent. Endure them, O Bharata. Krishna calls him Kunteya, son of Kunti, and tells him to endure. What he must endure is the heat and cold, the pleasure and pain, that come from the senses. He adds that these experiences are impermanent, coming and going, so the wise should bear them without distress.

en/2-14-intro-1ee1ba23.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna that the soul never dies. Now he turns to the body's daily experience and tells him what to do with it.

en/2-15-body-55326d31.mp3.text: The wise person who is not shaken by these, and remains equal in pain and pleasure, becomes fit for freedom. Listen to the word dhiram, steadfast. It names the person who stays even through pleasure and pain, and that steadiness is what makes him fit for freedom. Krishna now asks you to look at the boundary between what is real and what is not.

en/2-15-intro-40008283.mp3.text: The previous verse said to endure heat and cold. But how? Listen to how Krishna names the person who can do it.

en/2-16-body-2b9317d9.mp3.text: The unreal has no being; the real has no nonbeing. Seers have understood the boundary of both. Listen to the exact boundary between the unreal and the real. Nasato, what is unreal, has no permanent being, and nabhavo, the nonbeing of the real, never exists. Krishna then tells him to know the imperishable reality that pervades this whole world.

en/2-16-intro-4cbff7ac.mp3.text: Krishna now draws a hard line between what is real and what is not. Listen for the two sides of existence.

en/2-17-body-db78e4ee.mp3.text: Know that to be imperishable by which this entire world is pervaded. No one can destroy this imperishable reality. The word is avinashi, imperishable. It is the reality that pervades the entire world, and no one has the power to destroy it. Krishna now tells Arjuna that these bodies are temporary, but the being inside them cannot be harmed.

en/2-17-intro-57d6218c.mp3.text: Krishna is answering Arjuna's fear of killing. He asks him to focus on the one truth that can never be destroyed.

en/2-18-body-70261c1a.mp3.text: These bodies are said to be finite, but the embodied being is eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable. Therefore, fight, Arjuna. The verse sets up a direct pairing: the bodies are finite, but the embodied being is eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable. The command to fight follows directly from this truth. Krishna now asks Arjuna to stop thinking of the soul as either the killer or the killed.

en/2-18-body-ea687b23.mp3.text: These bodies are said to be finite, but the embodied being is eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable. Therefore, fight, Arjuna. The verse opens with a statement of fact, that these bodies are finite, and closes with a direct command, therefore fight. This structure shifts the focus from understanding the truth to acting on it. Krishna then explains that anyone who thinks the eternal being is killed does not understand the truth.

en/2-18-intro-5c7c5b5f.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna that the wise do not grieve for the living or the dead. Now he explains why that is true. Listen for the contrast between the body and the one inside it.

en/2-18-intro-7d143fb5.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the imperishable soul. Now he turns back to the body and tells Arjuna what to do with it.

en/2-19-body-0df8352c.mp3.text: Whoever thinks this imperishable being is the killer, and whoever thinks it is killed, both do not understand. It neither kills nor is killed. Notice how Krishna turns both statements into the same mistake. Whether you see the self as the killer or as the killed, both views miss the mark, because the self does neither. He then states the truth directly, that this being is unborn and never dies.

en/2-19-intro-3f627460.mp3.text: Krishna sharpens his point by rejecting both pictures of death and murder. Listen to how he frames the error.

en/2-2-body-807c4978.mp3.text: Krishna says: Arjuna, where has this delusion come from in this crisis? Noble people do not follow it. It does not lead upward, and it brings disgrace. Krishna calls the paralysis कश्मलम्, delusion. It is not the response of a noble person, it leads nowhere upward, and it brings disgrace. Krishna commands Arjuna to cast off this weakness and rise, scorcher of foes.

en/2-2-body-ee561713.mp3.text: Krishna says: Arjuna, where has this delusion come from in this crisis? Noble people do not follow it. It does not lead upward, and it brings disgrace. Krishna names the collapse as kashmalam, delusion. He says it has no place here because noble people do not follow it, it leads nowhere higher, and it brings disgrace. He tells Arjuna to cast off this petty weakness of heart and rise to fight.

en/2-2-intro-8ec8a41a.mp3.text: Krishna opens this chapter by naming exactly what has stopped Arjuna on the field. Listen for the word he uses for Arjuna's state.

en/2-2-intro-b4725da3.mp3.text: Krishna's first words are a direct rebuke. Listen for the one word he uses to name Arjuna's sudden collapse.

en/2-20-body-a79e4f8a.mp3.text: It is never born and never dies. It did not come into being, and it will not cease. Unborn, eternal, everlasting, ancient, it is not destroyed when the body is destroyed. The first word Krishna speaks is ajah, unborn. The self did not come into being, and it will not cease to be again. It is beyond the cycle of birth and death. If the self is unborn, Krishna then asks what happens when the body is destroyed.

en/2-20-intro-92b62849.mp3.text: How do you end what has no beginning? Krishna answers with a list of what the self is not. Listen for the first word.

en/2-21-body-2c928f12.mp3.text: One who knows the imperishable, eternal, unborn, and unchanging cannot think of killing or causing death. Krishna asks katham, how. If you truly see the self inside as unborn and imperishable, the very idea of killing collapses, because you cannot destroy what was never born. Krishna then gives the image of changing clothes to show what the body really is.

en/2-21-intro-c9cbfced.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from anatomy to vision, asking how anyone with true sight could even think of killing.

en/2-22-body-a7097bbf.mp3.text: As a person discards worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the embodied being discards worn-out bodies and enters new ones. Listen to one word, dehi, the embodied one. The body is not the self; it is merely a worn-out thing the embodied one leaves behind, just as a person leaves behind old clothes. Krishna now turns to what weapons and fire cannot touch, the self that never dies.

en/2-22-intro-c766bc03.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna to look past the death of the body. Listen to one word that makes the body sound like an everyday object.

en/2-23-body-0b6dc07d.mp3.text: Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, and wind cannot dry it. Krishna names the self by saying what it is not. He does not say the soul is safe from weapons, he says weapons cannot cut it. Krishna now tells Arjuna what this self actually is, beyond all physical limits.

en/2-23-intro-8e09777e.mp3.text: Krishna answers Arjuna's fear of killing by explaining what the soul is not. Listen for the four forces he names.
