en/2-24-body-782affb6.mp3.text: This embodied self cannot be cut, burned, wetted, or dried. It is eternal, all-pervading, unmoving, fixed, and timeless. Krishna uses the word ashosyah, undryable, to show that the inner being cannot be dried by any force. It is eternal, all-pervading, unmoving, and fixed, standing beyond the reach of any physical element. The next verse says this self is unseen and beyond thought, so Arjuna should stop grieving.

en/2-24-intro-015233a8.mp3.text: Krishna continues by listing exactly what physical force cannot do to the true self. Listen for the word that describes the limits of water.

en/2-25-body-1207fa77.mp3.text: It is unseen, beyond thought, and said to be unchanged. Therefore, knowing it this way, you should not grieve. Listen to the word ayam, this. It appears three times, pointing to the self, and each time it tells us the self is unseen, unthinkable, and unchanged, so grieving over it is useless. Krishna now asks what would happen if Arjuna still thought the self was born and died.

en/2-25-intro-ef7a5e0c.mp3.text: Krishna asks why Arjuna is grieving over bodies when the truth of the self is beyond sight and thought. Listen for three qualities of the inner reality.

en/2-26-body-157091ff.mp3.text: O mighty-armed one, even if you think this embodied being is always born and always dies, you still should not grieve like this. Krishna does not force his own view on Arjuna. He begins with 'even then', showing he is willing to argue from Arjuna's own assumptions. Krishna now points out that death is certain for the born, and birth for the dead.

en/2-26-intro-111dca79.mp3.text: Krishna offers Arjuna a second reason to stop grieving. Listen for how Krishna meets him where he is.

en/2-27-body-b15bb60b.mp3.text: For what is born, death is certain; for what dies, birth is certain. What cannot be avoided should not be grieved over. The word dhruvam, meaning certain, is used twice here. It marks two truths that never break: the born must die, and the dead must be born again. Krishna now points out that the self is unmanifest before birth and after death.

en/2-27-intro-e5ebff66.mp3.text: Krishna reminds Arjuna that the cycle of the body is fixed and asks him to stop grieving over it.

en/2-28-body-e84fc56c.mp3.text: All beings are unmanifest before birth and unmanifest after death; they are manifest only in between. Why grieve over that? Krishna uses the word avyaktam, the unmanifest. He says that before birth and after death, beings are simply unmanifest, and only briefly visible in between. He now turns to the inner self that is seen as wondrous by those who seek it.

en/2-28-intro-74a5dd5f.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna that death is certain for the born and birth for the dead. Now he speaks of the hidden state that frames all life.

en/2-29-body-1f70a3e9.mp3.text: Some behold the inner being as wondrous; some speak of it as wondrous; some hear of it as wondrous; and even after hearing, no one truly knows it. Even after hearing about the self, no one truly knows it. The self is wondrous to behold, describe, and hear about, yet it remains difficult to fully grasp. Krishna then tells Arjuna that the self in every body is eternal and cannot be slain. Listen to his next words.

en/2-29-intro-dace5a04.mp3.text: Krishna continues his teaching on the self, showing that it is beyond ordinary thought.

en/2-3-body-03578430.mp3.text: Do not yield to weakness, Partha. It does not suit you. Cast off this petty weakness of heart and rise, scorcher of foes. Krishna calls Arjuna by two names, Partha, son of Pritha, and Parantapa, scorcher of foes. He tells him to cast off the petty weakness of heart, because it does not suit who he is. Arjuna replies that he cannot raise his bow against Bhishma and Drona, who are worthy of his worship.

en/2-3-intro-704560e5.mp3.text: Arjuna has collapsed into grief and doubt. Krishna cuts through it with a sharp question and a direct command. Listen for how he names the moment.

en/2-30-body-12f5f753.mp3.text: O descendant of Bharata, the embodied one in every body is eternal and cannot be slain. Therefore you should not grieve for any being. Krishna closes with one word, dehi, the embodied one. The body may fall, but the one who lives inside every body is eternal, so there is no reason to weep. Krishna now turns from grief to duty, and tells Arjuna to consider his own role as a warrior.

en/2-30-intro-faad8fe1.mp3.text: Arjuna is drowning in sorrow, but Krishna answers with one truth. Listen for the word that ends the argument about grief.

en/2-31-body-ea09991c.mp3.text: Considering your own duty, you should not waver. For a warrior, no action is more beneficial than a righteous battle. Krishna uses the word svadharma, one's own duty. For Arjuna, that duty is not to avoid the fight, but to fight it, because no action serves a warrior better than a righteous battle. Krishna then describes this war not as a burden, but as an open gate to higher realms for the warrior who receives it.

en/2-31-intro-255aac76.mp3.text: Arjuna is frozen on the battlefield, and Krishna speaks directly to his hesitation. Listen to how Krishna defines the warrior's path.

en/2-32-body-9822624a.mp3.text: An unbidden battle is an open gate to higher realms. O Partha, fortunate are the warriors who receive such a war. The word to notice is yadrichchhaya, meaning unbidden. It means this war came to them without asking, yet Krishna calls it an open gate to higher realms, framing the conflict as a rare gift of duty. Krishna then warns that refusing this war would mean abandoning duty and honor.

en/2-32-intro-d55d09f7.mp3.text: Krishna points to one word that turns the war from a burden into a gift. Listen closely for what he calls this unbidden battle.

en/2-33-body-7e931161.mp3.text: If you do not fight this righteous war, you will abandon your duty and honor and incur blame. Krishna names two things, swadharma and kirti, your own duty and your honor, and says that abandoning both is the sin. The blame is not for fighting, but for running away from the role you were born to carry. He adds that everyone will speak of your everlasting disgrace. For an honored person, disgrace is worse than death.

en/2-33-intro-b080ba94.mp3.text: Krishna has just called this a righteous war. Now he warns Arjuna about the cost of refusing it. Listen to the two things he says will be lost.

en/2-34-body-0f9d127a.mp3.text: And all beings will speak of your everlasting disgrace. For an honored person, disgrace is worse than death. Krishna says the disgrace will be aviyam, everlasting. For a man honored as you are, that endless shame is worse than death. He shifts the argument from your inner duty to how the world will judge you. The great warriors will think you withdrew from battle out of fear, and those who once held you in high regard will see you as small.

en/2-34-intro-0b28bd2e.mp3.text: Krishna continues his argument by warning Arjuna about the world outside the chariot. Listen for the exact comparison he makes between dying and living with shame.

en/2-35-body-44e5838b.mp3.text: The great warriors will think you withdrew from battle out of fear. Those who once held you in high regard will see you as small. The word Maharathah means great chariot-warriors, and laabhavam means smallness or a drop in status. Those who once held him in high regard will see him reduced to nothing. Krishna asks what could be more painful than enemies mocking a warrior's strength.

en/2-35-intro-9485013e.mp3.text: What happens to a warrior's name when he stops fighting? Listen to how Krishna warns him that the great warriors will think he withdrew from battle out of fear.

en/2-36-body-8ba25557.mp3.text: Your enemies will speak many unworthy words, mocking your strength. What could be more painful than that? He names two things: unworthy words and mockers of your strength. The verse says your enemies will speak many such words, and asks what could be more painful. Krishna then shifts to the two possible results of the battle, death or victory.

en/2-36-intro-02be669b.mp3.text: Krishna asks what could hurt more than public shame. Listen to the exact words he uses.

en/2-37-body-2fbb8702.mp3.text: If you are killed, you will attain heaven; if you win, you will enjoy the kingdom. Therefore, rise, Kaunteya, and fight with resolve. The word is kritanishchayah, firm resolve. Krishna tells Arjuna to make up his mind and fight, because the decision itself is what matters. Krishna then tells Arjuna to treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as the same.

en/2-37-intro-b2659bb3.mp3.text: Listen for one word that turns Arjuna's fear into a command to stand up, no matter what the outcome is.

en/2-38-body-7676c2b7.mp3.text: Treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat alike. Then enter the battle; you will not incur wrongdoing. Listen to the word samam, equal. Krishna places pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat in a single line as equal. This is the exact condition he gives before Arjuna must fight. Krishna now turns to the method of yoga to help Arjuna cast off the bondage of action.

en/2-38-intro-c76aaca7.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna to treat victory and defeat, gain and loss, as equal before entering the battle.

en/2-39-body-91bbf341.mp3.text: This wisdom has been taught to you in Sankhya. Now hear it in yoga. Equipped with this understanding, Arjuna, you will cast off the bondage of action. The word buddhi, wisdom, appears twice in this verse. Krishna is not giving Arjuna new knowledge, but a new way to use the same understanding. He assures Arjuna that even a small effort in this path will protect him from the greatest fear.

en/2-39-intro-4315eb6d.mp3.text: Krishna turns the conversation from knowing to doing. He promises that this same wisdom will free Arjuna from the trap of his own actions.

en/2-4-body-29ef485c.mp3.text: Arjuna says: How can I fight Bhishma and Drona with arrows in battle, O Madhusudana? They are worthy of worship, O destroyer of enemies. Arjuna asks how he can fight Bhishma and Drona with arrows, and calls them worthy of worship, revealing the depth of his anguish. Sanjaya answers with the king's own son, Duryodhana, looking across at the Pandava army.

en/2-4-intro-4c81c6a0.mp3.text: After Krishna rebukes Arjuna for his despair, Arjuna answers with a deeper wound: how can he shoot arrows at the teachers he reveres?

en/2-40-body-6685bb1d.mp3.text: In this human world, no effort toward this steady wisdom is ever lost. No harmful result comes from it. Even a little practice of this dharma protects one from great fear. Even a little practice of this dharma protects one from great fear. This means the smallest step toward steady wisdom is never wasted, and it shields you from the deep fear that keeps you stuck. Krishna now describes the resolute mind that stays one-pointed, unlike the mind that branches endlessly in every direction.

en/2-40-body-933b8fff.mp3.text: In this human world, no effort toward this steady wisdom is ever lost. No harmful result comes from it. Even a little practice of this dharma protects one from great fear. The verse opens with a double negative, na abhiskrama-nasho nasti and na pratyavayo na vidyate, meaning there is no loss of beginning effort and no reverse result. It is a complete guarantee that a small start in this dharma never goes to waste and never backfires. Krishna then contrasts this resolute, one-pointed intellect with an endless, many-branched one. Listen for that distinction.

en/2-40-intro-1b52abe9.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that even a tiny step on this path is never wasted. Listen for the exact words of that promise.

en/2-40-intro-5ac09f81.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna to act with steady wisdom. Now he answers a doubt: is this path too risky?

en/2-41-body-b2057abd.mp3.text: O son of the Kurus, the resolute intellect is one-pointed here. The intellect of the irresolute is many-branched and endless. Krishna contrasts the resolute mind, aimed one way, with the irresolute mind branching endlessly. Krishna now explains that people with this scattered mind speak empty words about the Vedas, missing the truth entirely.

en/2-41-intro-00962dd4.mp3.text: Krishna sets up a stark choice between the mind that knows its target and the mind that cannot stop branching out. Listen for the word that names the endless path.

en/2-42-body-bb050b96.mp3.text: The unwise speak flowery words. They delight in the ritual sections of the Vedas and say nothing else exists. The word is pushpitam, flowery. These people dress up desire in polished, sacred language and treat reward-seeking as the whole of life, closing their minds to anything beyond it. Krishna immediately adds that this speech promises birth and action-fruit, describing many rites for enjoyment.

en/2-42-intro-31232a6f.mp3.text: Krishna points to a certain kind of talk that sounds sacred but hides a shallow aim. Listen for the word that marks it.

en/2-43-body-87981a8f.mp3.text: Those without clear seeing speak flowery words that promise birth and action-fruit, and describe many rites for enjoyment and power. Listen to the word kamatmanah, those whose minds are full of desire. It marks the speakers and the listeners, showing that a teaching born from craving can only offer more craving, birth, and action. Krishna then shows what happens when the mind is carried away by pleasure and power.

en/2-43-intro-d4bc7ddd.mp3.text: Krishna now names the listeners he is speaking to, the ones who get caught in flowery words. Listen for the mark of a teaching that keeps a person bound.

en/2-44-body-5db2948b.mp3.text: For those whose minds are carried away by pleasure and power, steadfast determination in meditation does not arise. The intellect, buddhi, is not established in steady meditation because the mind has been stolen by the attraction to pleasure and power. Krishna then tells Arjuna to rise above the three qualities and beyond opposites like gain and loss.

en/2-44-intro-407dfe8e.mp3.text: Krishna has just finished describing the flowery words of those who promise rewards. He now explains why the mind cannot hold steady.

en/2-45-body-89554196.mp3.text: The Vedas deal with the three qualities. Arjuna, rise beyond the three qualities, beyond opposites, fixed in lasting reality, free from concern for gain and security, and established in the true self. The word niryogakshema means free from worry about gaining things or protecting them. Krishna tells Arjuna to stop chasing security and comfort, and instead root himself in the unchanging self. Krishna explains that this inner freedom makes the vast Vedas as small as a puddle compared to the ocean of knowledge.

en/2-45-intro-a4fb6876.mp3.text: Arjuna is paralyzed by grief, and Krishna points to a way out. What is it that he must stop doing? Listen for the instruction.

en/2-46-body-5d4b4517.mp3.text: For one who understands, all the Vedas are as useful as a small puddle when a great reservoir of water is at hand. One Sanskrit word, udapane, means a small puddle. When a person stands beside a great reservoir that is full from all sides, that puddle offers nothing more. Krishna then tells Arjuna that his right is only to work, never to the results.

en/2-46-intro-ca6fb240.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from rules to a single image of water. Listen for how one full reservoir makes a puddle unnecessary.

en/2-47-body-a2f18485.mp3.text: You have a right to action alone, never to its fruits. Do not become the cause of the result, and do not cling to inaction. The word karma, action, appears three times here. It is the only thing that is yours to own, while the fruits and the cause of the fruits are not. Krishna now tells Arjuna to perform these actions while remaining established in yoga, equal in success and failure.

en/2-47-body-dfc712ab.mp3.text: You have a right to action alone, never to its fruits. Do not become the cause of the result, and do not cling to inaction. The word is अधिकारः, your right. It is bound only to कर्मणि, in action. It never reaches फलेषु, in fruits, showing that your claim stops where your effort ends. Krishna then tells Arjuna to abandon attachment to action itself while remaining steady in success and failure.

en/2-47-intro-01522018.mp3.text: Krishna gives a hard line about what belongs to you and what does not. Listen for the word that appears three times and holds the whole verse together.

en/2-47-intro-6cc69697.mp3.text: Krishna is drawing a hard line between what is yours and what is not. Listen for the single word that limits your claim.

en/2-48-body-56c8f95b.mp3.text: O Dhananjaya, perform actions while established in yoga, abandoning attachment. Remain equal in success and failure, for equanimity is called yoga. Krishna does not define yoga as a posture or a breath. He defines it as samatvam, evenness. The exact moment of success or failure does not have to shake the one who is established in yoga. Krishna now contrasts that steady state with action born of craving, and calls the craving-driven path pitiful. Listen.

en/2-48-intro-84ad49f9.mp3.text: Krishna has told Arjuna to act, but not to crave the results. Now he gives the precise inner state that makes that action true yoga. Listen to how he defines it.

en/2-49-body-1d1a2972.mp3.text: Action driven by craving is far below the steadiness of clear discernment. Seek refuge in clear discernment, for those who chase results are pitiable. The word kripanah means pitiable. Krishna calls those who chase results pitiable because their happiness depends on outcomes they cannot control. Krishna then explains how one united with discernment casts off both good and bad deeds in this life.

en/2-49-body-9bdacf78.mp3.text: Action driven by craving is far below the steadiness of clear discernment. Seek refuge in clear discernment, for those who chase results are pitiable. Krishna uses the word कृपणाः, pitiable, to describe those who act for results. They are weak because they have traded their inner steadiness for the gamble of outcomes. This distinction leads Him to explain why clear discernment is superior to chasing results.

en/2-49-intro-27a9a2df.mp3.text: Krishna carries the teaching forward, contrasting two kinds of action and the mind that guides them.

en/2-49-intro-dd04aaf1.mp3.text: Krishna has just taught Arjuna to remain steady in success and failure, and now He draws a hard line between two ways of acting.

en/2-5-body-62402a4e.mp3.text: It is better to live on alms in this world than to kill these great teachers. If I kill them, the pleasures I enjoy here will be stained with blood and bound to greed. Listen to how he weighs his duty against his respect. He says that winning these pleasures stained with blood is worse than living on alms, and that any victory he takes is bound to greed. Next, Arjuna continues.

en/2-5-intro-63522e17.mp3.text: Krishna has asked Arjuna to act, but Arjuna now answers with a moral cost. He names the people standing against him as his own teachers.

en/2-50-body-89a3dbda.mp3.text: One who is united with clear discernment casts off both good and bad deeds in this life. Therefore, devote yourself to yoga, for yoga is skill in action. The word yuktasva, be devoted, appears twice in this verse. First he tells Arjuna to be devoted to yoga, and then he defines yoga itself as skill in action. Krishna then explains how those united in wisdom reach a flawless state, free from the bondage of birth.

en/2-50-intro-9f5acf18.mp3.text: Krishna answers the fear of doing wrong: a steady mind changes how action binds. Listen for the reason he gives.

en/2-51-body-1295fc00.mp3.text: Wise people, united in clarity, abandon the fruit born of action and reach the flawless state, free from the bondage of birth. The verb is gacchanti, they go. The wise do not stay still; they move toward a flawless state, a place without affliction, simply by abandoning the fruit of what they do. Krishna now turns to the intellect itself, saying that when it crosses delusion, it grows dispassionate.

en/2-51-intro-81c580ea.mp3.text: Krishna speaks of a release that comes not from stopping action, but from letting go of what action produces. Listen to how the wise reach it.

en/2-52-body-ebbf9730.mp3.text: When your intellect crosses the swamp of delusion, you will grow dispassionate toward what has been heard and what remains to be heard. Listen for moha, delusion. Krishna does not call it a thought or a feeling; he calls it a swamp. Once your intellect crosses it, the pull of promised pleasures simply drops away. Next, Krishna describes the steady mind that has already crossed this swamp.

en/2-52-intro-2b3a2cb6.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that the root of his confusion is a swamp. Listen for the word that names this swamp.

en/2-53-body-24d274b6.mp3.text: When your intellect, unmoved by conflicting teachings, becomes steady in complete stillness, you will attain yoga. The word samadhi, complete stillness, names the exact state where the intellect finally arrives. It is not a vague calm, but the mind resting completely in one place. Arjuna asks what a person of steady wisdom looks like in daily life, and how they speak, sit, and walk.

en/2-53-intro-4ba28936.mp3.text: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna, taking him past the confusion of different teachings so he can see what a steady mind truly looks like.

en/2-54-body-9da5d212.mp3.text: Arjuna says: O Kesava, what are the marks of one whose wisdom is steady and who is absorbed in stillness? How does a person of steady understanding speak, sit, and walk? Arjuna asks a practical question, how does a steady man speak, sit, and walk, and Krishna answers by saying he is satisfied in the true self, a state where no desire remains. Krishna names this person steady in wisdom, setting out to describe the marks of such a state.

en/2-54-intro-45a05bcf.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the still mind. Now Arjuna asks how to recognize such a person in daily life.

en/2-55-body-55c65a94.mp3.text: The divine says: When a person gives up all desires that arise in the mind, and is satisfied in the true self by the true self alone, that person is called steady in wisdom. This verse answers Arjuna's question by showing the exact moment wisdom begins. The word yada, when, marks the inner turning point. When all desires are released, the person is no longer driven by the mind, but satisfied by the self. Krishna then lists the outer marks of this state: the sage is unshaken by sorrow and free from craving in joy.

en/2-55-intro-ffe90822.mp3.text: Arjuna asked what a steady person looks like. Krishna answers by pointing to the exact moment this change happens. Listen for the word that marks this inner turning point.

en/2-56-body-4dbf5097.mp3.text: The steady-minded sage is unshaken by sorrow, free from craving in joy, and beyond attachment, fear, and anger. Krishna lists three poisons that a steady person has left behind: attachment, fear, and anger. These three are named together as one single condition of being, gone beyond. Krishna then asks what such a steady person looks like when they speak, and next verse describes their behavior.

en/2-56-intro-dbc32e73.mp3.text: Krishna answers Arjuna's question by describing the outward behavior of a steady-minded person. Listen for the three states he names.

en/2-57-body-1e3eead0.mp3.text: One who feels no clinging anywhere, and neither rejoices nor hates when good or bad comes, has steady wisdom. The verb abhinandati means to rejoice or welcome. Krishna says the person of steady wisdom does not abhinandati when good fortune comes, because they do not cling to the pleasant. Krishna now shifts from the inside feeling to the outside action, comparing the senses to a tortoise withdrawing its limbs.

en/2-57-body-9f8c653c.mp3.text: One who feels no clinging anywhere, and neither rejoices nor hates when good or bad comes, has steady wisdom. The word is अनभिस्नेहः, without clinging. It is the root. Good and bad come and go, but because the person does not cling to anything, no outcome can make them rejoice or hate. Krishna now shows how this same steady wisdom pulls the senses inward, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs.

en/2-57-intro-0bdf3222.mp3.text: Krishna has been describing steady wisdom, and now he points to a specific reaction that marks it. Listen for the two things this person does not do when good or bad happens.

en/2-57-intro-764c524c.mp3.text: Krishna names the root of a steady mind. Listen for the word that means without clinging, and hear how it protects the wise from every joy and pain.

en/2-58-body-6f74b6dd.mp3.text: When this one draws the senses fully back from sense-objects, like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs, wisdom is steady. Krishna gives the image of a tortoise, कूर्मः, who draws in its limbs from all sides, सर्वशः, at will. The wise one does the same with the senses, pulling them away from the objects they chase so that wisdom remains steady. Krishna then adds that while the senses may still feel the pull of objects, the one who sees the supreme reality lets that taste fall away too.

en/2-58-body-d7e515fa.mp3.text: When this one draws the senses fully back from sense-objects, like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs, wisdom is steady. The verse is built on one image, that of a tortoise, and one result, steadfast wisdom. The tortoise draws in its limbs from all sides, and the wise person does the same with the senses, pulling them back from their objects. Krishna warns that even when objects fall away, the taste for them may remain, a danger the self-denying person must face.

en/2-58-intro-7ead3736.mp3.text: Krishna has just described a person who feels no clinging to anything. Now he gives the image of how that control actually works.

en/2-58-intro-d6b88ec9.mp3.text: Krishna has been describing a mind that no longer wavers. Now he gives a picture of how that steadiness is held.

en/2-59-body-6bcb42f4.mp3.text: Objects fall away from the self-denying person, but the taste for them remains. For the one who has seen the supreme reality, even that taste falls away. The verse hinges on rasah, the taste, which remains when the objects disappear. Krishna says that for the embodied one who has not seen the supreme, this taste does not turn away. Krishna now adds that even a wise person's mind can be pulled away by turbulent senses.

en/2-59-intro-019d98dd.mp3.text: Krishna has just shown the tortoise method, but he now warns that even this is not enough. Listen for the inner taste that survives.

en/2-6-body-99580e85.mp3.text: We do not know which is better for us: to fight or not to fight. We do not even know whether we will conquer them or they us. The sons of Dhritarashtra stand before us, and we do not wish to live after killing them. Arjuna admits he cannot tell whether fighting or not fighting is better, or which side would win. He now asks Krishna to tell him with certainty what is best, because he is confused about his duty.

en/2-6-intro-ae9062ac.mp3.text: Arjuna stands between two armies with his bow lowered. He admits he cannot tell which is better, or who will win.

en/2-60-body-d5842134.mp3.text: Even for a wise person who strives, the turbulent senses can forcibly carry away the mind. The word pramathini, meaning restless or turbulent, is used for the senses. They do not just tempt the body; they forcibly drag the mind, even from a wise person who is actively trying to control them. Krishna then gives the remedy for this very struggle: restraining the senses and fixing the mind on the divine.

en/2-60-intro-3e8036e9.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that even a wise person can be dragged off course by restless senses. Listen to the force of that word.

en/2-61-body-4760d17f.mp3.text: Having restrained all the senses, the disciplined one should sit devoted to Me. For one whose senses are under control, wisdom is firmly established. Krishna does not ask Arjuna to control the senses by force alone. The word matparah, devoted to Me, shows that restraint becomes firm only when the mind is turned toward the divine. Krishna warns that even thinking about sense objects creates attachment, which can lead to anger.

en/2-61-intro-e706b30e.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from the problem of the senses to the solution. He tells Arjuna to hold them in check and stay focused on the divine.

en/2-62-body-0fa77ad1.mp3.text: Thinking about sense objects creates attachment to them. Attachment gives rise to desire; desire gives rise to anger. The word sanga, attachment, is the second link that traps a person. It is born from mere thought, and from that attachment the desire for the object is born. From this desire, anger arises, and from anger comes delusion.

en/2-62-body-bbc5e708.mp3.text: Thinking about sense objects creates attachment to them. Attachment gives rise to desire; desire gives rise to anger. The verse opens with dhyayatah, while thinking. The mind does not need to act on the object yet; simply dwelling on it is enough to plant the seed of attachment. From that attachment, desire is born, and from desire, anger arises.

en/2-62-intro-3156b810.mp3.text: Listen for the word sanga, attachment. Krishna traces how a thought becomes a chain that destroys a person.

en/2-62-intro-83f6925e.mp3.text: Krishna points to the first step in a chain of ruin. Listen for the word that opens the door to attachment.

en/2-63-body-ae4a799f.mp3.text: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from confusion of memory, loss of discernment; from loss of discernment, ruin. Krishna traces a path from anger to ruin, showing how the mind collapses from the outside in. The next verse shows the disciplined person who avoids this collapse by keeping the senses under control.

en/2-63-intro-454cac8f.mp3.text: Krishna is answering Arjuna's question about what destroys a person. Listen for the chain of ruin that starts with a single emotion.

en/2-64-body-2a42635e.mp3.text: The disciplined person, moving among objects with senses under control and free from attraction and aversion, attains serenity. Listen to how the disciplined person, विधेय आत्मा, still moves among objects, subjects, and sense data, yet remains free from attraction and aversion, and attains serenity. In that serenity, all suffering falls away. For one whose mind is clear, understanding settles quickly.

en/2-64-body-3d1835d1.mp3.text: The disciplined person, moving among objects with senses under control and free from attraction and aversion, attains serenity. The disciplined person, the vidheyatma, keeps the senses under the control of the inner self. This inner alignment is what allows serenity to arise. Krishna now shows how this inner clarity brings an end to suffering and steadies the mind completely.

en/2-64-intro-ab835997.mp3.text: Krishna turns from the ruin of anger to the steadiness of the disciplined person. Listen to the condition of the one who moves through the world.

en/2-64-intro-f76bb729.mp3.text: Krishna just traced the ruin that follows a single moment of anger. Now he turns to the one who escapes that ruin.

en/2-65-body-3a717bc1.mp3.text: In inner clarity, all suffering falls away. For one whose mind is clear, understanding settles quickly. The word prasade means in clarity, and it is here that all sorrow ends for this one, because a clear mind quickly settles into understanding. Krishna then turns the chain around, showing that without peace there is no happiness at all.

en/2-65-intro-99ca63e0.mp3.text: When the mind grows still, what falls away first? Listen to how Krishna answers that.

en/2-66-body-e48a5589.mp3.text: A restless mind has no steady discernment, no steady purpose, no peace, and without peace, no happiness. Krishna builds a chain of loss: first steady discernment, then steady purpose, then peace, and finally happiness. Each loss depends on the one before it. One wandering sense is enough to wash away the mind's judgment, just as a wind sweeps a boat on water.

en/2-66-intro-882d5e17.mp3.text: Krishna describes the total loss of a mind ruled by restless senses. Listen to the exact chain of what disappears.

en/2-67-body-50f88d5b.mp3.text: As the winds carry a boat on water, even one roaming sense can sweep away the mind's discernment. The word vayu is the force that carries the boat off course, and Krishna uses that exact image to show how one sense can sweep away discernment. Krishna now turns to the one who controls the senses and finds a steady wisdom.

en/2-67-intro-e045b8c1.mp3.text: Krishna warns that a single sense can drag the whole mind off course. Listen for the exact force that sweeps away judgment.

en/2-68-body-2ac217c5.mp3.text: Therefore, O mighty-armed one, the wisdom of one whose senses are fully restrained from sense-objects is steady. Krishna calls Arjuna mighty-armed, reminding him that the strength to control the senses already lies within him. Once the senses are fully restrained in every way, wisdom stands firm and steady. Krishna then contrasts the inner state of the self-controlled with the ordinary waking and sleeping of the world.

en/2-68-intro-4a6b0840.mp3.text: Krishna has just warned that a single wandering sense can sweep away the mind's discernment. Now he states the result of true inner mastery.

en/2-69-body-7c234f61.mp3.text: What is night for all beings is wakefulness for the self-controlled one. What all beings wake toward is night for the seer who knows the real. The sage's day is the world's night. Where everyone else wakes up to chase things, the seer is awake in what is night for all beings, and what all beings wake toward is night for the seer. Krishna says that just as rivers pour into the sea, desires flow into a steady person without stirring their peace.

en/2-69-intro-30443466.mp3.text: Krishna carries on the idea of the steady mind, and now he tells Arjuna about the inner clock of the sage.

en/2-7-body-5c682520.mp3.text: My nature is overwhelmed by weakness, and my mind is confused about duty. I ask you: tell me with certainty what is best for me. I am your student; instruct me, for I have taken refuge in you. He calls himself your student, your disciple, and one who has taken refuge. With that single shift, the debate ends and the teaching begins. He then lists all the kingdoms and wealth he could win, and finds they cannot touch his grief.

en/2-7-intro-87291c28.mp3.text: Arjuna has dropped his bow. Listen for how he stops arguing and calls Krishna his teacher.

en/2-70-body-57288f16.mp3.text: As rivers flow into the sea and the sea remains steady, so desires may enter a disciplined person without disturbing inner peace. The person who wants pleasures does not find peace. Listen to the sea, samudram, and the word describing it, acala-pratishtam, unmoving. The rivers of desire pour in, yet the sea does not swell; that is the steadiness Krishna offers. Krishna now states plainly that the person who gives up craving and ego is the one who attains peace.

en/2-70-intro-0353689c.mp3.text: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to stay steady under pressure. Listen for the image he uses to show what inner peace looks like.

en/2-71-body-b4c05123.mp3.text: One who gives up all desires, moves without craving, without possessiveness, and without ego, attains peace. Three qualities are named in a row: without craving, without possessiveness, and without ego. The one who acts in this way is the one who attains peace. Krishna now names this state of freedom as the Brahmic state, the very state Arjuna must reach.

en/2-71-intro-bc548abe.mp3.text: Krishna describes the person who has found inner freedom. Listen to the three things this person leaves behind.

en/2-72-body-33bcb574.mp3.text: Arjuna, this is the Brahmic state. Having reached it, one is never deluded. Remaining established in it even at the end of life, one attains freedom in the supreme reality. Listen for the word स्थित्वा, meaning remaining established. The verse does not say that reaching this state is enough once. It says remaining established in it, even at the end of life, brings freedom. Arjuna hears this, and immediately asks why Krishna is urging him to fight at all.

en/2-72-body-aa11fc55.mp3.text: Arjuna, this is the Brahmic state. Having reached it, one is never deluded. Remaining established in it even at the end of life, one attains freedom in the supreme reality. Krishna names the brahmic state: once reached, delusion ends, and even at death it holds. Arjuna now asks why Krishna urges him to fight if understanding is better than action.

en/2-72-intro-78265a25.mp3.text: Krishna has just finished describing a mind at peace with itself. Now he gives this state a name, and with it a guarantee that even death cannot take it away.

en/2-72-intro-7c7ec764.mp3.text: Krishna has just finished describing the steady mind. Now he gives it a name. Listen for how that name changes the stakes of the whole conversation.

en/2-8-body-da3ceae7.mp3.text: Even if I gained an unrivaled, prosperous kingdom on earth or lordship over the gods, I see nothing that could remove this grief that dries up my senses. Listen to the scale of what Arjuna rejects. He is not talking about a small kingdom, but an unrivaled, prosperous earth and even lordship over the gods. Sanjaya then reports that after hearing this, Arjuna firmly tells Krishna he will not fight and falls silent.

en/2-8-intro-db417eb8.mp3.text: Arjuna has just confessed his weakness and confusion. Now he tells Krishna that no power on earth or in heaven can dry up his grief.

en/2-9-body-dec11c83.mp3.text: Sanjaya says: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha, Gudakesha, the scorcher of foes, said to Govinda, “I will not fight,” and fell silent. Sanjaya calls Arjuna Gudakesha, the conqueror of sleep, and then says he fell silent. The man who controlled sleep now surrenders to grief, and the battlefield holds its breath. Krishna then steps forward to speak to the silent Arjuna, and the crisis begins to shift.

en/2-9-intro-93091a55.mp3.text: Arjuna has refused to fight, and now the battlefield falls silent. Listen to how Sanjaya describes that sudden stillness.

en/3-1-body-2f02e418.mp3.text: Arjuna says: O Janardana, if you consider understanding superior to action, then why do you urge me to this terrible action, O Keshava? Your mixed words confuse my mind; tell me one clear thing by which I may attain what is good. Arjuna hears two different pulls, wisdom praised and battle commanded, and he calls them mixed words that confuse him. He asks for one clear statement that leads to the highest good. Arjuna insists on one clear instruction to cut through the confusion and find his path.

en/3-1-intro-89eb7a62.mp3.text: Krishna has praised steady wisdom, yet he still asks you to fight. Listen to how Arjuna points out the clash and asks for one clear path.

en/3-10-body-3f96bb20.mp3.text: In the beginning, Prajapati created beings together with sacrifice and said: “By this, you shall prosper. May this sacrifice be the wish-fulfilling cow for you.” Krishna names the speaker here as Prajapati, the lord of creatures. By recalling the creator, he shows that sacrifice and duty are not new rules but the original design of life itself. Krishna then explains that by nourishing others through this duty, they in turn nourish you.

en/3-10-body-b0a5c9ad.mp3.text: In the beginning, Prajapati created beings together with sacrifice and said: “By this, you shall prosper. May this sacrifice be the wish-fulfilling cow for you.” Krishna names Prajapati as the original speaker here, and the word सहयज्ञाः means together with sacrifice, showing that the act of giving back was part of the first creation. Krishna explains that this original sacrifice is what lets everyone prosper together.

en/3-10-intro-3311706d.mp3.text: Krishna moves Arjuna’s mind from the present battlefield to the very beginning of creation. Hear how the creator first ordered beings to prosper.

en/3-10-intro-852edbe7.mp3.text: Krishna is taking Arjuna back to the very start of the world, to the moment of creation, to show that duty is not a human invention. Listen for the name he gives to the first teacher.

en/3-11-body-250b51ab.mp3.text: By nurturing the radiant beings through this duty, let them nurture you. Nurturing one another, you will attain the highest good. Nourish the devas and they will nourish you; mutual care leads to the highest good. Krishna then warns that anyone who takes these gifts without giving back is nothing but a thief.

en/3-11-body-5b32d4d7.mp3.text: By nurturing the radiant beings through this duty, let them nurture you. Nurturing one another, you will attain the highest good. In this verse, the key word is परस्परम्, one another. The radiant beings and humans do not act alone; they sustain each other, and only through that mutual exchange do they reach the highest good. Krishna then names the radiant beings and warns that taking from them without giving back is theft.

en/3-11-intro-6225f3d9.mp3.text: Krishna continues the cycle of giving, showing how duty creates a bond of mutual care. Listen for the two sides of this exchange.

en/3-11-intro-e18a6217.mp3.text: Having explained how sacrifice began, Krishna now shows how it must continue as a relationship.

en/3-12-body-3e85f351.mp3.text: The radiant beings, nourished by sacrifice, will give you the enjoyments you need. One who enjoys their gifts without offering back is a thief. Listen to one word, अप्रदायैभ्यो, without giving back. The verse says the radiant beings give you everything you need, but if you enjoy what they give and do not offer it back, you are a thief. Krishna then says those who eat the leftovers of sacrifice are freed from all faults. Those who cook only for themselves eat only wrongdoing.

en/3-12-body-a7667f59.mp3.text: The radiant beings, nourished by sacrifice, will give you the enjoyments you need. One who enjoys their gifts without offering back is a thief. The verse turns on a single Sanskrit word, apradaya, which means without giving back. It names the exact moment when a person stops participating in the exchange of life and becomes a thief. The next verse draws a sharp line between those who eat the leftovers of sacrifice and those who cook only for themselves.

en/3-12-intro-22fab84a.mp3.text: Krishna answers a quiet question many people ask: why is sacrifice necessary, and what happens when we stop giving back? Listen to how he answers.

en/3-12-intro-53371c6f.mp3.text: This verse answers a simple question: how does the world keep giving? It says the exchange depends on your part.

en/3-13-body-e7ef8657.mp3.text: Those who eat the leftovers of sacrifice are freed from all faults. Those who cook only for themselves eat only wrongdoing. The verb pachanti means to cook. Krishna says those who cook only for their own sake eat only agha, wrongdoing. The act of preparing food becomes the act of consuming sin. The cycle of action and return is explained next, beginning with food itself.

en/3-13-intro-8f51f8fa.mp3.text: Krishna contrasts two ways of eating. One leads to freedom, the other to sin. Listen to how the word for cooking is turned into a word for eating wrongdoing.

en/3-14-body-4eb729f7.mp3.text: All beings arise from food. Food comes from rain. Rain comes from sacrifice. Sacrifice arises from action. The chain begins with a single word, annat, from food. Food is the first link, and from it all beings come into being, so the whole world rests on what we eat and how it is produced. Krishna then asks Arjuna to see how action itself is born from the Vedas and the imperishable.

en/3-14-intro-8c1ab837.mp3.text: Krishna points to one word that begins a long chain of life. Listen for where this chain starts.

en/3-15-body-2ddf272e.mp3.text: Know that action comes from the Vedas, and the Vedas come from the imperishable. Therefore, the all-pervading supreme reality is always established in sacrifice. Notice the word viddhi, know. Krishna commands Arjuna to know that action is born from the Vedas, and the Vedas from the imperishable, making sacrifice the root of all existence. If anyone ignores this cycle of sacrifice and action, they live only for the senses and their life becomes empty.

en/3-15-intro-5f2eeadb.mp3.text: Krishna has just shown how sacrifice sustains all life. Now He traces action back to its source. Listen for how the chain of existence is rooted in the divine.

en/3-16-body-472994c4.mp3.text: O Partha, the one who does not follow this cycle set in motion here lives in vain, delighting only in the senses and living a life of wrongdoing. The word indriyarama, delighting in the senses, names the one who refuses the cycle. He seeks pleasure alone and therefore lives a life that is agha, tainted by wrongdoing. Krishna now speaks of the one who has already found the true self, and so has no duty left to perform.

en/3-16-intro-2b62dffd.mp3.text: Krishna explains how life itself depends on a shared cycle of action. Listen to the warning he gives about refusing that order.

en/3-17-body-70812685.mp3.text: The person who delights in the true self, is satisfied in the true self, and is content in the true self has no duty left. Krishna points to the one who has found fullness within. For this person, no duty remains to be done. Krishna then asks what the perfected person, who has no purpose in doing, should do next.

en/3-17-intro-e40f3826.mp3.text: If work is for the world, what happens when the world is no longer needed? Listen for the one who has found fullness within.

en/3-18-body-3001c384.mp3.text: For the perfected person, no purpose remains in doing, and no purpose remains in not doing. No being in the world is a source of personal gain. For the one who is complete, Krishna says, doing and not doing both gain nothing. Krishna then commands Arjuna to always perform his duty without attachment, because acting this way leads to the supreme.

en/3-18-body-47435852.mp3.text: For the perfected person, no purpose remains in doing, and no purpose remains in not doing. No being in the world is a source of personal gain. Listen to the paired words कृतेन and अकृतेन, doing and not doing. For the completed person, neither action nor inaction brings any personal purpose. Krishna then tells Arjuna that he must still perform his duty, but without attachment.

en/3-18-intro-5967fcfe.mp3.text: Krishna describes the person who has reached inner completeness. Listen to how this state changes everything about action and gain.

en/3-18-intro-f356762d.mp3.text: Picture a person who needs nothing. Krishna says that for such a one, acting and resting are the same. Listen for who this person is.

en/3-19-body-798ee14a.mp3.text: Therefore, always perform your duty without attachment; by acting without attachment, a person reaches the supreme. Listen to the word asaktah, without attachment. Krishna places this condition on every duty, and by doing so he makes freedom from clinging the very path to the supreme. Janaka and others attained perfection through action itself, and you should act too.

en/3-19-intro-e403ecb2.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the person who needs nothing. Now he turns that into practice, telling Arjuna to act steadily. Listen for the single condition he places on every action.

en/3-2-body-055e71d8.mp3.text: Arjuna says: Your words seem mixed and confusing to me. Tell me one thing clearly, so I may find the highest good. Arjuna tells Krishna his words feel mixed and asks for one clear teaching. Krishna answers by naming two paths already taught in this world, one for the contemplative and one for the active.

en/3-2-body-6d2e1636.mp3.text: Arjuna says: Your words seem mixed and confusing to me. Tell me one thing clearly, so I may find the highest good. Arjuna says your words confuse my understanding not by their nature, but because my own mind is entangled. He asks for one teaching not as a student, but as a man demanding a single way out. Krishna answers by telling Arjuna that he has already taught two paths, the path of knowledge and the path of action.

en/3-2-intro-c41645a7.mp3.text: Arjuna has already collapsed in despair. Now he pushes Krishna with a direct demand: tell me one clear path that leads to the highest good.

en/3-2-intro-ebfda2dd.mp3.text: Arjuna admits he is stuck. He asks Krishna to cut through the noise and give him one clear instruction that leads to the highest good.

en/3-20-body-96bfb33b.mp3.text: Janaka and others attained perfection through action itself. You should act too, while keeping the welfare of the world in view. The verse names Janaka and others, janakaadayah, meaning Janaka and the rest. These are the great kings and sages who proved that perfection comes through action. Krishna reminds Arjuna that he must act for the welfare of the world, lokasangraha, just as great figures have done.

en/3-20-intro-0b6e099c.mp3.text: Krishna turns from private hesitation to public duty. Listen to how he names the great figures who proved action leads to perfection.

en/3-21-body-01f281cb.mp3.text: Whatever the best person does, others follow. Whatever standard they set, the world copies. The verse states that whatever the best person does, others copy. It also shows that the world follows the standard set by that person. Krishna then tells Arjuna that he has nothing to gain yet remains engaged in action.

en/3-21-body-39b1c6db.mp3.text: Whatever the best person does, others follow. Whatever standard they set, the world copies. The word shreshtha, the best, is the key here. It is not about being the strongest, but about being the most respected, and your example becomes the standard that everyone else copies. Krishna then asks Partha how the world would be led if he, the best, were to stop working.

en/3-21-intro-010c7f6a.mp3.text: Krishna explains that a leader's actions become a model for everyone else. Listen for the exact words of the standard that the world copies.

en/3-21-intro-a6563b42.mp3.text: Krishna continues by explaining why Arjuna must act, reminding him that his conduct is watched by the world.

en/3-22-body-03f3195f.mp3.text: O Partha, there is nothing in the three worlds that I must do, and nothing I have not yet gained that must be gained. Yet I remain engaged in action. He says he has no duty left in the three worlds and no desire left to fulfill, yet he still engages in action. This shows that action does not need a personal reward to be right. He then warns that if he stops acting, the whole world will copy that laziness.

en/3-22-intro-60ae76c5.mp3.text: Why does Krishna keep fighting if he needs nothing? This verse answers that question by naming his very own reason for acting.

en/3-23-body-0debba72.mp3.text: For if I ever stopped acting with care, people would follow my path in every way, Arjuna. Here he says that if he ever stopped working, people would copy that inaction, and he would be the cause of disorder. He then explains that if he stopped, the whole world would fall into ruin.

en/3-23-intro-ee4e7751.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that he works with care because everyone watches him. Listen for the warning hidden inside that reason.

en/3-24-body-4f9f80b7.mp3.text: If I did not act, these worlds would fall into ruin. I would create disorder and destroy these people. This verse uses the word sankarasy, of mixed confusion. Krishna says his own inaction would create this same social disorder that Arjuna feared, proving that action is the only way to prevent collapse. Krishna now says the wise should act like the ignorant, but without attachment, to set an example for the world.

en/3-24-intro-221ba22f.mp3.text: Krishna says his own inaction would ruin the worlds. Listen for the word that names this ruin.

en/3-25-body-6cfa715a.mp3.text: As the ignorant act with attachment to action, so should the wise act without attachment, seeking the welfare of the world. The word asaktah, without attachment, is the key here. The wise must act with the same energy as the ignorant, but stripped of personal clinging. Krishna then warns the wise not to unsettle the minds of those still attached to action.

en/3-25-intro-fe8fff2d.mp3.text: Krishna now turns from his own example to the duty of the wise. Listen for the rule he sets for how they should act.

en/3-26-body-17a504f4.mp3.text: An awakened person should not unsettle the minds of those attached to action. Instead, acting skillfully, such a person should engage them in all work. An awakened person should leave others' faith in action intact and lead by working well. Krishna then explains that all actions are driven by the qualities of nature.

en/3-26-intro-6fb1e55d.mp3.text: Krishna continues his teaching on how a wise person should behave in society.

en/3-27-body-0a543955.mp3.text: All actions are carried out in every way by the qualities of nature. Deluded by ego, a person thinks, 'I am the doer.' The verse reveals a split between the doer and the deed. The qualities of nature act upon the qualities of nature, yet the ego, deluded by itself, insists upon the claim, 'I am the doer.' Krishna then explains that this false ownership is what binds a person to the results of their work.

en/3-27-intro-a9d145d2.mp3.text: Krishna asks what truly drives action, and points to the ego that claims ownership over work performed by nature.

en/3-28-body-6705c33f.mp3.text: The one who truly understands the division of qualities and actions does not cling, seeing that qualities act upon qualities. Krishna points to one truth, guna acting on guna. The wise person sees that the gunas are moving the gunas, and with that sight, the ego who claims to be the doer simply vanishes. Next, Krishna shows what happens when a person forgets this truth and clings to the ego of doing.

en/3-28-intro-25020bec.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from action to awareness, showing the wise person how to stand apart. Listen to how he names the true actor.

en/3-29-body-cdaefbc7.mp3.text: The ignorant, deluded by the qualities of nature, cling to actions born of those qualities. The wise should not unsettle those who do not yet understand fully. Krishna uses kritsnavit, the one who knows fully, to describe a wise person, and then commands them not to unsettle the dull-minded. The wise should not disturb those who do not yet understand fully. Krishna then turns to the knower's own duty, asking them to surrender all action to him and fight without attachment.

en/3-29-intro-6220e505.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna to listen for the word kritsnavit, the one who knows fully, and to hear what this knower is told not to do to the ignorant.

en/3-3-body-0113986b.mp3.text: The divine says: In this world, I have already taught two kinds of steadfast practice: the path of knowledge for the contemplative, and the path of action for the active. Krishna names two temperaments, the contemplative knowers and the active yogis, and assigns each its own path, knowledge and action, before the teaching has even begun. He then warns that simply avoiding action does not lead to freedom.

en/3-3-body-43bae770.mp3.text: The divine says: In this world, I have already taught two kinds of steadfast practice: the path of knowledge for the contemplative, and the path of action for the active. Krishna addresses Arjuna as अनघ, sinless one. This marks him as a pure seeker ready to hear the distinction between the two paths. Krishna now explains why neither avoiding action nor renouncing it alone is enough.

en/3-3-intro-24badb3d.mp3.text: Krishna begins his reply by telling Arjuna that human beings differ in make-up, and that two valid paths already exist.

en/3-3-intro-c47219c3.mp3.text: Krishna answers Arjuna's plea for clarity by naming two paths. One is for the contemplative knowers, the other for the active yogis.

en/3-30-body-e239e1a1.mp3.text: Surrender all actions to me with the disciplined mind. Free from desire, possessiveness, and sorrow, fight. Surrender every action to Krishna, drop desire and 'mine', and fight without fever, he tells Arjuna. Krishna names the exact state that must be present before the battle: free from desire, free from possessiveness, and free from distress.

en/3-30-intro-526f12eb.mp3.text: Krishna offers a path to act without inner collapse. Listen to how he tells Arjuna to surrender every action inward.

en/3-31-body-21e5eb88.mp3.text: Those who always follow this teaching of Mine with trust and without fault-finding are freed from the bonds of action. Notice the word anusuyantah, without fault-finding. The teaching does not free the one who watches for flaws; it frees the one who simply accepts and follows. Krishna immediately warns that those who do find fault are lost, turning the teaching into a clear choice.

en/3-31-intro-1571ecb5.mp3.text: Krishna carries forward the promise of freedom, now naming the exact inner state required to break the chains of karma.

en/3-32-body-957b204d.mp3.text: But those who, finding fault with this teaching, do not follow it, know them to be deluded in all knowledge and ruined in understanding. The word is abhyasuyantah, finding fault. It is the closed mind that refuses to listen and instead looks for flaws, leaving the person lost in every kind of knowledge. Krishna then turns to the wise, explaining that even they act according to their own nature, making restraint impossible to force.

en/3-32-intro-d9ad1877.mp3.text: Why does Krishna warn that rejecting his teaching leads to ruin? Listen to the exact state he assigns to those who refuse it.

en/3-33-body-73d8c08f.mp3.text: Even the wise act according to their own nature. All beings follow nature; what can restraint do? Even the wise, the ones who know the truth, still act from their own nature. Krishna admits that force and suppression cannot change this deep-rooted pattern. He then names the two forces that control the senses, attachment and aversion. He calls them your enemies. Listen to how he describes them.

en/3-33-intro-428bb741.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from blaming Arjuna to describing human nature. Listen for the single word that surprises him.

en/3-34-body-6e2e0cc5.mp3.text: Attachment and aversion sit in every sense-object. Do not come under their power, for they are your enemies on the path. Listen for the word paripanthinau, the two enemies on the path. Attachment and aversion sit established in every sense-object, and Krishna calls them the two enemies on the path. Krishna then says that even the wise act according to their own nature, and asks where a person should focus their effort.

en/3-34-body-ac7f774a.mp3.text: Attachment and aversion sit in every sense-object. Do not come under their power, for they are your enemies on the path. Krishna calls them enemies, परिपन्थिनौ, the two who lie in wait on the path. They do not stand outside you; they sit established in every object your senses meet. He now turns from this inner struggle to the choice of duty, saying one's own duty is better than another's.

en/3-34-intro-21f6bd0f.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna to watch the inner reactions that follow every sense experience. Listen for the two forces he names.

en/3-34-intro-b53d43f5.mp3.text: Krishna warns Arjuna that two enemies are already waiting in every object he touches. Listen for the exact names of these two forces.

en/3-35-body-f6fb8d8a.mp3.text: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than another's duty well performed. Better death in one's own duty; another's duty is dangerous. Listen to one word, svadharmah, one's own duty. Krishna ranks your own role, done imperfectly, above someone else's role done well. Krishna now warns Arjuna against the peril of adopting another's path, no matter how perfect it looks.

en/3-35-intro-4d69f470.mp3.text: Krishna speaks to Arjuna, who is frozen between his warrior role and his fear of killing relatives. Listen for the logic Krishna uses to pull him back to his own role.

en/3-36-body-e6939c3a.mp3.text: Arjuna says: O descendant of the Vrishni clan, what drives a person to commit wrongdoing, even unwillingly, as if forced? The word bhavitavya means appointed, and Arjuna uses it to describe himself. He is saying he feels like a puppet, driven by some outside force to do wrong, even though he does not want to. Krishna answers by naming desire as the force that drives a person into anger and destruction.

en/3-36-intro-89c9fbb3.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna to do his own duty, so Arjuna pushes back, asking what power moves a person against their own will.

en/3-37-body-26bc22bf.mp3.text: Krishna says: Desire, born of rajas, turns into anger. It is all-consuming and deeply destructive. Know it as your enemy here. Notice the word kamah, desire. The Lord presents it as the force that turns into krodha, anger, and warns Arjuna to recognize this single enemy within himself. Krishna then shows how this desire covers clear seeing like smoke covers a fire.

en/3-37-intro-008b644e.mp3.text: Arjuna asked why a person commits sin even unwillingly. Krishna answers with one word: what is that force? Listen for it.

en/3-38-body-c800a81f.mp3.text: As fire is covered by smoke, a mirror by dust, and a womb by a membrane, so clear seeing is covered by desire. The verse lists three objects that are covered, and the word avrtam, covered, appears twice. The first covering is smoke over fire, the second is dust on a mirror, and the third is a membrane over a womb. Krishna moves from the covering to the covering agent, calling desire the eternal enemy of the wise.

en/3-38-intro-dbfc4055.mp3.text: Krishna compares the way desire hides wisdom to three everyday coverings. Listen for how the third object is paired with its cover.

en/3-39-body-e1d3310b.mp3.text: O son of Kunti, wisdom is covered by this desire, the eternal enemy of the wise, as fire is never satisfied. Krishna names desire the eternal enemy of the wise. He calls it a fire that can never be satisfied. He then shows exactly where this fire lives, inside the senses and the mind.

en/3-39-intro-fcc7bda6.mp3.text: Krishna points to one force that hides wisdom. Listen for the image of a fire that never says enough.

en/3-4-body-6554672b.mp3.text: A person does not reach actionless freedom by avoiding action, nor by renouncing action alone does one reach perfection. Avoiding action does not bring freedom, Krishna says, and renouncing alone does not bring the highest state. Krishna then explains that no one can stay still even for a moment, because nature itself drives everyone to act.

en/3-4-intro-962f9d24.mp3.text: Krishna is correcting a false choice. Listen for the word san-nyasanat, renunciation, and hear why simply giving things up is not the answer.

en/3-40-body-3f70a435.mp3.text: The senses, the mind, and the discerning mind are said to be its seat. Through them, it deludes the embodied person by veiling understanding. Krishna names three instruments, the senses, the mind, and the discerning mind, as the seat of desire. All three together form the base through which knowledge is veiled and the embodied person is deluded. Krishna now tells Arjuna to first control the senses and then destroy this great sinner.

en/3-40-intro-133da85c.mp3.text: Krishna is tracing the enemy inside the human system. Listen to the exact instruments desire uses to cloud a person's judgment.

en/3-41-body-4cf33a05.mp3.text: Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, first control the senses, and then destroy this great sinner, the destroyer of knowledge and wisdom. Notice the word adau, first. Krishna does not ask Arjuna to strike down desire immediately. He sets a clear order. First restrain the senses, because they are the gateway through which desire enters and clouds judgment. Senses are only the first line of defense, for the mind and the discerning mind sit even higher.

en/3-41-intro-e21fcdbe.mp3.text: Krishna has just described desire as the force that blinds judgment from within. Now he gives the first practical step to fight it.

en/3-42-body-4db56140.mp3.text: The senses are higher than the body; the mind is higher than the senses; the discerning mind is higher than the mind. And beyond the discerning mind is the self. The word parah means higher than the one below, and Krishna builds a ladder with it. The senses are higher than the body, the mind is higher than the senses, the discerning mind is higher than the mind, and the self is higher than the discerning mind. Krishna now tells Arjuna to use this knowledge to steady the self and destroy desire.

en/3-42-intro-fcda465a.mp3.text: Krishna asks which enemy is hardest to conquer, and answers by mapping the inner layers. Listen for the ladder that leads upward.

en/3-43-body-56ad209a.mp3.text: Thus, knowing the higher beyond the intellect, steady the lower self by the higher self, and destroy that enemy in the form of desire, which is hard to conquer. He calls desire an enemy, दुरासदम्, hard to conquer. It is the same force that drove the war, and now Krishna tells Arjuna to slay it from within. Krishna now turns to the chain of this knowledge, passing it down through the ages to Manu and Ikshvaku.

en/3-43-body-aed0c458.mp3.text: Thus, knowing the higher beyond the intellect, steady the lower self by the higher self, and destroy that enemy in the form of desire, which is hard to conquer. Krishna commands Arjuna to steady the lower self, atmanam, with the higher self, atmana. The battle is not won by fighting the senses but by letting the deeper self hold the reins. Krishna now turns to the lineage of this teaching, passing the imperishable knowledge down from Vivasvan to Manu.

en/3-43-intro-f84767d3.mp3.text: Krishna maps the inner battlefield from senses to mind to intellect. Listen for the moment he names the real enemy.

en/3-43-intro-fc650fd2.mp3.text: Krishna has mapped the inner chain from senses to mind to intellect, and now names the real enemy. Listen for the target of his final command.

en/3-5-body-e99b5b1d.mp3.text: No one can remain without action even for a moment. Everyone is driven to act by the qualities born of nature. Notice the word avashah, helpless. No one is in charge of their own stillness. Even when a person sits perfectly still, the qualities of nature move them from the inside. Krishna then moves from the impossibility of inaction to the danger of pretending to act while only thinking of results.

en/3-6-body-6c273421.mp3.text: One who restrains the organs of action but keeps thinking of sense objects in the mind is deluded and called a hypocrite. Krishna calls such a person a mithyachari, a false actor, because he restrains his organs of action but keeps his mind feasting on sense objects. Krishna then points to the true path, where a person truly restrains the senses and begins action without attachment.

en/3-6-intro-a6680961.mp3.text: Krishna rejects the idea that stopping your hands is enough. Listen to the word he uses for the person who pretends.

en/3-7-body-f4778bcd.mp3.text: Arjuna, the one who restrains the senses with the mind and begins karma yoga without attachment is श्रेष्ठ. Krishna praises the one who reins in the senses with the mind and works without attachment. Krishna then states that even the body cannot be kept alive by pure inaction, so action is unavoidable.

en/3-7-intro-cb52c401.mp3.text: How does a person act in the world without drowning in desire? Listen to Krishna's answer about where true control begins.

en/3-8-body-1df62c33.mp3.text: Do the duty prescribed for you. Action is better than inaction, and even your body cannot be sustained by inaction. Listen to one word: अकर्मणः, inaction. Krishna does not ask Arjuna to invent a new path; he says even keeping the body alive requires action. Krishna then explains that actions done for sacrifice free a person, while actions for personal gain bind them.

en/3-8-body-d0c55fae.mp3.text: Do the duty prescribed for you. Action is better than inaction, and even your body cannot be sustained by inaction. Listen to the word akarma, inaction. Krishna says that even keeping the body alive is not possible through inaction, turning the argument from ethics into biology. He then explains that the only difference is whether actions are done for sacrifice or for personal gain.

en/3-8-intro-45180460.mp3.text: Krishna answers the paralysis directly: do the duty that is already yours. Listen for how he turns the argument from fear into action.

en/3-8-intro-c5a203de.mp3.text: Krishna turns the argument from fear into motion. Listen for the practical reason he gives for why action is unavoidable.

en/3-9-body-088621f0.mp3.text: Actions done for sacrifice free a person; actions done for personal gain bind. Therefore, Arjuna, do your duty without attachment for that purpose alone. The word karmabandhanah means bound by action. The world is bound by action not because we work, but because we work for ourselves. Krishna then explains that this was the original law, set at the beginning of time by Prajapati.

en/3-9-intro-ac4f38dc.mp3.text: Krishna points to the motive behind your work. Listen closely to the word that names the trap we fall into.

en/4-1-body-fba7042c.mp3.text: The Lord says: I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvan. Vivasvan taught it to Manu, and Manu taught it to Ikshvaku. Notice the word avyayam, imperishable. Krishna calls this yoga imperishable because it has survived across ages, even though it was lost and is now being restored to Arjuna. Krishna continues by explaining that this imperishable teaching was passed down through royal sages before being lost to time.

en/4-1-intro-ed6151b1.mp3.text: After teaching the path of action, Krishna now turns to an ancient inheritance. Listen to the chain of teachers he names.

en/4-10-body-1cd2b034.mp3.text: Many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, free from attachment, fear, and anger, absorbed in Me and taking refuge in Me, have attained My being. Listen for jnanatapasa, the austerity of knowledge. It is not a physical penance but the steady discipline of wisdom that burns away impurity and leads to the divine. Krishna now states that he responds directly to the way people approach him, so every path leads back to him.

en/4-10-intro-d617e062.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from his divine birth to the inner state of those who reach him. Listen for the austerity that purifies the mind.

en/4-11-body-31ce5202.mp3.text: As people approach Me, so I respond to them. All people follow My path in every way, O Arjuna. Listen to the verb bhajami, meaning I favor or respond to. It shows that the divine is not a distant judge but an active presence that meets every seeker according to their own approach. Krishna now explains why people who want quick results worship radiant beings instead of him.

en/4-11-intro-d07a4a58.mp3.text: Krishna has just described how purified seekers take refuge in him. Now he explains how he responds to anyone who approaches, and how every person is already following his path.

en/4-12-body-371d95f3.mp3.text: People who want quick success worship radiant beings, because results from action come quickly in the human world. The word kanksantah, desiring, reveals the restless pull of the mind. People do not worship the devas because they are wise; they do so because they want fast results, and in the human world action can indeed produce quick fruit. Krishna now turns to the very origin of these divisions and the social orders that bind them together.

en/4-12-intro-0cc27aa2.mp3.text: Krishna carries on from his teaching that all paths lead to Him, and now He shows why people still look elsewhere for quick fixes.

en/4-13-body-baead92a.mp3.text: The four social orders were created by Me according to qualities and actions. Though I am their maker, know Me as the unchanging non-doer. The strongest tension is in two words, कर्तारम् and अकर्तारम्. Krishna is the maker, yet also the non-maker, and he is unchanging. Krishna now explains that he does not crave the fruits of these actions.

en/4-13-body-f8eb0131.mp3.text: The four social orders were created by Me according to qualities and actions. Though I am their maker, know Me as the unchanging non-doer. Here is the core paradox: Krishna says he is the maker of the four orders, yet he asks Arjuna to know him as the changeless non-doer. The creator of the system is not trapped inside it. Krishna then adds that actions do not stain him, because he has no craving for their fruits. One who knows this is not bound.

en/4-13-intro-0e6788c2.mp3.text: If social order comes from the Divine, why does it create division? This verse answers that question directly.

en/4-13-intro-fb927bbe.mp3.text: Krishna answers why the world is divided into roles by revealing that even the maker of those roles remains untouched by them. Listen for that paradox.

en/4-14-body-759c1879.mp3.text: Actions do not stain me, and I do not crave their fruits. One who knows me this way is not bound by actions. Actions do not stain Krishna because he has no craving for their fruit, and knowing this frees you. He shows that even ancient seekers of freedom acted this way, so you must do your duty.

en/4-14-intro-675b211a.mp3.text: Krishna explains why he remains untouched by action. Listen to how he separates the work from the hunger for results.

en/4-15-body-bcd156bb.mp3.text: Even seekers of freedom acted after knowing this. Therefore, do the work that your ancestors always did. purumukshubhi means seekers of freedom, and Krishna names them to show that even those who seek freedom still do their work. Krishna now promises to explain the very nature of action and inaction.

en/4-15-body-d97fe6cc.mp3.text: Even seekers of freedom acted after knowing this. Therefore, do the work that your ancestors always did. Listen to the word मुमुक्षुभिः, seekers of freedom. These are not ordinary people, but those who already knew the truth of action and still chose to act, setting the standard for Arjuna. Krishna then asks what is action and what is inaction, and promises to explain it clearly to free Arjuna from harm.

en/4-15-intro-ab102186.mp3.text: Krishna wants Arjuna to hear one specific kind of person who already knew this and still worked. Listen for who they are.

en/4-15-intro-c227886e.mp3.text: Listen for a word that shows even those seeking freedom still did their work.

en/4-16-body-12801ab4.mp3.text: What is action, and what is inaction? Even the wise are confused here. I will explain that action to you, knowing which you will be freed from what is harmful. The verse begins by naming kavayo, the wise, and stating that even they are mohita, deluded. Krishna does not hide the difficulty, but names it fully before offering the way out. Krishna now names action, forbidden action, and inaction to show that all three must be understood. Listen closely.

en/4-16-intro-61b37a38.mp3.text: Krishna has just said that the wise are confused. Now he names the very problem that traps them, to show Arjuna that he alone has the answer.

en/4-17-body-2b93d9a7.mp3.text: Action, forbidden action, and inaction must all be understood, because the movement of action is hard to grasp. Krishna repeats the word बोद्धव्यम्, must be understood, three times, for action, forbidden action and inaction. He does not tell Arjuna to choose between them, but to sort them out, because the way action works is deep. Krishna now tells Arjuna that the wise person sees action inside inaction, and inaction inside action.

en/4-17-body-e4218707.mp3.text: Action, forbidden action, and inaction must all be understood, because the movement of action is hard to grasp. Krishna names three things Arjuna must sort out: action, forbidden action and inaction, because karma moves in hidden ways. Krishna then shows the wise person who can see action within inaction and inaction within action.

en/4-17-intro-1a93e4e7.mp3.text: Krishna returns to the confusion about action and inaction, and adds a third term to the problem. Listen for the hidden nature of karma.

en/4-17-intro-a2c0a119.mp3.text: Krishna continues from his previous warning that even the wise are confused about action. Listen for how he names the three things Arjuna must sort out.

en/4-18-body-48f01e21.mp3.text: One who sees action in inaction, and inaction in action, is wise among people; that person is disciplined and complete in action. The verse names one who sees action in inaction. That seer is called yuktah, disciplined and united, which means inner discipline is not the opposite of action, but the very mark of a wise person. Krishna next names the person who acts without desire, whose deeds are burned by the fire of knowledge.

en/4-18-intro-1f3d680e.mp3.text: How can a person act without being bound by the action? Listen for the secret Krishna reveals about what it means to truly act.

en/4-19-body-68e0fd14.mp3.text: The wise call that person learned whose actions begin without desire or personal planning, and whose deeds are burned by the fire of knowledge. The wise, बुधाः, are the ones who make this judgment. They look at a person whose undertakings begin free from personal desire and then call them learned. The next verse shows how such a person acts without attachment while fully engaged in the world.

en/4-19-body-e77cbda3.mp3.text: The wise call that person learned whose actions begin without desire or personal planning, and whose deeds are burned by the fire of knowledge. The verse gives us one exact image, the fire of knowledge burning up the person's deeds. This tells us that knowledge itself can consume the binding force of those deeds. Krishna then describes the one who has already dropped all craving and lives without dependence, even while acting.

en/4-19-intro-2ec54b19.mp3.text: Krishna now names the person the wise truly respect. Listen for how knowledge itself acts on their deeds.

en/4-19-intro-43b8967b.mp3.text: Krishna now tells Arjuna what the wise call a learned person, focusing on how actions begin.

en/4-2-body-4f9f1395.mp3.text: O scorcher of foes, this yoga was known by the royal sages through an unbroken lineage. In the course of great time, this yoga was lost in this world. Arjuna is called Parantapa, scorcher of foes, and with that single name Krishna reminds him of his warrior nature as he speaks of a yoga once passed down by royal sages. Krishna says that because Arjuna is his friend and devotee, this ancient yoga is now being taught to him today.

en/4-2-intro-4fa47f1a.mp3.text: Carry on from the line of kings, and listen to the word Krishna uses to call Arjuna.

en/4-20-body-89e6b59d.mp3.text: One who has abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, remains ever content, and depends on nothing, does nothing at all even while fully engaged in action. Listen to the phrase abhipravritto api, even while fully engaged. Krishna is describing a person who is completely active, yet because they are without attachment and inner contentment, they do not perform any binding action. Krishna then explains that the person who gives up all hope and possessions is free from fault even while doing bodily work.

en/4-20-intro-4312f3af.mp3.text: Krishna now points to a person who is busy with work but does not do anything. Listen to the word that makes this possible.

en/4-21-body-4a8692d8.mp3.text: One who has no hope, who has controlled the body and mind, and who has given up all possessions, does only bodily action and incurs no fault. Notice the word yatacittatma, one whose mind and inner being are controlled. This is a person whose mind is held in hand, so even ordinary bodily action leaves no trace of fault. Krishna adds that a person who is content with whatever comes, beyond opposites, is not bound even while acting.
