en/4-21-intro-ef5cfe1c.mp3.text: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to act without being stained, even when the body is busy. Listen for the one who is fully in control.

en/4-22-body-e02245d0.mp3.text: Content with whatever comes by itself, beyond opposites, free from envy, equal in success and failure, such a person is not bound even while acting. The word samah, equal, sits at the center. By staying equal in success and failure, a person stops the mind from tying itself to outcomes and stays free. Krishna then names the next quality, vimatsarah, freedom from envy, as the inner state that makes action clean.

en/4-22-intro-47b412d8.mp3.text: Krishna has just described a person who acts without hope of gain. Now he names the inner state that keeps a person unbound, even while doing work.

en/4-23-body-13f07ac0.mp3.text: For one who has given up attachment, is freed, and whose mind rests in knowledge, all action melts away when done only for sacrifice. The word pragliyate means melts away, and it shows that for a person free of attachment and established in knowledge, all action simply disappears instead of remaining as a burden. Krishna then says that the offering itself is Brahman, and the person who sees it this way becomes one with Brahman.

en/4-23-intro-c1450206.mp3.text: Krishna asks how to act without being trapped by the results, and here he gives a clear answer about what happens to a person's actions.

en/4-24-body-bc6892e7.mp3.text: In such sacrifice, the offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, and the act of offering into the fire of Brahman is Brahman. One whose action is absorbed in Brahman reaches Brahman alone. The verse names every part of the sacrifice, and every part is Brahman. The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, the fire is Brahman, and the one who offers is also Brahman. Krishna then shows two different paths of sacrifice that both lead to this same ultimate reality.

en/4-24-intro-309dbfa5.mp3.text: On the battlefield, Krishna explains how to act without losing sight of the ultimate reality. Listen to how he dissolves every part of the sacrifice back into Brahman.

en/4-25-body-e79bf237.mp3.text: Some yogis offer sacrifice to the divine alone. Others offer the self into the fire of Brahman through sacrifice itself. The word अपरे, others, appears twice. It marks two different yogis, showing that the path of yoga has more than one way to approach the absolute. Krishna now describes a third kind of offering, this time using the senses themselves as the sacrifice.

en/4-25-body-f8e34a30.mp3.text: Some yogis offer sacrifice to the divine alone. Others offer the self into the fire of Brahman through sacrifice itself. One word appears twice, yajna, sacrifice, binding both lines of action together. In the first line, the offering goes to the divine alone, while in the second, the offering is the self into the fire of Brahman. The next verse will describe yet another way yogis offer their senses into the fire of restraint.

en/4-25-intro-204d2870.mp3.text: Krishna is laying out two paths for the yogi. Listen for one word that names the people who walk each path.

en/4-25-intro-8dd2c095.mp3.text: Krishna is describing two paths of yoga. Listen for one word that appears twice, the word yajna, sacrifice.

en/4-26-body-1b369f08.mp3.text: Some yogis offer the senses into the fires of restraint. Others offer sound and the other sense-objects into the fires of the senses. Krishna uses the word others, anye, to mark a sharp turn. He is describing two different yogis and their two different fires. Sanjaya will now describe the army formations, beginning with Duryodhana's actions.

en/4-26-body-3480f6e9.mp3.text: Some yogis offer the senses into the fires of restraint. Others offer sound and the other sense-objects into the fires of the senses. The verb जुह्वति means to offer as a sacrifice. One group offers the senses into the fire of restraint. The other offers sound and sights into the fire of the senses, burning up craving through direct experience. Krishna then adds a third path, offering life-force and action into the fire of self-control.

en/4-26-intro-4e24ef78.mp3.text: Krishna explains to Arjuna how to train the mind using a Vedic fire sacrifice. Listen for the two different offerings.

en/4-26-intro-923331ed.mp3.text: Krishna has been describing different paths of sacrifice. Now he tells Arjuna about two inner methods of offering, showing that the goal is one even if the method differs.

en/4-27-body-3eddcc6c.mp3.text: Others offer all the activities of the senses and the life-force into the fire of self-control, lit by knowledge. Listen to the role of knowledge here. It is knowledge that kindles the fire of self-control, and into that flame they offer every activity of the senses and the life-force. Krishna then names the material offerings others make, from wealth to study, as a further form of sacrifice.

en/4-27-intro-21987600.mp3.text: Krishna has shown many ways to sacrifice. Now he speaks of a deeper fire. Listen for who offers what into it.

en/4-28-body-874e3a7a.mp3.text: Others offer wealth, austerity, yoga, and the study of sacred texts as sacrifice, while disciplined seekers make these offerings with firm vows. The verse lists four paths, wealth, austerity, yoga, and study, and it calls all of them yajnas. The key is not the offering itself, but that these are done by disciplined seekers with firm vows. Krishna then turns to the breath itself, showing how even the movement of air can become a sacrifice.

en/4-28-intro-1639713e.mp3.text: If sacrifice is not just ritual, what else can it be? Listen to how the text names four different offerings that people make.

en/4-29-body-48f4ed14.mp3.text: Some offer the outgoing breath into the incoming breath, and the incoming breath into the outgoing breath, restraining the movement of both through breath-control as their aim. Others, with regulated food, offer the breaths into the breaths. All of them know sacrifice and are cleansed by sacrifice. Krishna names breath-control itself as a form of sacrifice. He describes practitioners restraining the movements of the incoming and outgoing breaths and offering them into each other. He then adds regulated eating, showing that every disciplined act is a form of sacrifice.

en/4-29-intro-b5a718fc.mp3.text: Krishna shows that sacrifice is not only a fire ritual. Here he speaks of breath-control and disciplined eating.

en/4-3-body-c91e687e.mp3.text: Because you are my devotee and my friend, I have taught you today this ancient yoga. It is a supreme secret. Krishna shares this supreme secret only with Arjuna because they share the bond of a devotee and a close friend. That relationship makes the hidden knowledge possible. Arjuna now questions how an ancient teaching can come from a friend born recently.

en/4-3-intro-5dde42cb.mp3.text: Krishna has just claimed that this teaching is ancient. Now he tells Arjuna exactly why he is hearing it. Listen to the reason.

en/4-30-body-443e1337.mp3.text: Some offer the breath into the breath through regulated breathing; some, with regulated food, offer the life-forces into the life-forces. All of them know sacrifice, and sacrifice has washed away their impurities. Krishna names them yajnavidah, knowers of sacrifice. He does not limit the word to priests with fire; he means anyone whose breath or food is measured is already doing the rite. He then says those who eat the nectar left over from that sacrifice attain the eternal supreme reality.

en/4-30-intro-9a5b171e.mp3.text: Krishna is explaining that sacrifice is not just fire. He points to two specific practices. Listen for how he names the people who do them.

en/4-31-body-07886e8e.mp3.text: Those who partake of the nectar left over from sacrifice attain the eternal supreme reality. This world is not for the one who does not perform sacrifice; how then the next world? Krishna calls the remainder of sacrifice nectar, and says a life without sacrifice fails even in this world. Krishna says knowing these many kinds of sacrifice born of action frees you from the bondage of action.

en/4-31-intro-1f2eb4dc.mp3.text: Krishna has been showing Arjuna many ways to offer action into action. Now he names the one who receives the blessed remainder.

en/4-32-body-9f658417.mp3.text: In this way, many kinds of sacrifice are described in the sacred teaching. Know them all as born of action; knowing this, you will be freed from the bondage of action. Krishna gives Arjuna one single command, विद्धि, know. He tells him to see that every ritual, every offering, every sacrifice is born of action, and that recognition alone loosens the grip of karma. Krishna then tells Arjuna that the sacrifice of knowledge is higher than the sacrifice of material things.

en/4-32-body-badc5b89.mp3.text: In this way, many kinds of sacrifice are described in the sacred teaching. Know them all as born of action; knowing this, you will be freed from the bondage of action. The key is that every sacrifice is a karma. When Arjuna sees that even sacred ritual belongs to the realm of action, he stops clinging to the results of any ritual. Krishna now turns to the sacrifice of pure knowledge, declaring it greater than any material offering.

en/4-32-intro-95b20990.mp3.text: Krishna has shown many paths. Now he gathers them into one command. Listen for it.

en/4-32-intro-cf996f0b.mp3.text: Krishna gathers all the sacrifices he has taught and points to their common source.

en/4-33-body-2cd4584f.mp3.text: O Arjuna, knowledge-sacrifice is better than sacrifice made of material things. All action and all matter end in knowledge. The word is jnana yajna, knowledge-sacrifice, and it is declared better than any sacrifice made of material things. Every action and every object ends in that knowledge. Krishna explains exactly how a seeker approaches this knowledge, through prostration, questioning, and service.

en/4-33-body-ea26c9ca.mp3.text: O Arjuna, knowledge-sacrifice is better than sacrifice made of material things. All action and all matter end in knowledge. The verb ज्ञाने परिसमाप्यते means ends, and it ends every action. Every deed and every material thing finds its completion in knowledge alone. Krishna then says that this knowledge comes through prostration and sincere questioning.

en/4-33-intro-6278cb67.mp3.text: Krishna asks: if rituals with material goods are not the highest path, what is? Listen for the term that replaces them.

en/4-34-body-c20a4c86.mp3.text: Know that by prostration, by sincere questioning, and by service. The wise who see reality will teach you that knowledge. Krishna lists three ways to receive knowledge. He calls them prostration, sincere questioning, and service. This is how one approaches those who see reality. Krishna says that with this knowledge, you will see all beings first in yourself, and then in me.

en/4-34-intro-490581fd.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from giving knowledge to showing how it is received. Listen for the three steps that open the door to wisdom.

en/4-35-body-f1790781.mp3.text: Knowing which, you will not fall into confusion again. Through which, you will see all beings without remainder first in yourself, and then in me. Once this knowledge is gained, Arjuna will see all beings in himself and then in Krishna, without confusion. Krishna says that with the raft of knowledge you will cross all wrongdoing.

en/4-35-intro-652c0d94.mp3.text: Listen for a single word that marks a complete shift in how you see everything.

en/4-36-body-8e6cb868.mp3.text: Even if you are the worst of wrongdoers, you will cross all wrongdoing by the raft of knowledge alone. Krishna does not say the raft of knowledge washes away your wrongdoing. He says you cross over all wrongdoing by using that raft. The next verse shows that this fire of knowledge burns even action itself to ashes.

en/4-36-intro-a655aa55.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna that seeing the self in all beings removes all confusion. Now he goes further. Listen for the one thing that can save even the worst wrongdoer.

en/4-37-body-fb5c57dd.mp3.text: As a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes, Arjuna. The verse sets up one exact parallel, the blazing fire of knowledge and the blazing fire of the body. The first makes firewood into ash, and the second makes all actions into ash. Krishna declares that no other purifier in this world compares to this knowledge.

en/4-37-intro-d7f44150.mp3.text: Krishna carries on from his promise to Arjuna, offering one clear image of how knowledge works. Listen for the parallel.

en/4-38-body-25140bb2.mp3.text: No purifier compares to knowledge in this world. The one perfected in yoga finds that knowledge within the self in time. The word pavitram, purifying, is used here, and Krishna says no purifier equals knowledge. The yogi finds this truth inside the self, by oneself, in time. Krishna then names the exact qualities that let a person gain this knowledge and reach supreme peace.

en/4-38-intro-c3e39276.mp3.text: Arjuna has been told that knowledge burns action to ashes. Now listen to how Krishna says nothing else can wash a person clean like that knowledge.

en/4-39-body-a9998699.mp3.text: The person with trust, discipline, and controlled senses gains knowledge. Having gained knowledge, that person quickly reaches supreme peace. The word shraddhavan, full of trust, names the person who receives knowledge. This inner trust opens the door to knowledge, while lack of it closes it. Krishna now names the opposite type, the doubter who has no faith and is already lost.

en/4-39-intro-8d0ddf27.mp3.text: Krishna speaks from the battlefield about the one who receives knowledge. Listen to the three qualities that open the door.

en/4-4-body-dca98c12.mp3.text: Arjuna says: Your birth is recent, while the birth of the Sun is ancient. How am I to understand that you taught this yoga at the beginning of creation? Arjuna hears that the yoga was taught at the beginning of creation, yet he sees Krishna standing before him as a living charioteer, while the Sun is ancient. He asks how this can be. Krishna answers that many births have passed for both of them, and only he remembers them all.

en/4-4-intro-7fd9481e.mp3.text: Arjuna has heard Krishna call this yoga ancient and secret. Now Arjuna points to the gap between Krishna's youth and the Sun's age.

en/4-40-body-77f26496.mp3.text: The ignorant and faithless person who doubts is ruined. For the doubter, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. The word संशयात्मा, a doubting inner being, is repeated at the end of the verse. It shows that the one whose soul is split by doubt loses this world, the next, and happiness. Krishna next describes the person who has cut away these doubts and found the true self.

en/4-40-body-bc6d3678.mp3.text: The ignorant and faithless person who doubts is ruined. For the doubter, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. The word sankhyatma means a doubting inner being. Krishna says such a person is ruined. Then he repeats that this same person finds no world, no next world, and no happiness, showing that doubt empties a person from the inside out. Krishna then says that a person whose doubts are cut away by knowledge is not bound by action, and he names Arjuna once more.

en/4-40-intro-4a1221e6.mp3.text: Krishna names a single condition that destroys a person completely, from this life to the next. Listen for the word that traps the mind inside doubt.

en/4-40-intro-a5ba9248.mp3.text: Krishna points to a single inner state that destroys a person, a state you can hear named twice in this verse. Listen for it.

en/4-41-body-328631c2.mp3.text: O Dhananjaya, actions do not bind the one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts have been cut away by knowledge, and who abides in the true self. Notice how Krishna names Arjuna, Dhananjaya, the one who won wealth. He reminds him that he is the warrior who can stand free, because yoga has loosened his hold and knowledge has cut his doubt. Krishna now commands him to cut away the final doubt with the sword of knowledge and rise to fight.

en/4-41-intro-85620656.mp3.text: Krishna has spent the last few verses dismantling Arjuna's confusion. Now he gives the turning point: action still happens, but it no longer leaves a binding mark.

en/4-42-body-939ce6d2.mp3.text: Therefore, O Bharata, cut away this doubt in your heart, born of ignorance, with the sword of knowledge. Stand in yoga and rise up for battle. Sanjaya, the sword of knowledge, jnanasinA (with the sword of knowledge), is not a weapon for the body but a blade of clear understanding used to cut away the doubt, samshayam (doubt), that sits in the heart, hRtstham (situated in the heart). Arjuna still cannot choose, so he asks which path is truly better for him.

en/4-42-body-c4d6b83a.mp3.text: Therefore, O Bharata, cut away this doubt in your heart, born of ignorance, with the sword of knowledge. Stand in yoga and rise up for battle. Krishna tells Arjuna to take the sword of knowledge, which is the knowledge of the self, and cut the doubt sitting in his heart. Only after cutting it should he stand in yoga and rise up. Arjuna now asks which path is truly better for him: the renunciation of action or the yoga of action.

en/4-42-intro-04c84005.mp3.text: Krishna closes this teaching by naming the exact tool Arjuna must use to break free. Listen for it.

en/4-42-intro-0e7044cf.mp3.text: Krishna has just finished his teaching on the nature of action and the self, and now he gives one last command. Listen to how he tells Arjuna to act.

en/4-5-body-5f1fdd0b.mp3.text: Krishna says: Many births of yours and mine have passed, Arjuna. I know them all, but you do not, enemy-burner. Krishna and Arjuna have both lived many births; Krishna remembers them all, Arjuna does not. Krishna now explains how you can know this truth, even though you do not remember your own past.

en/4-5-body-f427a60e.mp3.text: Krishna says: Many births of yours and mine have passed, Arjuna. I know them all, but you do not, enemy-burner. The word is वेत्थ, know. Krishna says he knows all those births, but you do not. It is not a claim of magic; it is the difference between two memories of the same long road. Krishna now steps further back, saying that though he is the unborn lord, he still appears in the world by his own power.

en/4-5-intro-623dce1c.mp3.text: Krishna widens time to answer Arjuna. Listen for the word that names what Krishna knows and Arjuna does not.

en/4-5-intro-cea72a46.mp3.text: Krishna opens a vast frame. He says they have both crossed many births. Listen for the sharp difference between what he knows and what you know.

en/4-6-body-c8d694d2.mp3.text: Though unborn and imperishable, and though I am the lord of all beings, I manifest myself by controlling my own nature through my own power of appearance. Unborn and imperishable, Krishna still appears, taking form through his own power over nature. He explains that he appears whenever dharma declines and adharma rises.

en/4-6-intro-5605b406.mp3.text: Arjuna has asked how Krishna could have taught the sun at the dawn of time. The answer is that ordinary birth does not bind this speaker at all. Listen to how he describes his own power.

en/4-7-body-7d834234.mp3.text: Whenever there is a decline of dharma and a rise of adharma, I manifest myself. Listen to the word यदा यदा, meaning whenever. Krishna ties his own appearance to a fixed law of the world: whenever dharma declines, he must manifest himself. He follows this rule with a second verse explaining exactly what he does to restore the balance.

en/4-7-body-9ea6c3c3.mp3.text: Whenever there is a decline of dharma and a rise of adharma, I manifest myself. Whenever dharma declines and adharma rises, Krishna says, he manifests himself. He then names the precise purpose of this repeated appearance: to protect the good, destroy the wicked, and establish dharma.

en/4-7-intro-09d1174a.mp3.text: Krishna has just explained his eternal nature, and now he turns to the moment he steps into history. Listen for the condition that brings him down.

en/4-7-intro-a72a72e7.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna he is unborn and knows all births. Now he explains exactly when he enters the world.

en/4-8-body-26c2aa1f.mp3.text: For the protection of the righteous, for the destruction of wrongdoers, and for the establishment of dharma, I appear age after age. Krishna comes age after age to protect the good, destroy wrongdoers and re-establish dharma. Krishna then tells Arjuna that understanding this cycle of appearing and acting in the world is the key to liberation.

en/4-8-intro-658619f1.mp3.text: Krishna has just said he appears when dharma declines. Now he tells Arjuna the exact purpose behind that appearing. Listen for the three tasks that drive his descent.

en/4-9-body-42013430.mp3.text: Arjuna, my birth and action are divine. One who truly understands this does not take birth again after leaving the body, but comes to me. The word divyam means divine. Krishna is saying that his birth and his actions are not bound by the laws of nature, and knowing this truth is what frees a person. Many purified beings have already reached this state by taking refuge in him. Listen to how they did it.

en/4-9-intro-8953044d.mp3.text: Krishna speaks of his own birth and action as something beyond the ordinary. Listen to how he links this knowledge to a person's fate.

en/5-1-body-9fd287c1.mp3.text: Arjuna says: Krishna, you praise both renunciation of action and yoga of action. Tell me clearly which one is definitely better for my welfare. Arjuna points out that Krishna praises both renunciation and action, and asks him to choose one path that is clearly better for his welfare. Krishna replies that both paths lead to the highest good, but acting with discipline is better than renouncing action.

en/5-1-intro-24356ba7.mp3.text: Krishna has spoken at length about acting and renouncing, and Arjuna now asks him to stop praising both. He wants to know which single path is truly better.

en/5-10-body-c6c7622b.mp3.text: One who offers actions to Brahman, renounces attachment, and acts is not stained by wrongdoing, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water. The word tyaktva, having abandoned, is the key. It is not the act that binds, but the attachment to the result. By leaving that behind, a person acts in the world like a lotus leaf in water, and remains unstained. Krishna then explains that this inner purification is the true purpose of performing action with the body and mind.

en/5-11-body-d3a318b4.mp3.text: Yogis perform action with body, mind, intellect, and the senses, giving up attachment, only for inner purification. The word tyaktva means having given up, and it is the turning point of the verse. The yogi performs action with body, mind, intellect, and senses, yet the one thing dropped is attachment. Krishna then explains what happens when this letting go is done, and what happens when it is not.

en/5-11-intro-aba9c582.mp3.text: Picture a practitioner who keeps working but stays untouched by the outcome. This verse lists every part of a person that acts, and the one thing that is left behind.

en/5-12-body-82628605.mp3.text: The disciplined one gives up the fruit of action and attains steady peace. The undisciplined one, clinging to results through desire, becomes bound. The word tyaktva, having given up, stands between the fruit of action and steady peace. This single word marks the shift from craving to release. Krishna now turns to the one who has not given up, showing how desire becomes the chain that binds.

en/5-12-intro-4609678d.mp3.text: Listen for the word tyaktva, having given up. Notice how Krishna places it right before the peace that follows.

en/5-13-body-5d44fd8f.mp3.text: The embodied one, who has mastered the senses and mind, dwells happily in the city of nine gates, mentally renouncing all actions, neither doing nor causing action. Krishna calls the body a city with nine gates. Inside that city, the self-mastered one dwells happily by letting go of all actions in the mind, never acting and never causing others to act. Krishna then explains that nature alone performs all actions, leaving the self free from doership.

en/5-13-body-bb42d01b.mp3.text: The embodied one, who has mastered the senses and mind, dwells happily in the city of nine gates, mentally renouncing all actions, neither doing nor causing action. The word पुरे means city. Krishna calls the body a city of nine gates, a place where the self-mastered dweller lives happily even while letting go of all action in the mind. Krishna now reveals that the supreme being creates no link between action and result, and it is nature alone that keeps moving.

en/5-13-intro-069f016b.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna that the disciplined find peace while the undisciplined are bound to results. Now he describes the inner state of that peaceful person.

en/5-13-intro-131544e3.mp3.text: Krishna has been teaching Arjuna about action without attachment, and now he points to a deeper state. Listen to how he describes the self-mastered person's inner stillness.

en/5-14-body-6b0b724c.mp3.text: The supreme being creates neither doership nor actions nor the link between action and result for people. Nature alone keeps moving. The key actor here is svabhava, nature. While the Lord creates no doer, no action, and no binding result, nature alone keeps moving forward on its own. Krishna then explains that the all-pervading Lord takes neither wrongdoing nor good deeds, and that knowledge is covered by ignorance.

en/5-14-intro-429a3efa.mp3.text: Krishna carries on from the idea of mental renunciation by explaining what the supreme being actually creates.

en/5-15-body-46092f8c.mp3.text: The all-pervading one takes neither anyone's wrongdoing nor anyone's good deed. Knowledge is covered by ignorance, and that is why living beings are deluded. Notice the word jantavah, living beings. It places the blame for confusion not on the divine taking away their deeds, but on their own limited state of being. Krishna then shows how destroying that ignorance through knowledge reveals the supreme truth.

en/5-15-intro-62a2a0b7.mp3.text: Arjuna feels crushed by the weight of his own actions on the battlefield. What is the divine's true role in all of this? Listen to how Krishna answers.

en/5-16-body-93cb6310.mp3.text: But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the true self, that knowledge reveals the supreme reality like the sun. Notice the word 'but', तु. It marks a sharp turn from the previous verse, where knowledge was said to be covered, to this one, where knowledge destroys that very covering. Those who fix their minds on the supreme reality reach a state of no return, their impurities washed away.

en/5-16-body-c0206ded.mp3.text: But for those whose ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the true self, that knowledge reveals the supreme reality like the sun. The word is Adityavat, like the sun. Just as sunlight instantly removes darkness without effort, knowledge of the Atman reveals the supreme reality the moment ignorance is gone. Krishna now says that those who are fully devoted to that reality reach a state of no return.

en/5-16-intro-1332338f.mp3.text: Krishna contrasts the darkness of ignorance with the clarity of knowledge. Listen to how the text describes the moment of revelation.

en/5-16-intro-a7f54a99.mp3.text: Krishna is describing what happens when a person truly understands. Listen for the image he uses to show this.

en/5-17-body-98a54648.mp3.text: Those whose intellect is fixed in That, whose mind is That, who are established in That, and who are devoted to That, go to the state of no return, their impurities washed away by knowledge. That single word is tad, That, and it appears four times in this verse. It binds the intellect, the mind, the footing, and the devotion into one single focus on the supreme. Krishna then broadens this vision to show how the wise see that same reality in every living being.

en/5-17-intro-068c26e1.mp3.text: Krishna is drawing a line between knowing the truth and living it. Listen for the single word that returns four times, binding the mind and intellect together.

en/5-18-body-860e1ff1.mp3.text: The wise see the same reality in a learned, humble brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste. Listen to the word samadarshinah, equal-seeing. The wise do not rank beings. They see the same single reality in a learned brahmin and in an outcaste, in a dog and in an elephant. Krishna explains that those who rest in this sameness conquer rebirth here itself, because the supreme reality is flawless and equal.

en/5-18-intro-9379210c.mp3.text: Krishna has just described a mind fixed in the supreme reality. Now he shows what that mind looks like in practice, as it looks past every social label.

en/5-19-body-02d1b0b9.mp3.text: Those whose mind rests in sameness conquer rebirth here itself. The supreme reality is flawless and equal, so they are established in it. Those whose minds rest in sameness have conquered rebirth here, Krishna says, because Brahman itself is flawless and even. The next verse describes the person who does not rejoice at the pleasant nor shrink from the unpleasant.

en/5-19-body-c2d5d8bc.mp3.text: Those whose mind rests in sameness conquer rebirth here itself. The supreme reality is flawless and equal, so they are established in it. Those whose minds rest in sameness have conquered rebirth here, Krishna says, because Brahman itself is flawless and even. Krishna now shows the outward sign of this inner steadiness, the lack of reaction to what feels good or bad.

en/5-19-intro-3fc5671b.mp3.text: Krishna continues, raising the standard from the wise person's sight to the steady mind. Listen for where this victory actually takes place.

en/5-19-intro-8c4523c4.mp3.text: Krishna now draws the line between seeing sameness and living it. Listen for the exact moment of conquest.

en/5-2-body-cecfb49c.mp3.text: Renunciation and karma yoga both lead to the highest good, but karma yoga is better than renouncing action. The word is visishyate, which means is superior. Krishna first says both paths bring the highest good, and then he adds that karma yoga is superior to renunciation of action. Krishna then describes the person who is truly free from desire and hate, and is always a true renunciant.

en/5-2-intro-6d9bdf56.mp3.text: Listen for the word that makes one path outrank the other, right after Krishna says both paths lead to the highest good.

en/5-20-body-9ef1a50c.mp3.text: One who does not rejoice at the pleasant, and does not shrink from the unpleasant, is steady in understanding, free from delusion, and established in the supreme reality. Krishna gives a direct test for a steady mind: the person does not rejoice at the pleasant, and does not shrink from the unpleasant, and this freedom from delusion is what establishes them in the supreme reality. Krishna now asks what happens when a person finds joy inside the true self instead of in outer contacts.

en/5-20-intro-2bec3d2a.mp3.text: After explaining how the supreme reality is flawless, Krishna now tells what it looks like inside a person. Listen for the mark of a steady mind.

en/5-21-body-983b62f7.mp3.text: One who is not attached to outer contacts finds the joy within the true self. Unified with the supreme reality, that person enjoys unending happiness. The word akshayam means imperishable, and it points to a happiness that does not run out. The verse says this joy is found not in the world outside, but within the true self. Next, Krishna turns to the senses themselves and shows that the pleasures they offer are only sources of suffering.

en/5-21-intro-f0fd081b.mp3.text: Krishna shows Arjuna how to step out of the restless chase of outer pleasures and find a joy that never fades.

en/5-22-body-fa03bbce.mp3.text: The pleasures born from contact with the senses are only sources of suffering. They have a beginning and an end, O Arjuna, and the wise do not delight in them. Listen to one word, duhkha yoni. It means a womb or source of suffering, and Krishna uses it to say that every pleasure born of the senses is merely a source of pain. The wise do not delight in these pleasures. Krishna now turns to the next obstacle, desire and anger, and how to withstand them.

en/5-22-intro-221d04f4.mp3.text: Krishna asks Arjuna to look closely at the pleasures of the senses. Listen to the word that names their true origin.

en/5-22-intro-59b6adb3.mp3.text: Krishna points to one specific word to show what sense pleasures really are. Listen for how he names the suffering hidden inside them.

en/5-23-body-1eec76ae.mp3.text: Whoever can withstand the surge of desire and anger here before the body falls, is a disciplined person and is truly happy. Whoever can bear the surge of desire and anger before the body falls is a yogi and happy. The next verse describes the person who finds happiness within and reaches the supreme reality.

en/5-23-body-3845ae32.mp3.text: Whoever can withstand the surge of desire and anger here before the body falls, is a disciplined person and is truly happy. Listen to इह एव, here itself. Krishna is not promising a reward after death; he is saying the struggle with desire and anger must be won in this very body, before the body falls. The person who wins that inner battle becomes truly happy, and that happiness comes from a source that never ends.

en/5-23-intro-31787873.mp3.text: Krishna asks Arjuna to look inward, to the rush of desire and anger that arises inside a person before the body falls.

en/5-23-intro-fd3e748f.mp3.text: Arjuna has just been told that sensory pleasures are fleeting and painful. Now Krishna points to the inner storm that actually ruins life. Listen to the urgency in his words.

en/5-24-body-a4b2f000.mp3.text: One who finds happiness within, delights within, and has inner light alone, becomes one with the supreme reality and reaches freedom in the supreme reality. The verse names three inner sources. The yogi finds happiness within, delight within, and light within. This marks a person who needs nothing from the outside world. Krishna then tells us that sages who are pure and devoted to the welfare of all beings also attain this same freedom.

en/5-24-intro-9d3395fb.mp3.text: After explaining how to master desire and anger, Krishna now names the person who has already won. Listen for the three inner qualities that mark such a yogi.

en/5-25-body-4d6da326.mp3.text: Sages who are free of impurity, free of doubt, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings attain freedom in the supreme reality. Rishis free of stain and doubt, self-controlled and devoted to the welfare of every being, reach nirvana in Brahman. Krishna then says that for those who are free from desire and anger, freedom in Brahman is near on both sides.

en/5-25-body-7439ce95.mp3.text: Sages who are free of impurity, free of doubt, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings attain freedom in the supreme reality. The verse names three states, क्षीणकल्मषाः, whose impurities are diminished, छिन्नद्वैधाः, whose doubts are cut away, and यतात्मानः, self-controlled. The inner cleansing of stain and doubt and the control of the self go together. Krishna then adds the outward sign of such a person, that they delight in the welfare of all beings. He then moves to the next quality.

en/5-25-intro-c875cb8e.mp3.text: Krishna answers Arjuna's doubt with the qualities of a sage. Listen for the inner and outer marks of the one who reaches freedom.

en/5-26-body-c5c4373f.mp3.text: For those free from desire and anger, with disciplined minds and self-knowledge, freedom in the supreme reality is near on both sides. The word abhitah, on both sides, means this peace is immediate, whether the body still lives or has already fallen away. Krishna then gives the exact physical posture and breath control used by such a seeker.

en/5-26-intro-f69309f2.mp3.text: Krishna describes a mind at peace with itself, free from craving and rage. Listen for the two states this freedom covers.

en/5-27-body-135d8470.mp3.text: Leaving outer objects outside, fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, and balancing the inward and outward breaths moving through the nose. The word प्राणापानौ, the inward and outward breaths, is made equal. This equalizing of the two main breaths is the physical anchor for the mind's withdrawal. Krishna then describes the state of the one who has mastered this discipline.

en/5-27-body-def8a1fd.mp3.text: Leaving outer objects outside, fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, and balancing the inward and outward breaths moving through the nose. Krishna balances the inward and outward breaths, the prana and apana, making them equal as they move within the nose. This equalizing of the breath is the physical anchor that steadies the mind. With the breath balanced, Krishna describes the person who is forever free, having mastered the senses, mind, and intellect.

en/5-27-intro-4b9d2943.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from describing the liberated state to giving a practical method. Listen for the way he pairs the inward and outward breaths.

en/5-27-intro-8a81c7ea.mp3.text: Krishna offers a practical method for the mind. Listen for the word that pairs the two breaths.

en/5-28-body-c804ac5a.mp3.text: One who has controlled the senses, mind, and intellect, who seeks freedom as the highest aim, and who is free from desire, fear, and anger is forever free. The sage is not waiting for death to be free. He is already free, because his senses, mind, and intellect are fully mastered. Krishna now says that the person who knows him as the enjoyer of all sacrifice and austerity attains peace.

en/5-28-intro-e89218e0.mp3.text: Krishna has just described how a sage sits with senses and breath held. Now he states the result of that discipline.

en/5-29-body-6a781687.mp3.text: Knowing me as the enjoyer of all sacrifice and austerity, the great lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace. The word maheshvaram, great lord of all worlds, names the supreme ruler of the universe; knowing this ruler as one's own friend brings a peace that needs no further proof. Krishna now defines the true yogi as one who acts without clinging to the fruit of action.

en/5-29-intro-3e2384f7.mp3.text: Krishna's final reassurance on Kurukshetra tells Arjuna that peace arrives from knowing the true nature of the one receiving all offerings, and the next verse begins to describe the yogi.

en/5-3-body-ba632b6b.mp3.text: One who neither hates nor desires is always a renunciant. Free from opposites, such a person is easily released from bondage, O mighty-armed one. Listen to nir-dvandva, free from opposites, and what that word reveals here. A true renunciant is not someone who abandons action, but someone who drops hatred and craving. Freedom comes when inner opposites no longer pull the mind. Krishna now shows that the wise see no conflict between renunciation and yoga, because both paths lead to the same fruit.

en/5-3-intro-3608b75a.mp3.text: Krishna now sharpens the teaching. Real renunciation means inner freedom from hatred, craving, and the tug of opposites, whatever one's outward life.

en/5-4-body-4e7fa7c3.mp3.text: The unwise say that renunciation and yoga lead to different results. The wise see that one who is firmly established in either reaches the same fruit. The word balah means the unwise or childish. It is not a polite disagreement, but a dismissal of those who see renunciation and yoga as separate roads. The wise see that one established in either path reaches the same fruit, and the next verse shows what that fruit is.

en/5-4-intro-27e49213.mp3.text: Krishna now calls the idea that two paths lead to different places a childish mistake. Listen to who he calls childish and why.

en/5-5-body-257c332c.mp3.text: The state reached by the wise is also reached through yoga. One who sees wisdom and yoga as one sees rightly. Krishna says the state reached by wisdom is also reached through action. The one who sees both as a single path sees clearly, and that clarity is the true sight. Krishna then says that renunciation without action is hard, and the disciplined path of yoga leads to the supreme reality.

en/5-5-intro-43272f62.mp3.text: Arjuna is still stuck on whether to fight or to renounce. What does Krishna say to untangle this? Listen to how he joins the two paths.

en/5-6-body-e995f950.mp3.text: But, mighty-armed one, renunciation without yoga is hard to attain. The disciplined seeker in yoga quickly reaches the supreme reality. Mighty-armed Arjuna hears that renunciation without yoga is hard, while a disciplined yogi reaches Brahman quickly. The disciplined yogi sees the same self in all beings and acts without being tainted by action.

en/5-7-body-50bdd9a8.mp3.text: A disciplined yogi, pure in mind, self-mastered, and senses conquered, sees the same self in all beings and is not tainted by action while acting. The word is visuddhatma, pure inner being. A person acts without being stained not because the work is light, but because the inner being itself has been made pure, so no action can stick to it. Krishna then shows that even while doing all this, the knower of reality should think, 'I do nothing at all.'

en/5-7-intro-8aeeb194.mp3.text: Krishna asks Arjuna to listen for one Sanskrit word that shows exactly where the stain on action comes from.

en/5-8-body-2523bb17.mp3.text: The knower of reality should think, "I do nothing at all," while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, taking, speaking, discarding, sleeping, breathing, and opening and closing the eyes. The knower of reality thinks, 'I do nothing at all,' while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, and breathing. The body is active, but the knower claims no doership for it. Krishna adds that the senses move among their objects, even while the wise person is speaking, eating, or sleeping.

en/5-8-intro-1dff6d65.mp3.text: Arjuna is frozen between action and collapse. Krishna now describes the inner vision of the wise person who still moves through the world.

en/5-9-body-effedc0e.mp3.text: Even while speaking, releasing, taking, opening, and closing the eyes, the wise know: the senses move among their objects. Notice the exact phrase 'the senses move among sense-objects.' Krishna says that speaking, taking, and blinking are not the self acting, but the senses simply moving among their objects. Krishna now turns to the one who offers every action to Brahman and remains untainted by sin.

en/5-9-intro-7b100a3c.mp3.text: Krishna carries on from the idea of non-action, showing how the body and senses keep moving.

en/6-1-body-1f9ec17d.mp3.text: One who performs the required action without taking shelter in the fruit of action is a renunciate and a yogi. Not one who merely gives up fire, and not one who merely stops acting. Krishna's renunciant does the required work without leaning on its fruit; giving up the ritual fire is not enough. Next, Krishna will explain what it means to act without leaning on the fruit.

en/6-1-intro-9b2d012f.mp3.text: Krishna begins by redefining what a renunciate and a yogi truly are. Listen to how he describes the inner state of the one who acts.

en/6-10-body-223f5550.mp3.text: The disciplined yogi, dwelling alone in seclusion, should constantly unite the mind with the supreme being, free from desire and possessiveness, with body and mind under control. Notice the word nirashiraparigrahah, without desire and possessiveness. Krishna is not asking for a feeling of emptiness, but for the removal of attachment to results and things. He tells the yogi to find a clean spot and set up a firm seat. But where is this seat placed?

en/6-10-intro-6ece0421.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the yogi who sees everyone equally. Now he tells the yogi what to actually do. Listen for the conditions the yogi must create.

en/6-11-body-2f675d4e.mp3.text: Having placed a firm seat for himself on a clean spot, neither too high nor too low, with cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass laid in layers. The verse uses the word na atyucchritam, meaning not too high, to describe the height of the seat. A seat that is not too high keeps the body steady and the mind from wandering. Sitting on that seat, the yogi must make the mind one-pointed and restrain its movements to begin the practice of yoga.

en/6-11-body-fa2a9445.mp3.text: Having placed a firm seat for himself on a clean spot, neither too high nor too low, with cloth, deerskin, and kusha grass laid in layers. The word उत्तरम् means laid above. The seat is prepared in layers, with kusha grass at the bottom, deerskin next, and cloth on top, creating a firm support for the body. Once this steady seat is prepared, Krishna then explains how to sit on it and steady the mind.

en/6-11-intro-b360c45d.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna to prepare a steady seat in a clean place, neither too high nor too low. Listen for the layers he describes.

en/6-11-intro-d227f97c.mp3.text: Krishna describes the physical setup for meditation, a simple seat on clean ground. Listen for the exact material details.

en/6-12-body-86e8c1ad.mp3.text: Sitting on that seat, with the mind made one-pointed and the movements of mind and senses restrained, one should practice yoga for inner purification. Listen to the long compound word yatacittendriyakriyah. It gathers the mind and the senses into a single act of restraint. This is the condition Krishna sets for the practice. Next, Krishna tells Arjuna to hold the body, head, and neck perfectly still, fixing the gaze on the tip of the nose.

en/6-12-intro-e558c947.mp3.text: Krishna now tells Arjuna to sit down. Listen for the exact state of mind and body he demands before the practice begins.

en/6-13-body-d474a5c4.mp3.text: Holding the body, head, and neck straight and still, and gazing only at the tip of the nose without looking around. The word samam means holding the body straight and even. It is a rule of balance, because the body is held straight so the mind can become steady. With the body still, Krishna now tells the yogi to fix the mind on Him and sit devoted to the Supreme.

en/6-13-intro-4f92de59.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna to sit on the seat and steady the mind. Now He shifts to the body, showing how the posture must match the inner state.

en/6-14-body-345035a4.mp3.text: The yogi, with a peaceful mind, free of fear, and firm in celibate discipline, restrains the mind, fixes awareness on Me, and sits devoted to Me as the supreme aim. The word madhuparah, for whom I am the supreme aim, shows that the yogi's meditation is directed toward Krishna as the highest goal, and this devotion is the very purpose of his sitting. Krishna now says that by keeping the mind united in this way, the yogi attains the supreme peace that comes from Him.

en/6-14-intro-d6721bbd.mp3.text: The previous verse fixed the body, and this one turns to the inner conditions of the mind before it can rest in peace.

en/6-15-body-e86f21c7.mp3.text: The disciplined yogi, always uniting the mind in this way, attains the supreme peace of freedom rooted in Me. Listen to the word shanti, peace. Here it is the supreme freedom that ends all inner disturbance and rests in the divine. Krishna now turns to the daily habits that either build or break this steady mind.

en/6-15-intro-482ffff9.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the physical discipline of yoga. Now he tells Arjuna what this steady practice actually produces.

en/6-16-body-c6842e18.mp3.text: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who eats nothing at all. It is not for one who sleeps too much, nor for one who stays awake too long, Arjuna. Krishna names four extremes, too much, too little, too much sleep, too much wakefulness, and says yoga is not for any of them. He then tells Arjuna that yoga that destroys suffering comes from a balanced life.

en/6-16-intro-c2715543.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that the practice of yoga cannot survive on an empty stomach or an overfed one. Listen to what he says next.

en/6-17-body-55e03020.mp3.text: Yoga that destroys suffering comes from balanced eating, balanced activity, balanced work, and balanced sleep and waking. Measured food, measured effort, measured sleep and waking: from these, yoga that ends sorrow becomes possible. Krishna now moves from balanced living to the mind itself, describing what a controlled mind resting in the true self looks like.

en/6-17-body-cbd1b0e7.mp3.text: Yoga that destroys suffering comes from balanced eating, balanced activity, balanced work, and balanced sleep and waking. Listen to युक्ताहारविहारस्य, balanced eating and movement. The verse does not speak of extreme fasting or overeating, but of measured food and activity as the foundation of yoga. Krishna then shows what the mind looks like once it rests, free from craving, in the true self.

en/6-17-intro-744b55bb.mp3.text: Listen for the word that tells how a steady daily routine makes the practice possible.

en/6-17-intro-746c20a2.mp3.text: Krishna lists four things that must be balanced. Listen to the last one, the one about sleep and waking, and hear what it promises.

en/6-18-body-18265a5a.mp3.text: When the controlled mind rests in the true self alone and is free from craving for all pleasures, that person is called united in yoga. The controlled mind rests in the true self alone, and the person is called united in yoga. The mind does not rest on objects, but on the self alone. Krishna compares this steady mind to a lamp that does not flicker in a windless place.

en/6-18-intro-4c23f51d.mp3.text: Krishna now tells Arjuna how to recognize true yoga. Listen for the mark of a mind that has found its home.

en/6-19-body-748eeda4.mp3.text: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, so the disciplined mind of a yogi does not waver while practicing yoga of the true self. A lamp in a windless place does not flicker, and that is the yogi's steadied mind. When that steadiness is fully reached, the person rests in the true self alone and is free from all craving.

en/6-19-intro-f9748126.mp3.text: Krishna continues his teaching on the yogi's steady mind by giving it a single, clear image of a lamp.

en/6-2-body-f7b08a5d.mp3.text: Arjuna, what people call renunciation is yoga. No one becomes a yogi without giving up intentions. The word sankalpa, intention, is the only inner obstacle to becoming a yogi. Krishna says that without dropping these inner intentions, no one becomes a yogi, and true renunciation is simply giving up these intentions. Krishna now explains that action is the way up, but stillness is the way to stay there.

en/6-2-intro-15c2170d.mp3.text: Krishna asks Arjuna to listen for one Sanskrit word that shows exactly why a person cannot become a yogi.

en/6-20-body-255712e2.mp3.text: When the restrained mind becomes still through yoga practice, and the person sees the true self by the true self, one is content in the true self alone. The verse repeats yatra, meaning where, to describe a single state. In that state, the restrained mind rests, and the true self sees the true self, and is content there. Krishna then explains that this boundless joy is beyond the senses and grasped by the mind.

en/6-20-intro-d3c99bc4.mp3.text: What does it feel like to be truly at peace? Listen to how the state of yoga is described.

en/6-21-body-6fcb9d10.mp3.text: One knows the boundless joy beyond the senses and grasped by the discerning mind; established in it, one never truly falls away. The word atyantikam means boundless or ultimate. The verse says this joy is grasped by the mind and is beyond the senses, so the yogi who reaches it stands firm and never wavers from truth. Krishna says that once a person finds this state, they feel no greater gain exists, and they are not shaken by sorrow.

en/6-21-intro-8ceb6032.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that the highest joy is beyond the senses, grasped only by the mind, and once reached, a person never truly falls away.

en/6-22-body-e38b324b.mp3.text: Having attained it, one thinks no greater gain exists. Established in it, one is not shaken even by great sorrow. The word is labham, gain. Krishna says that once you have this, you consider no other gain greater than that. It is a state where even heavy sorrow, duhkhena, cannot shake you. Krishna now names this state: know it as yoga, the severance of union with suffering.

en/6-22-intro-b4b405e9.mp3.text: Krishna asks you to notice one gain, and why no other gain can match it. Listen for how heavy sorrow is treated.

en/6-23-body-86c5ee6e.mp3.text: Know that as yoga: the severance of union with suffering. Practice that yoga with certainty, with an undiscouraged mind. Here, Krishna names yoga as the severance from union with suffering. The word yoga points to the ending of the mind's bond with sorrow, and he commands that it be practiced with certainty and without discouragement. He then urges that this practice be undertaken with certainty and a mind that has not lost heart.

en/6-23-intro-acaf31ba.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the peace that meditation brings, and now he gives it a name. Listen for how he defines yoga.

en/6-24-body-ca734158.mp3.text: Abandon every desire born of resolve, and restrain the whole field of the senses on all sides with the mind alone. The verse names one tool, manas, the mind. It is not the senses that pull the senses back, but the mind acting alone that gathers them on all sides. Krishna then explains that this mind is quieted only little by little through steady discernment.

en/6-24-intro-c9d14eed.mp3.text: Krishna tells us to drop the desires that spring from our own plans, and to pull the senses back with the mind alone.

en/6-25-body-83334876.mp3.text: Little by little, the mind should be quieted by steady discernment. Fix the mind in the true self and think of nothing else. Listen to the word कृत्वा, having made. First you establish the mind in the self, and only then, after that fixing, it stops thinking of anything else. Whenever the mind wanders again, Krishna says, simply bring it back to the self.

en/6-25-body-ae3fac1b.mp3.text: Little by little, the mind should be quieted by steady discernment. Fix the mind in the true self and think of nothing else. Krishna says to use buddhi, the discerning mind, and hold it with dhriteh, firmness. First you quiet the mind, then you place it in the true self, and only then you stop thinking at all. Krishna now says to bring the wandering mind back into the true self.

en/6-25-intro-59e247fd.mp3.text: Arjuna has asked how to steady the mind. This verse gives the exact method. Listen to the steps.

en/6-25-intro-c468352f.mp3.text: How does a restless mind stop? Krishna gives a method here, and the first word tells you it is not a single leap but a gradual settling.

en/6-26-body-118d18ba.mp3.text: Whenever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, bring it back under the control of the true self. The Sanskrit repeats yato yato, wherever, which means the mind will wander again and again. The remedy is just as plain: bring it back to the true self, and only to the true self. The yogi who masters this wandering mind is the one who reaches the highest joy.

en/6-26-intro-e1c5cd66.mp3.text: Krishna knows the mind will keep slipping away. Listen to the exact instruction for bringing it back.

en/6-27-body-ad730e67.mp3.text: The yogi whose mind is peaceful, whose passion is stilled, and who is free from impurity attains the highest joy. The word is shantarajasam, with passion stilled. Passion here is the restless force that pushes the mind to constantly seek and grasp, and when it settles, the yogi reaches the highest joy. Krishna then describes how the yogi who has become Brahman and is spotless reaches that joy.

en/6-27-intro-2d301e95.mp3.text: Krishna is teaching Arjuna how to master the restless mind. Listen for the word that describes the mind once it is completely stilled.

en/6-28-body-19d9f871.mp3.text: Thus, the disciplined yogi, free from impurity, always unites the self with the supreme reality and attains limitless joy through that contact. Notice the word सुखेन, with ease. The contact with Brahman is an effortless experience for the yogi who is free from impurity. Krishna now shows the result of this union as the yogi begins to see the true self in all beings.

en/6-28-body-5b6d1d89.mp3.text: Thus, the disciplined yogi, free from impurity, always unites the self with the supreme reality and attains limitless joy through that contact. The word yogi here means one who unites, and the word vitakalmasah means free from impurity. It is the yogi who is free from impurity who attains that limitless joy. Krishna then explains that this yogi sees the true self in all beings and all beings in the true self.

en/6-28-intro-3089b427.mp3.text: Krishna continues teaching Arjuna how a mind trained in yoga experiences the highest joy. Listen for how the contact with the supreme reality is described.

en/6-28-intro-5038ea12.mp3.text: Krishna is speaking to Arjuna after having described how the mind settles and the highest joy is found. He now explains the condition of the yogi who has reached that state.

en/6-29-body-3875b791.mp3.text: The one united in yoga sees the true self in all beings and all beings in the true self, seeing everything with equal vision. The word ईक्षते, sees, shows that this is direct sight and not thought. The yogi united in yoga sees the same true self in every living being and every living being within that self. Krishna now speaks of an even closer bond, saying he is never lost to those who see him in all beings.

en/6-29-body-5aac4202.mp3.text: The one united in yoga sees the true self in all beings and all beings in the true self, seeing everything with equal vision. The verse turns on two words, sarvabhutastham and atmani. The yogi sees the self situated in all beings, and all beings situated in the self. It is the same self, the same beings, held in one gaze. Krishna now asks who truly sees him, and he answers with the same equal vision.

en/6-29-intro-41141f71.mp3.text: Krishna continues the teaching on the inner vision of the meditator, moving from the quiet mind to the way that mind sees the world.

en/6-29-intro-fafbc70f.mp3.text: Carrying on from the settled mind, Krishna now shows the vision that meditation reveals on the battlefield. Listen for the equal eye.

en/6-3-body-4df27ef9.mp3.text: For the sage who seeks to rise into yoga, action is the means. For the one who has risen in yoga, stillness is the means. Notice how the word karanam, cause, is used for both stages, yet the tool changes. For the one seeking to rise, action is the cause, and for the one who has risen, stillness is the cause. Krishna next describes the person who has let go of sense pleasures and actions entirely.

en/6-3-intro-e290f501.mp3.text: Krishna shifts from what renunciation is to how to practice it. He now divides the path into two stages, and names the tool for each.

en/6-30-body-02084e40.mp3.text: Who sees Me in all beings and sees all beings in Me, I am never lost to that person, and that person is never lost to Me. The word pranasyaami means to disappear or be lost. Krishna says he will never disappear from the yogi's sight, and the yogi will never disappear from his. Krishna then says this united yogi lives in him and acts in the world without losing that vision. Listen to verse thirty-one.

en/6-30-intro-14d3b31b.mp3.text: What happens to a person who truly sees the divine in every living thing? Krishna answers with a promise of unbreakable closeness.

en/6-31-body-f3d63bd3.mp3.text: The yogi who abides in unity and worships Me in all beings lives in Me, even while acting in every way. Here is the word vartate, abides. It means the yogi is rooted inside Krishna, even while doing everyday tasks. Krishna then calls out to Arjuna to hear the highest standard of yoga.

en/6-31-intro-54f30402.mp3.text: Krishna has just taught Arjuna to see the divine in every being. Now he describes what happens to a person who truly lives in that unity.

en/6-32-body-0b9316cc.mp3.text: O Arjuna, the yogi who sees all beings as equal through the measure of the true self, and sees pleasure and pain alike, is considered the highest yogi. The word is आत्मौपम्येन, by comparison with the self. The yogi measures every being by his own inner self and sees pleasure and pain with the same steady mind. Arjuna replies that he cannot see this steady practice in himself because his mind is restless.

en/6-32-body-11ccd516.mp3.text: O Arjuna, the yogi who sees all beings as equal through the measure of the true self, and sees pleasure and pain alike, is considered the highest yogi. The word samam, equally, is the hinge of this verse, showing that the highest yogi does not favor pleasure over pain. Arjuna immediately doubts that anyone can keep a steady mind when it is so restless.

en/6-32-intro-89cb963a.mp3.text: Krishna points to the inner test of a true meditator. Listen for how he pairs pleasure with pain.

en/6-32-intro-d2dec127.mp3.text: Krishna names the highest yogi by what he sees. Listen closely for the word that tells you exactly how he measures the world.

en/6-33-body-c2e22e0f.mp3.text: Arjuna says: Krishna, you have described this yoga as balanced, but I do not see its steady practice, because the mind is restless. Arjuna addresses Krishna as Madhusudana, the slayer of the demon Madhu, and then admits that because of his restless mind, he simply cannot see how to keep such a steady state. He admits that controlling this turbulent mind is as hard as taming the wind.

en/6-33-intro-0225f4e5.mp3.text: Arjuna has just heard Krishna praise the highest yogi, the one who sees all beings as equal. Listen to how Arjuna responds to that ideal.

en/6-34-body-d695a08b.mp3.text: The mind is restless, turbulent, stubborn, and strong. I think controlling it is as hard as controlling the wind. Listen to one word, pramathi. It means churning, and it shows how the mind agitates the body and the senses until they are restless. Krishna answers that the mind is hard to tame, but it can be mastered through practice and detachment.

en/6-34-intro-0263f287.mp3.text: Arjuna carries on from his last complaint, naming the four qualities of the mind that make it so hard to master.

en/6-35-body-19336b7e.mp3.text: The mind is hard to control, but it is mastered through practice and detachment. Krishna does not argue with Arjuna here. He agrees the mind is restless and hard to restrain, then names the two tools that master it: practice and detachment. He now explains that yoga is hard to reach without this control, but possible for the one who strives.

en/6-35-intro-67436ca7.mp3.text: Arjuna has just said controlling the mind is as hard as controlling the wind. What does Krishna say is possible instead?

en/6-36-body-524fb8f0.mp3.text: Yoga is hard to attain for one whose mind is not fully controlled. But for one who controls the mind and strives with the right method, it can be reached. The Sanskrit word upayat (उपायतः) means by right means. Krishna does not offer a magic key here, but a method that requires a controlled mind and steady effort to work. The next verse asks what happens to someone who has faith but lacks steady effort and turns away before reaching success.

en/6-36-body-8fdfa997.mp3.text: Yoga is hard to attain for one whose mind is not fully controlled. But for one who controls the mind and strives with the right method, it can be reached. Listen to the word yogah. It is the subject of the whole verse. Krishna is not talking about a posture, but about the very state of union, and he says it is hard to attain for the uncontrolled mind. Arjuna asks what happens to the person who begins with faith but then turns away before reaching the goal.

en/6-36-intro-509151b6.mp3.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga is out of reach for the undisciplined, but he offers a clear path for the dedicated. Listen to how he sets this condition.

en/6-36-intro-a1e62db0.mp3.text: Krishna speaks plainly to Arjuna about the conditions that make yoga either impossible or possible. Listen to the two kinds of people he describes.

en/6-37-body-a7e47f29.mp3.text: Arjuna says: What happens to a person who has faith but lacks steady effort, whose mind turns away from yoga before full success is reached, O Krishna? The key word here is ApAya, which means without attaining. Arjuna is asking what becomes of a person who fails to attain yoga-siddhi. He is not asking about the faithless, but the sincere one who falls short, and he wants to know if that effort is lost. Next, Arjuna continues.

en/6-37-intro-d77c59c8.mp3.text: Arjuna now asks about a different kind of traveler on the path, one who begins with faith but loses his footing. Listen for how he names this state.

en/6-38-body-c2224f1e.mp3.text: O mighty-armed one, does a person who has fallen from both sides, like a torn cloud, perish without support, deluded on the path of the supreme reality? Arjuna uses a single image, a torn cloud. He asks what becomes of a person who loses support in both the world and on the path to liberation, left floating and scattered in the sky. Next, Arjuna continues.

en/6-38-intro-770cc48a.mp3.text: Arjuna has already asked what happens to someone who starts the spiritual path but loses faith before success. Now he asks a darker question.

en/6-39-body-ea908c7b.mp3.text: O Krishna, only you can fully cut away this doubt. No one else is able to remove it. Arjuna tells Krishna that no one else is able to remove this doubt; he is not asking for an answer he can find with his own mind, but for a complete cutting away that only Krishna can provide. Krishna answers that such a person finds no destruction either here or hereafter.

en/6-39-intro-b6cf6c7f.mp3.text: Arjuna has just asked about the fate of a seeker who falls from the path, and now he admits he cannot resolve this alone.

en/6-4-body-586085d3.mp3.text: When one no longer clings to sense pleasures or to actions, that person is called established in yoga, having renounced all intentions. The key word is yogarudhah, one mounted on yoga. The verse shows that this is the state of a person who does not cling to sense objects or to actions, because he has renounced all intentions. Krishna then turns to how the self must lift itself up without letting itself fall.

en/6-4-intro-dac66109.mp3.text: Krishna now tells Arjuna how to know he has reached that height. Listen for the state of the mind that is no longer caught.

en/6-40-body-5feea321.mp3.text: Krishna says: O Partha, there is no destruction for him either here or hereafter. No one who does good ever comes to a bad end, my dear. Krishna addresses Arjuna as Partha, son of Pritha, and then makes a promise. The one who does good practice, kalyanakrit, will never reach a bad end, durgatim. Krishna explains where that person goes after falling from yoga, to the worlds of good deeds, before being born again in a pure and prosperous home.

en/6-40-intro-dbc91758.mp3.text: Arjuna asked what happens to the person who falls short in yoga. Listen to Krishna's direct answer.

en/6-41-body-8083fd3b.mp3.text: The one who falls from yoga reaches the worlds earned by good deeds, dwells there for many long years, and is then born again in the house of the pure and prosperous. The word yoga-bhrastah means one fallen from yoga. Instead of ruin, this person is born into a pure and prosperous house, carrying the memory of the path. Krishna adds that such a birth among wise yogis is very rare.

en/6-41-intro-d72c9a77.mp3.text: Krishna speaks of a soul who tries the path of yoga but fails. Listen to the place this person returns to.

en/6-42-body-02cf9e0c.mp3.text: Or he is born into the family of wise yogis. Such a birth is very rare in this world. Listen for the word yoginam, of the yogis. Instead of being born into a wealthy or pure house, the one who fell returns straight into a family shaped by wisdom and discipline, where the path can continue. Sanjaya now says that in that family he regains his old understanding and strives again toward success.

en/6-42-intro-aa6db9b0.mp3.text: Krishna has just described the fate of the yogi who slips. Now listen for a different possibility, one that offers a rare advantage for the one who fell.

en/6-43-body-6d8567ed.mp3.text: O son of Kuru, there he effortlessly regains the spiritual understanding from his previous life. Then he strives again, with greater force, toward complete success. Krishna says the yogi regains the buddhisanyoga, the spiritual understanding from his former body, effortlessly. Then he strives again with greater force toward complete success. Even against his will, he is drawn onward by that earlier practice.

en/6-43-intro-18a6f667.mp3.text: Arjuna has just asked if a failed yogi is lost forever. Krishna answers by describing what happens in the next life. Listen for the two stages of recovery.

en/6-44-body-cc5484d8.mp3.text: Even against his will, he is drawn onward by that earlier practice. Even the seeker of yoga goes beyond the sound of ritual words. The word avashah api means even against his will. Krishna says that past practice is so strong that it pulls a person forward even when they are not in control. Krishna then explains that this very practice also carries a seeker past the mere sound of ritual words.

en/6-44-intro-9876ef4e.mp3.text: Carrying on, Krishna tells Arjuna that the pull of past practice is so strong that a person is drawn back even when they are not in control. Listen for the word that marks this involuntary pull.

en/6-45-body-470b78e0.mp3.text: But the yogi who keeps striving with effort, whose impurities have been cleared, and who has been perfected through many births, reaches the highest goal. The word yatamanah, striving, shows that the yogi is not resting on past skill. The effort is present, continuous, and active right now. Krishna then places the yogi above all other paths of spiritual life.

en/6-45-intro-65bf44da.mp3.text: Krishna answers the fear that effort can be lost. Listen to how the yogi moves from one birth to the next.

en/6-46-body-dc6dd36e.mp3.text: The yogi is greater than ascetics, greater than scholars, and greater than workers. Therefore, Arjuna, become a yogi. Listen to the rhythm of the word yogi. It is named three times, each time placed higher than the last, and the verse ends with a direct order to Arjuna to become one. Krishna now names the one who worships him with trust and complete absorption.

en/6-46-intro-abce7265.mp3.text: Krishna has just shown how a yogi's practice survives failure. Now he ranks the yogi above all other paths and gives a direct command.

en/6-47-body-1a3b7208.mp3.text: Among all yogis, the one who worships me with trust, with the inner self absorbed in me, is considered the most fully united. The word to hear is shraddhavan, trustful. It is not the skill of the posture but the trust of the heart that makes the worshipper the highest of all yogis. Krishna now explains how this trust is born, by revealing his divine knowledge to Arjuna.

en/6-47-intro-2bbc753d.mp3.text: Krishna has taught the method of meditation. Now listen for the single word that crowns the entire path.

en/6-5-body-53ce4d13.mp3.text: Lift yourself by yourself; do not let yourself fall. The true self is its own friend, and the true self is its own enemy. The word is atmanah, of the self. The self is its own friend and its own enemy. The same self that saves you can also destroy you. Krishna now shows the exact way the higher self acts as a friend, and the lower self acts as an enemy.

en/6-5-intro-2ebaeb5e.mp3.text: If yoga is a state of peace, what breaks that peace? Krishna asks Arjuna to look inside, because the enemy is not out there.

en/6-6-body-0799e05c.mp3.text: For one who has conquered the lower self by the true self, the true self is a friend. For one who has not conquered the lower self, the true self behaves like an enemy. The word atma is used twice in one breath. The true self is a friend only when the lower self, the restless mind, is conquered by the true self. Without that victory, the self itself becomes the enemy. Krishna says that for the one who has conquered the self, the supreme reality is present in heat and cold, pleasure and pain.

en/6-6-intro-aac4eed4.mp3.text: Krishna asks how one can be a friend to oneself. Listen to how he defines the inner battle.

en/6-7-body-be276b0c.mp3.text: For one who has conquered the self and is serene, the supreme reality is ever present in heat and cold, pleasure and pain, honor and dishonor. The word is manaapamaanayo, honor and insult. The supreme reality is present to the self-conquered person, whether they experience praise or blame. Krishna says that person is called a yogi because they see clay, stone, and gold as the same.

en/6-7-intro-bfbbd0f8.mp3.text: Krishna states that the Supreme Reality is present to the self-conquered. Listen for the pairs of opposites that frame this state.

en/6-8-body-cdda84fc.mp3.text: One whose mind is satisfied by knowledge and realization, who remains steady, who has conquered the senses, and who sees clay, stone, and gold alike is called a yogi in union. Listen to one compound, samaloshtashmakanchanah. It means equal in clay, stone, and gold. The yogi does not rank the world by greed. Krishna now adds another sign of the one who stands firm, equal to friend and enemy.

en/6-8-intro-c55d1dfd.mp3.text: Arjuna is still learning how to stand firm without being pulled by fear or desire. Listen to how Krishna names the one who is satisfied by understanding.

en/6-9-body-3f12351a.mp3.text: The one whose understanding is equal toward friend, enemy, neutral person, mediator, hateful person, relative, the virtuous, and the sinful is श्रेष्ठ. Friend, enemy, neutral, relative, saint or sinner: whoever sees them with an even mind stands out among yogis. Next he turns from people to the yogi's own place of dwelling, asking him to sit alone and fix his mind on the supreme.

en/6-9-body-d45bda73.mp3.text: The one whose understanding is equal toward friend, enemy, neutral person, mediator, hateful person, relative, the virtuous, and the sinful is श्रेष्ठ. The word samabuddhih, equal understanding, is what makes a person श्रेष्ठ. Krishna lists seven kinds of people, from a well-wisher to a hateful enemy, and says the one who holds them all in the same even mind is the best. Next, Krishna tells the yogi to leave everything behind and constantly unite the mind with the supreme being.

en/6-9-intro-41dd5922.mp3.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna that a yogi sees clay, stone, and gold with the same eye. Now he asks what it means to see people with that same steady gaze.

en/6-9-intro-584524d7.mp3.text: In the last verse Krishna spoke of seeing clay, stone, and gold with the same eye. Now he speaks of seeing people.

en/7-1-body-0a4473a0.mp3.text: The Blessed Lord says: Arjuna, fix your mind on Me, take refuge in Me, and practice yoga. Hear how you will know Me fully, without doubt. Krishna states three conditions for knowing him: a mind attached to me, practicing yoga, and taking refuge. The word mad-ashrayah, taking refuge in me, shows that the practice of yoga happens within the shelter of the divine. Krishna says he is the source of all knowledge and direct realization, and that knowing him leaves nothing else to be known.

en/7-1-intro-254b8502.mp3.text: Krishna carries on the promise from the last verse, showing Arjuna exactly how to know him fully and without doubt.

en/7-10-body-a63e1b9f.mp3.text: Know Me, O Partha, as the eternal seed of all beings. I am the intelligence of the intelligent and the brilliance of the brilliant. He calls himself the seed, sanatana, eternal, of all beings, and then says he is the intelligence in the intelligent and the brilliance in the brilliant, so every clear mind and bright strength comes from him. He now moves from the source of life to the source of strength, naming what he is in those who are strong.

en/7-10-intro-536028a8.mp3.text: Krishna has just shown that he is the fragrance in the earth and the radiance in fire. Now he names his own origin. Listen for the source he names for all beings and for the qualities he holds in people.

en/7-11-body-4986bce1.mp3.text: Among the strong, I am strength free from desire and attachment. In beings, I am desire that does not oppose dharma, O best of the Bharatas. Krishna says he is strength, balam, but not ordinary strength, balavatam, of the strong; he is that strength free from craving. He also says he is desire, kamah, but only desire that does not oppose dharma. Sattva, rajas, and tamas are not outside him, but live inside him.

en/7-11-intro-890400c8.mp3.text: Krishna continues describing his nature, and this time he takes two opposites and makes them his own. Listen for how he redefines them.

en/7-12-body-5bbdbbc7.mp3.text: Know that all states of being, sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic, arise from Me. I am not in them; they are in Me. Krishna says that sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic states all arise from him. Yet he is not contained within them, because they rest in him and he remains beyond them. Krishna then explains that the whole world is deluded by those same qualities and does not know him as the imperishable one beyond them.

en/7-12-intro-75424418.mp3.text: Krishna asks what state of mind or nature any person truly comes from. Listen for his answer about where all qualities begin.

en/7-13-body-6d676a01.mp3.text: Deluded by these three qualities, the whole world does not know me, who am beyond them and imperishable. Listen for the word mohitam, deluded. It names the state of being trapped by the three qualities so tightly that the world cannot recognize Krishna as the imperishable reality outside them. Krishna then says this divine illusion is hard to cross, and only those who take refuge in Him go beyond it.

en/7-13-intro-44ecb682.mp3.text: Krishna says the world is caught in nature's qualities and cannot recognize who is beyond them. Listen for the word that names this trap.

en/7-14-body-0562d758.mp3.text: My divine illusion, made of the three qualities, is hard to cross. Only those who take refuge in Me go beyond it. The word is duratyaya, hard to cross. Krishna says his maya, made of the three gunas, is duratyaya, and only those who surrender to him can cross beyond it. Krishna then explains that the deluded and wrongdoers do not surrender to him, but take refuge in a shadowed nature instead.

en/7-14-intro-62221aab.mp3.text: Krishna names the obstacle and the only way past it. Listen for the one word that tells you exactly how hard the battle is.

en/7-15-body-07bc7567.mp3.text: The deluded, the lowest among people, the wrongdoers, and those whose understanding has been stolen by the veil do not turn to me. They take refuge in a shadowed nature instead. Here is one word, apahrita-jnana, whose understanding has been stolen. The veil does not just confuse them; it takes their knowledge away, so they cannot even look toward the truth. Krishna now turns to the other side of the same gate, naming the four kinds of people who do seek him out.

en/7-15-intro-0e7f2a3b.mp3.text: Right after Krishna says only those who take refuge in him can cross the veil, he names the ones who never will. Listen to how he describes the minds that stay trapped.
